questions.stem: Oedometer is used to measure:
questions.solution:
**Consolidation.**

> The source draws the distinction that this question exists for: **an OEDOMETER measures the CONSOLIDATION of soil; an ODOMETER is a device that measures the DISTANCE travelled by a vehicle.**

> **The two words differ by one letter**, and options (b) and (c) — speed and velocity — are there precisely to catch a candidate who has read "odometer".

**What the oedometer does:**

> A soil specimen is **confined laterally in a rigid ring** and loaded **vertically in increments**, with the settlement measured against time for each increment.

> **The lateral confinement is the essential feature**: it reproduces the **ONE-DIMENSIONAL** condition of a wide loaded area on a clay layer, where the soil cannot spread sideways — which is exactly the field situation being modelled.

**What it yields:**

| Parameter | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **C_c — compression index** | Slope of the **virgin e–log σ′** curve — governs **HOW MUCH** settlement |
| **C_r — recompression index** | Reloading slope, about **C_c/5 to C_c/10** |
| **σ′_c — preconsolidation pressure** | Maximum past effective stress, from **CASAGRANDE's construction** |
| **c_v — coefficient of consolidation** | From the time–settlement curve — governs **HOW FAST** |
| **m_v** | Used directly in settlement: **S = m_v Δσ H** |
| **k — permeability** | Indirectly, from **k = c_v m_v γ_w** |

> **C_c says HOW MUCH; c_v says HOW FAST.** Keeping those two questions apart is the organising idea of consolidation — a clay may be highly compressible yet drain quickly, or barely compressible yet take decades.

**And only the second is helped by vertical drains**, which shorten the drainage path without changing the total settlement at all.

**The settlement expression:**

> **S = (C_c H/(1 + e₀)) log₁₀[(σ′₀ + Δσ)/σ′₀]** for a normally consolidated clay.

> **For an OVER-consolidated clay the calculation SPLITS at σ′_c** — C_r below it, C_c above. **Using C_c throughout can overestimate the settlement five-fold** and buy a piled foundation that was never needed.

**The distinction from COMPACTION**, which is the other pairing examined here:

| | **COMPACTION** | **CONSOLIDATION** |
|---|---|---|
| Expels | **AIR** | **WATER** |
| Applies to | Partially saturated soil | **Fully SATURATED** soil |
| Cause | **MECHANICAL energy** — rolling, ramming | **Sustained LOAD** |
| Time | **Instantaneous** | **Years** |
| Test | **PROCTOR** | **OEDOMETER** |

examTip.trap: **ODOMETER (vehicle distance) versus OEDOMETER (soil consolidation)** — one letter apart, and options (b) and (c) exist entirely to catch the misreading.
examTip.trick: The **lateral confinement in a rigid ring** is the whole point — it reproduces the **one-dimensional** field condition of a wide load on a clay layer.
examTip.mnemonic: **C_c says HOW MUCH settlement; c_v says HOW FAST.** One test gives both. And **compaction expels AIR by machine in minutes; consolidation expels WATER under load over years.**

questions.stem: The fore poling method is generally adopted for tunneling:
questions.solution:
**In soft ground.**

> The source describes it precisely: **fore poling is a method of supporting a mine or tunnel's weak roof, typically used in SOFT, LOOSE or CAVING earth. Poles, lumber, steel tube or slabs are driven into the ground BEFORE or DURING excavation.**

> And it adds the decisive point: **fore poling is the only method used if the ground is RUNNING.**

**How it works:**

> **Poles or spiles are driven AHEAD of the working face**, at a slight upward angle, forming a **protective canopy** over the ground still to be excavated.

> **The excavation then proceeds BENEATH that canopy**, so the roof is supported **before** it is exposed rather than after.

> **That is the essential idea: in ground that will not stand even for minutes, support must PRECEDE excavation.**

**Why it suits soft and running ground:**

| Ground | Behaviour | Support needed |
|---|---|---|
| **Competent rock** | **Stands for hours or days** | Support can follow excavation |
| **Soft / loose** | Stands only briefly | Prompt support |
| **RUNNING ground** | **Flows like a liquid — will not stand at all** | **Support must PRECEDE excavation — fore poling** |

> **Running ground is dry cohesionless sand or silt that simply flows into the opening.** Nothing can be excavated and then supported, because there is no interval between the two.

**The soft-ground tunnelling methods, as a family:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **FORE POLING** | Poles driven **ahead of the face** — for the worst ground |
| **Needle beam** | A beam supported at the face and behind, carrying the roof supports |
| **SHIELD tunnelling** | A **steel shield advanced by jacks**, with segmental lining erected inside its tail |
| Compressed air | Balances water pressure in wet ground |
| Ground freezing / grouting | Temporarily stabilises the ground |

> **All of these exist because the ground will NOT stand on its own** — which is the single distinction between soft-ground and hard-rock tunnelling.

**The hard-rock methods, for contrast:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **Drill and blast** | Flexible; suits variable rock and any shape |
| **Heading and benching** | A drill-and-blast sequence for a large section |
| **Full face** | Smaller sections in good rock |
| **TBM** | Fast and smooth-bored, but inflexible and costly to mobilise |
| **NATM** | Uses the rock's **own arching capacity**, supported flexibly by shotcrete and rock bolts, with **convergence monitored** |

> **NATM is the instructive contrast with fore poling**: it **depends on the rock supporting itself**, allowing a small controlled deformation so the ground forms its own arch.

> **Fore poling exists because there is no such capacity to rely on.** The ground condition, not the diameter or the depth, chooses the method.

examTip.trick: **In running ground, support must PRECEDE excavation** — there is no interval in which to excavate and then support. That is exactly what driving poles ahead of the face achieves.
examTip.trap: Options (b) and (c) both name competent ground, where support can **follow** excavation. Fore poling would be pointless there — and NATM, which relies on the rock arching, is the opposite philosophy.
examTip.mnemonic: **The GROUND CONDITION chooses the method, not the diameter.** Rock stands → NATM with shotcrete and bolts. Soft or running → fore poling, needle beam or a shield.

questions.stem: The procedure of removal of rock protrusions by hammering immediately after the blasting:
questions.solution:
**Mucking.**

> The source defines it: **the process of removing all the excavated rocks, debris and bulk material during tunnelling is known as MUCKING.**

> And it notes why it matters: **it becomes an important task because the space in the tunnel is very limited, and it may create discomfort for the workers and equipment.**

**The distinctions the source draws:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **MUCKING** | **Removing excavated rock and debris** |
| **Skimming** | Differentiating **greasy material from water** |
| **Trimming** | Cutting the **edges** of rocky material or stones |
| **Scaling** | **Moulding into a suitable size** for convenience |

> **All four are real operations**, which is what makes this a genuine discrimination rather than a recognition test.

> Note that **SCALING has a second and more common tunnelling meaning**: knocking down **loose rock from the roof and walls after blasting**, which is a safety operation performed before anyone works beneath.

**Why mucking so often controls the tunnel's progress:**

> The excavation **CYCLE is: drill → charge → blast → VENTILATE → SCALE → MUCK → SUPPORT → survey → repeat.**

> **The cycle time is set by the SLOWEST of those steps**, and **muck removal frequently governs**, alongside ventilation.

| Constraint | Note |
|---|---|
| **Only ONE working face** | Nothing else can proceed while mucking occupies it |
| **Very restricted space** | Plant cannot pass; haulage is single-track |
| **Large volume** | A single blast round produces many tonnes |
| **Long haul** | Growing steadily as the tunnel advances |

> **That is why the advance rate of a tunnel is so often a LOGISTICS problem rather than an excavation one** — the rock can be broken faster than it can be carried out.

> **The same reasoning explains why a second heading, an adit, or a shaft is driven** on a long tunnel: it multiplies the number of working faces and shortens the haul from each.

**Ventilation is the other cycle constraint:**

> **Blasting fumes must be cleared before anyone can return to the face**, and the tunnel atmosphere must satisfy:

| Gas | Limit |
|---|---|
| **Oxygen** | **NOT LESS than 19.5%** |
| **Carbon dioxide** | Not more than **0.5%** |
| **Hydrogen sulphide** | Not more than **0.001% (10 ppm)** |

> **A BLOWING (forcing) ventilation system clears the face fastest**, which is why reversible systems are used — blow to clear after the blast, exhaust during mucking to control dust.

**And the safety operation that precedes mucking:**

> **SCALING the roof and walls to bring down loose rock** — because the greatest danger in a tunnel immediately after a blast is a **fall of ground onto the men and machines working below.**

examTip.trick: The tunnelling cycle is **drill → charge → blast → ventilate → scale → MUCK → support**, and the cycle time is set by the **slowest** step. Muck removal and ventilation frequently govern.
examTip.trap: **All four options are real operations** — skimming (greasy material from water), trimming (cutting edges), scaling (sizing, and also knocking down loose roof rock). This is a genuine discrimination.
examTip.mnemonic: **A tunnel's advance rate is usually a LOGISTICS problem, not an excavation one** — rock can be broken faster than it can be carried out. Which is why long tunnels are driven from **multiple faces**.

questions.stem: Why is the E-coli test performed?
options: To confirm presence of colored bacteria
To confirm presence of bad odor
To confirm the water has been contaminated by feces
questions.solution:
**To confirm whether the water has been contaminated by faecal matter.**

> The source states it directly: **E. coli is commonly found in human and animal faeces. Testing water or food for E. coli helps to confirm whether it has been contaminated by faecal matter or not.**

**Why E. coli is used as the INDICATOR rather than testing for pathogens directly:**

| Requirement of a good indicator | E. coli |
|---|---|
| **Abundant in faeces** | ✓ — present in enormous numbers |
| **Easy and cheap to detect** | ✓ |
| **Survives about as long as the pathogens** | ✓ |
| **Does NOT multiply in water** | ✓ — so its presence means recent contamination |
| Not normally present otherwise | ✓ |

> **Testing for every pathogen individually would be impossibly slow, expensive and unreliable** — cholera, typhoid, hepatitis and dozens of others, each needing its own method, most present in small numbers.

> **E. coli answers the one question that covers them all: has faecal matter reached this water?** If it has, any of those pathogens may be present.

**The standard is ABSOLUTE:**

> **ZERO E. coli per 100 ml.** There is no permissible level.

> **That is unlike every other water quality parameter**, which has a numerical limit. **The reason is that the presence of any faecal indicator means faecal contamination has occurred**, and no safe dose of pathogens can be assumed.

**The related tests:**

| Test | Detects |
|---|---|
| **Total coliform** | A broader group — **includes organisms from soil and vegetation**, so a positive is not necessarily faecal |
| **Faecal (thermotolerant) coliform** | Narrower; grows at 44.5 °C |
| **E. COLI** | **The most specific faecal indicator** |

> **Total coliforms can occur naturally without faecal contamination**, which is why E. coli — a subset — is the more meaningful test.

**Methods:** the **Most Probable Number (MPN)** multiple-tube method, and the **membrane filtration** method, which is faster and gives a direct count.

**Why the other options are wrong — each names a different parameter with its own test:**

| Option | Correct test |
|---|---|
| Turbidity | **Nephelometric — NTU**, limit **5 NTU** |
| Odour | **Threshold Odour Number (TON)** — a dilution ratio judged by the human nose |
| Colour | **Hazen units (Pt-Co scale)** |

**And the connection that makes turbidity relevant to this test:**

> **Turbidity SHIELDS pathogens from disinfection** — micro-organisms hide inside suspended particles where chlorine cannot reach them.

> **So a turbid water can show E. coli despite an adequate chlorine residual**, which is why the sequence is invariably **clarify FIRST, disinfect LAST**, and why **filtration is what makes disinfection work.**

**The residual that protects the supply afterwards:** **0.1–0.2 mg/l free chlorine**, maintained throughout the distribution system — which is exactly what decays to nothing at a **dead end**, and why dead ends are where contamination shows up first.

examTip.trick: **E. coli is an INDICATOR, not the hazard itself.** Testing for every pathogen would be impossibly slow — E. coli answers the one question that covers them all: **has faecal matter reached this water?**
examTip.trap: **The standard is ZERO per 100 ml — there is no permissible level**, unlike every other parameter. Any faecal indicator means contamination has occurred.
examTip.mnemonic: **Total coliforms occur naturally in soil and vegetation; E. coli does not.** That specificity is why E. coli is the meaningful test — and why turbidity must be removed first, since it **shields pathogens from chlorine.**

questions.stem: COD/BOD of country sewage in general is:
questions.solution:
**Greater than 1.**

> The source states the reason in one line: **COD is ALWAYS greater than BOD, so the COD/BOD ratio is always greater than one.**

**Why COD always exceeds BOD:**

| | **BOD** | **COD** |
|---|---|---|
| Measures | **BIODEGRADABLE** organic matter — what micro-organisms can consume | **ALL chemically oxidisable** matter |
| Method | **Biological** — 5 days at 20 °C | **Chemical** — strong oxidant, ~3 hours |
| Value | **Lower** | **HIGHER — always** |

> **COD oxidises everything BOD does, plus material that bacteria CANNOT break down** — lignin, many synthetic organics, and some inorganic reducing agents.

> **Since COD's scope strictly contains BOD's, the ratio can never fall below 1.** That makes option (b) impossible in principle, not merely unusual.

> **And option (c), −1, is impossible on sight** — both quantities are concentrations and cannot be negative, so their ratio cannot be negative either.

**What the RATIO tells you — this is where its value lies:**

| COD/BOD | Interpretation |
|---|---|
| **Close to 1** | **Highly BIODEGRADABLE** — nearly everything present can be treated biologically |
| **1.5 – 2.5** | **Typical DOMESTIC sewage** — biological treatment is appropriate |
| **High (>3–4)** | **Much non-biodegradable matter** — suspect **INDUSTRIAL** waste; biological treatment alone will not suffice |

> **Equivalently, a BOD/COD ratio above about 0.5 indicates a waste suitable for biological treatment.**

> **That single ratio is the quickest guide to which treatment process to use**, and it is why both tests are run rather than just the cheaper one.

**Why COD is useful despite BOD being the regulated parameter:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **3 hours instead of 5 days** | **Usable for process CONTROL** — a plant operator cannot wait five days |
| Reproducible | Chemical, not biological — no seed variability |
| **Works on toxic wastes** | Where bacteria would be killed and BOD would read falsely low |

> **A toxic industrial waste can give a misleadingly LOW BOD** because it poisons the very organisms performing the test. **COD is unaffected**, and a large gap between the two is itself the warning.

**Typical values:**

| Wastewater | BOD₅ | COD |
|---|---|---|
| **Weak domestic** | ~110 mg/l | ~250 |
| **Medium domestic** | **~220 mg/l** | **~500** |
| Strong domestic | ~400 mg/l | ~1000 |

**And the BOD test itself:** **5 days at 20 °C**, capturing about **68% of the ultimate BOD** (from **1 − 10^{−0.1×5}**).

> **Temperature changes the RATE of BOD exertion but not the ULTIMATE demand** — a warmer sample exerts its BOD faster; the total oxygen required is the same.

examTip.trick: **COD's scope strictly CONTAINS BOD's** — it oxidises everything bacteria can, plus what they cannot. So the ratio can never fall below 1; option (b) is impossible in principle.
examTip.trap: **Option (c), −1, is impossible on sight** — both are concentrations and cannot be negative. Discarding it costs no thought at all.
examTip.mnemonic: **BOD/COD above ~0.5 means biological treatment will work; a high COD/BOD suggests INDUSTRIAL waste.** And a toxic waste gives a falsely **LOW BOD** because it poisons the test organisms — COD is unaffected.

questions.stem: Where does the maximum ordinate on a mass haul diagram occur?
options: The point where excavation ends and embankment starts
questions.solution:
**At the point where excavation (cutting) ends and embankment (filling) starts.**

**The characteristics of a mass haul diagram**, as the source lists them:

| Feature | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **A RISING curve** | **CUTTING** — the volume of excavation is increasing |
| **A FALLING curve** | **FILLING** — the volume of embankment is accumulating |
| **A MAXIMUM point** | **The END of a CUT / the BEGINNING of a FILL** |
| **A MINIMUM point** | **The END of a FILL / the BEGINNING of a CUT** |

> **The reasoning is pure calculus**: the curve plots **CUMULATIVE volume**, so it rises while material is being cut and falls while it is being placed. **A turning point is where the sign changes** — that is, where cut becomes fill.

> **Options (b) and (c) name single events**, but a maximum requires the curve to stop rising **and start falling** — which needs **both** conditions together.

**What a mass haul diagram is FOR:**

> **Earthwork is expensive to MOVE, not merely to dig.** The diagram is the tool for planning that movement economically.

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Balancing cut and fill** | Minimising both borrow and spoil |
| **Determining HAUL distances** | And therefore the plant required |
| **Identifying BORROW and SPOIL** | Where the earthwork cannot balance |
| Selecting plant | Short haul → dozer; long haul → scraper or truck |

> **The horizontal axis is chainage; the vertical is CUMULATIVE volume**, with cut positive and fill negative.

**The key construction — the BALANCING LINE:**

> **A horizontal line cutting the curve at two points defines a section where cut and fill EXACTLY BALANCE** — because the cumulative volume is the same at both ends.

> **The horizontal distance between those intersections is the HAUL distance**, and **the area between the curve and the balancing line is the HAUL (volume × distance)** — the quantity that actually costs money.

> **That area, not the volume alone, is what the design seeks to minimise.**

**FREE HAUL and OVERHAUL:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **FREE HAUL distance** | The distance within which **moving material is included in the excavation rate** |
| **OVERHAUL** | Material moved **BEYOND** that distance — **paid for separately** |

> **That contractual distinction is why the diagram is drawn at all**: it determines what the contractor may charge extra for, and it is a routine source of measurement dispute if not agreed in advance.

**And the practical judgement it supports:**

> **Beyond a certain haul distance it becomes CHEAPER to borrow locally and spoil the excavated material than to move it.** The mass haul diagram is what identifies that point.

> **Moving earth a long way is often the most expensive thing on an earthworks contract** — which is why the diagram, despite being a simple cumulative plot, earns its place.

examTip.trick: The curve plots **CUMULATIVE volume** — it **rises in CUT and falls in FILL**. A maximum is therefore where the curve stops rising and starts falling: **cut ending, fill beginning**.
examTip.trap: Options (b) and (c) name **single events**, but a turning point needs **both** — the end of one operation and the start of the other. A maximum is a change of sign, not an event.
examTip.mnemonic: **The AREA between the curve and the balancing line is the HAUL (volume × distance)** — and that, not the volume alone, is what costs money. Beyond the **free haul** distance it becomes **OVERHAUL**, paid separately.

questions.stem: Formula of SPI is:
questions.solution:
**SPI = BCWP/BCWS — Earned Value ÷ Planned Value.**

> The source gives both indices together: **SPI = BCWP/BCWS** and **CPI = BCWP/ACWP.**

**The three earned value quantities:**

| Abbreviation | Modern name | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **BCWS** | **PV — Planned Value** | **What we PLANNED to have done by now** |
| **BCWP** | **EV — Earned Value** | **What we HAVE actually done, valued at budget rates** |
| **ACWP** | **AC — Actual Cost** | **What we have actually SPENT** |

> **The old names spell out their meaning**: **Budgeted Cost of Work Scheduled / Performed**, and **Actual Cost of Work Performed.**

**The two indices, and how to keep them apart:**

| Index | Formula | Compares | Answers |
|---|---|---|---|
| **SPI — Schedule** | **BCWP/BCWS = EV/PV** | **Work done vs work PLANNED** | **Are we on TIME?** |
| **CPI — Cost** | **BCWP/ACWP = EV/AC** | **Work done vs money SPENT** | **Are we on BUDGET?** |

> **Both have EARNED VALUE (BCWP) as the numerator** — because the question in each case is "what have we actually achieved, compared with...?"

> **Only the DENOMINATOR changes: SCHEDULE index divides by the SCHEDULE (BCWS); COST index divides by the COST (ACWP).**

> **That mnemonic settles both formulae at once**, and it immediately rules out option (b) — which puts **actual cost** over **scheduled cost**, mixing the two comparisons and answering neither question.

**Reading the indices:**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **> 1** | **AHEAD** of schedule / **UNDER** budget — good |
| **= 1** | Exactly on plan |
| **< 1** | **BEHIND** schedule / **OVER** budget |

**The corresponding variances:**

> **SV = BCWP − BCWS** (schedule variance) and **CV = BCWP − ACWP** (cost variance)

> **The indices are RATIOS and the variances are DIFFERENCES** — of the same pairs. **A ratio shows the proportion; a difference shows the amount.**

**Why earned value is worth the trouble:**

> **Comparing spend against budget alone is meaningless.** A project that has spent half its budget may be half complete, or a tenth complete, or nearly finished.

> **Earned value introduces the third quantity — WHAT HAS ACTUALLY BEEN ACHIEVED** — and only with that can cost and schedule performance be separated.

> **That is the whole insight of the method**: two numbers cannot distinguish being behind schedule from being over budget; three can.

**A genuine limitation worth knowing:**

> **SPI is measured in COST units, not time** — and it **converges to 1.0 at project completion** regardless of how late the project actually is, because eventually all the planned work is earned.

> **So SPI becomes unreliable toward the end of a project**, and the **critical path** — not SPI — remains the authority on the completion date.

**Forecasting:** **EAC = BAC/CPI** estimates the cost at completion, assuming performance continues at the rate observed so far.

examTip.trick: **Both indices have EARNED VALUE (BCWP) on top.** Only the denominator changes: the **SCHEDULE** index divides by the **schedule (BCWS)**; the **COST** index divides by the **cost (ACWP)**.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) puts ACTUAL COST over SCHEDULED cost** — mixing the two comparisons so it answers neither question. Earned value must be the numerator in both.
examTip.mnemonic: **Two numbers cannot separate "behind schedule" from "over budget"; three can.** That is the whole insight. But **SPI converges to 1.0 at completion** however late — so trust the **critical path** for the date.

questions.stem: When is duty maximum?
options: Highest in the field and lowest at the head of the main canal
Highest in the field and lowest at the head of the main capital
Lowest in the field and Highest at the head of the main canal
questions.solution:
**Highest in the field and lowest at the head of the main canal.**

> The source explains why: **at the HEAD of the canal there are numerous losses still to occur, which requires MORE water to irrigate a particular field. However, if considered AT the field, all losses have ALREADY occurred and a LESSER amount of water is required to irrigate the same area.**

**What duty means:**

> **The number of hectares irrigated for the full growth of a crop by a supply of 1 cumec running continuously through the base period.**

> **Duty = area ÷ discharge**, so **a HIGHER duty means one cumec serves MORE land — that is, LESS water per hectare.**

**Why duty rises toward the field:**

| Point | Losses still ahead | Water needed per hectare | Duty |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Head of main canal** | **All of them** | **MOST** | **LOWEST** |
| Distributary | Some | Intermediate | Intermediate |
| **Field** | **NONE — all already occurred** | **LEAST** | **HIGHEST** |

> **The source's own diagram states it as D₅ > D₄ > D₃ > D₂ > D₁** — duty increasing steadily from the main canal (D₁) through distributary, branch and outlet to the field (D₅).

> **So duty must ALWAYS be quoted with the point at which it is measured**, or the number is meaningless.

**The reasoning in one line:**

> **Water is lost between the head and the field, so more must be released at the head to deliver the same amount at the field.** More water released for the same area means a lower duty there.

**Note that option (b) is a typographical trap:**

> It reads **"head of the main CAPITAL"** instead of "canal" — otherwise identical to the correct answer. **A misprint, but one that makes the option meaningless as written.**

**The related quantities:**

> **Δ = 8.64 B/D** metres, with **B in days** and **D in hectares per cumec.**

> The **8.64 is simply 86 400 s/day ÷ 10 000 m²/ha** — knowing that means never mis-remembering it.

| Crop | Delta |
|---|---|
| **Rice** | **1200 – 2000 mm** |
| Sugarcane | 1500 – 2000 mm |
| **Wheat** | **350 – 400 mm** |
| **Millet / maize** | **300 – 500 mm** |

**Factors that IMPROVE duty:**

| Factor | Note |
|---|---|
| **CANAL LINING** | Cuts conveyance losses directly |
| **Efficient application** (drip, sprinkler) | Cuts field losses |
| Suitable crop choice | Millet over rice |
| Good soil (less percolation) | — |
| Careful scheduling | Avoiding over-irrigation |

> **Lining is usually the single most effective measure**, because conveyance losses in an unlined canal commonly reach **30–50%** of the water diverted.

**And the efficiency chain that connects it all:**

> **η_overall = η_conveyance × η_application** — and **efficiencies MULTIPLY, never average.**

> Two stages at 70% give **49%**, so **the water released at the head can be TWICE what the crop consumes.** Sizing a canal on the crop's own requirement guarantees a scheme that cannot deliver.

examTip.trick: **Losses occur BETWEEN the head and the field.** At the field they have all already happened, so less water is needed per hectare — and less water per hectare means a **HIGHER duty**.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) reads "head of the main CAPITAL"** — a misprint of "canal", otherwise identical to the answer. Read the options letter by letter where they look the same.
examTip.mnemonic: **D₅ > D₄ > D₃ > D₂ > D₁** — duty rises steadily from main canal to field. So **always state WHERE the duty is measured**, or the number means nothing.

questions.stem: Given w/c = 0.8 and volume of cement = 2 m³, the water required in litres is:
questions.solution:
**2304 litres.**

**Working.**

> **Weight of cement in 2 m³** = 2 × 28.8 bags × 50 kg = **57.6 bags × 50 = 2880 kg**
>
> (since **1 m³ of cement = 28.8 bags = 28.8 × 50 kg = 1440 kg**)
>
> **Water required = 0.8 × 2880 = 2304 litres** ✓

> **The two constants do all the work: 28.8 bags per m³, and 50 kg per bag** — and **28.8 is simply 1440 kg/m³ ÷ 50 kg**, so only the bulk density need be remembered.

> **1 litre of water = 1 kg**, which is why the answer converts directly.

**A shortcut worth seeing:**

> **Water = w/c × volume × 1440 = 0.8 × 2 × 1440 = 2304** — bypassing bags entirely.

> **The bag count is a distraction here**; the calculation is simply cement **mass** × the ratio.

**Why the water–cement ratio matters so much:**

> **ABRAMS' LAW: strength depends primarily on the w/c ratio, and INVERSELY** — lower w/c gives higher strength, almost regardless of the mix proportions.

| w/c | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **0.35 – 0.45** | **High strength, LOW permeability, durable** — but stiff |
| **0.6 – 0.7** | Workable — but **weak and PERMEABLE** |

> **A w/c of 0.8, as in this question, is very high** — appropriate to a lean or non-structural mix, and well outside what IS 456 permits for any exposure class.

| Exposure | Max w/c |
|---|---|
| **Mild** | **0.55** |
| Moderate | 0.50 |
| **Severe** | **0.45** |
| **Extreme** | **0.40** |

**Where the excess water goes:**

> **Only about 0.25 of water per unit of cement is chemically needed for HYDRATION.** Everything above that is added for **workability**, and it eventually **evaporates, leaving CAPILLARY PORES.**

> **Those pores are the mechanism of both the strength loss and the durability loss** — and permeability is the master durability property, since carbonation, chlorides, sulphates and freeze–thaw all require something to get **in**.

**The right way to gain workability:**

| Admixture | Water reduction |
|---|---|
| **Plasticiser** | **5 – 15%** |
| **SUPERPLASTICISER** | **15 – 30%** |

> **They break the conflict between placeability and durability** — the workability of a wet mix at the w/c of a dry one.

**The related quantity constants**, for a nominal mix:

| Constant | Value | Origin |
|---|---|---|
| **Dry volume factor** | **1.54** | Dry aggregates contain **voids** that vanish on mixing and compaction |
| **Bags per m³** | **28.8** | **1440 ÷ 50** |
| Cement bulk density | **1440 kg/m³** | — |

> **Omitting the 1.54 factor understates the cement by a third** in a volume-based calculation — though it is not needed here, since the cement volume is given directly.

examTip.trick: Shortcut past the bags: **water = w/c × volume × 1440 = 0.8 × 2 × 1440 = 2304 litres.** And **1 litre of water = 1 kg**, so the mass converts directly.
examTip.trap: **28.8 bags per m³ is just 1440 ÷ 50** — only the bulk density need be remembered. The bag count is a distraction in a calculation that only needs cement **mass**.
examTip.mnemonic: **w/c = 0.8 is very high** — outside what IS 456 allows for any exposure (mild 0.55, severe 0.45, extreme 0.40). **Only ~0.25 is needed for HYDRATION**; the rest leaves capillary pores behind.

questions.stem: We cannot draw an angle using a set square:
questions.solution:
**20 degrees.**

> The source gives the rule in one line: **only multiples of 15 can be drawn using a set square.**

> **20 is not a multiple of 15**, so it cannot be constructed — while **15, 30 and 60 all are.**

**Why 15° is the unit:**

> A drawing set contains **two set squares:**

| Set square | Angles |
|---|---|
| **45° square** | **45, 45, 90** |
| **30–60 square** | **30, 60, 90** |

> Used singly they give **30, 45, 60, 90**. **Used in COMBINATION — one against the other, adding or subtracting — they give every multiple of 15:**

| Angle | How |
|---|---|
| **15°** | **45 − 30** |
| 30° | Directly |
| 45° | Directly |
| 60° | Directly |
| **75°** | **45 + 30** |
| 90° | Directly |
| **105°** | **60 + 45** |
| 120°, 135°, 150° | Combinations |

> **The 15° arises from the DIFFERENCE 45 − 30**, and every other constructible angle is a sum or difference of the six basic ones. **That is why the set is limited to multiples of 15 and no finer.**

> **Anything else — 20°, 25°, 40° — requires a PROTRACTOR.**

**Why this matters in practice:**

> **Set squares are faster and more accurate than a protractor for the angles they can produce**, because they are used against a T-square or drafting machine and need no reading of a scale.

> **A protractor requires reading a graduated arc**, which introduces both a reading error and a positioning error. **For a multiple of 15° the set square is simply better.**

**The related drawing conventions:**

| Convention | Value |
|---|---|
| **Hatching** | **Thin lines at 45°** — a set square angle, which is why it is used |
| **Isometric axes** | **120° apart**; the horizontal axes at **30°** to the horizontal |
| **Inclined lettering** | **75°** — also a set square angle |
| Vertical lettering | 90° |

> **Notice that the standard drawing angles — 30, 45, 75, 120 — are all multiples of 15**, and that is not a coincidence: **the conventions were designed around what the instruments could produce.**

**And the isometric details:** axes at **120°**, isometric scale **≈ 0.816 (√2/√3)** — though **isometric DRAWINGS use true lengths** at full scale, because the 0.816 reduction adds work for no practical gain.

> **Circles become ELLIPSES in isometric**, which is tedious to construct — and that is precisely the reason **OBLIQUE projection** exists, placing the face with the circles at the front so they stay circles.

**The other drawing standards** worth carrying: lettering heights **2.5, 3.5, 5, 7, 10, 14, 20 mm** in a **√2** progression matching the A-series (**A0 = 1 m²**); **only ONE lettering style per drawing**; and the **projection symbol** in the title block, since **first angle (top view BELOW) and third angle (top view ABOVE) give mirror-image readings.**

examTip.trick: **Set squares give only MULTIPLES OF 15°** — because the two squares (45-45-90 and 30-60-90) combine by addition and subtraction, and **15 = 45 − 30** is the finest step available.
examTip.trap: Three options (15, 30, 60) are all multiples of 15 and therefore constructible. Only **20** is not — anything else needs a **protractor**.
examTip.mnemonic: **The standard drawing angles are all multiples of 15 — hatching 45°, isometric 30° and 120°, inclined lettering 75°.** The conventions were designed around what the instruments could produce.

questions.stem: NDRRMA falls under which ministry?
questions.solution:
**The Ministry of Home Affairs (MOHA).**

> The **National Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Authority (NDRRMA)** is the executive agency for disaster risk management in Nepal, and it falls under MOHA.

**Why Home Affairs and not a technical ministry:**

> **Disaster response requires the coordination of MANY agencies simultaneously** — Nepal Police, Armed Police Force, Nepal Army, local government, health services and the district administration.

> **MOHA already commands the security forces and the district administration structure** (Chief District Officers), which is precisely the machinery a multi-agency emergency response needs.

> **A technical ministry could design mitigation works but could not mobilise a response**, which is why disaster management sits with Home Affairs in most countries.

**The institutional structure under the Disaster Risk Reduction and Management Act 2074 (2017):**

| Body | Chaired by |
|---|---|
| **National Council for DRRM** | **The PRIME MINISTER** — policy level |
| **Executive Committee** | **The HOME MINISTER** |
| **NDRRMA** | The executive agency, **under MOHA** |
| Province / District Disaster Management Committees | Regional coordination |
| Local Disaster Management Committees | Mayor / chairperson |

> **Note that option (a), the Prime Minister's Office, is not absurd** — the **National Council IS chaired by the Prime Minister.** But **the AUTHORITY itself sits under MOHA**, and the question asks about the NDRRMA.

> **Policy level under the PM; executive agency under MOHA** — that division is what the question tests.

**The significance of the 2074 Act:**

> **It marked a shift from RESPONSE to RISK REDUCTION** — from managing disasters after they occur to reducing the risk beforehand.

> **That shift is the substantive point worth knowing**, and it reflects the international consensus (the Sendai Framework) that prevention is far more cost-effective than relief.

**The DRM cycle:**

| Phase | Activities |
|---|---|
| **PREVENTION / MITIGATION** | **Building codes, land use planning, structural measures** |
| **PREPAREDNESS** | Early warning, drills, stockpiles, contingency plans |
| **RESPONSE** | Search and rescue, relief, emergency medical care |
| **RECOVERY** | Reconstruction — **"BUILD BACK BETTER"** |

> **The engineering contribution is concentrated in the FIRST phase, and it is by far the most cost-effective.** Every rupee spent on prevention saves several spent on response.

**Where engineering enters:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Building code enforcement** | **NBC 105** (seismic), **NBC 109 and 202** (masonry) |
| **Land use planning** | Keeping development off hazardous ground |
| **Retrofitting** | Especially schools and hospitals |
| Structural mitigation | Embankments, slope stabilisation, check dams |
| **Lifeline protection** | Water, power, roads and hospitals must survive |

**And the terminology underlying it all:**

> **RISK = Hazard × Exposure × Vulnerability**

> **Engineering cannot reduce the HAZARD** — an earthquake will happen regardless. **What engineering reduces is VULNERABILITY**; **planning reduces EXPOSURE.**

> **That is why building codes and land use planning are complementary rather than alternative measures**, and it is the whole logic of disaster risk reduction.

**Nepal's hazard profile:** **earthquake** (the whole country is seismically active), **LANDSLIDE** (the most frequent by number of events), **flood**, **GLOF** (glacial lake outburst flood), fire, drought and epidemic.

examTip.trick: **MOHA already commands the security forces and the district administration (CDOs)** — exactly the machinery a multi-agency disaster response needs. A technical ministry could design works but not mobilise a response.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) is not absurd** — the **National Council IS chaired by the Prime Minister**. But the **AUTHORITY sits under MOHA**: policy level under the PM, executive agency under Home Affairs.
examTip.mnemonic: **RISK = Hazard × Exposure × Vulnerability.** Engineering cannot reduce the hazard — it reduces **VULNERABILITY**; planning reduces **EXPOSURE**. The 2074 Act shifted the emphasis from **response to risk reduction**.

questions.stem: Formula of flexure equation?
questions.solution:
**M/I = σ/y** — and the full relation is **M/I = σ/y = E/R.**

**The three terms and what each connects:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **M/I** | **Moment ÷ second moment of area** |
| **σ/y** | **Bending stress ÷ distance from the neutral axis** |
| **E/R** | **Elastic modulus ÷ radius of curvature** |

> **The equality of all three is the complete flexure formula**, and each pairing gives a useful result:

| From | Gives |
|---|---|
| **M/I = σ/y** | **σ = My/I** — the bending stress at any fibre |
| **M/I = E/R** | **1/R = M/EI** — the **curvature**, which integrates to the deflection |
| σ/y = E/R | The strain distribution |

**The assumptions behind it** — worth knowing because they define where it applies:

| Assumption | Note |
|---|---|
| **Plane sections remain plane** | Fails for **deep beams** (span/depth < ~4) |
| **Material is homogeneous and elastic** | Fails beyond yield |
| **Hooke's law holds** | — |
| **PURE BENDING** — constant moment, no shear | Strictly true only in that case |
| The beam is initially straight, of constant section | — |

> **The pure bending assumption is why flexural strength is measured in the MIDDLE THIRD of a four-point loading test** — that region has **constant moment and zero shear**, exactly matching the theory.

> **For a slender beam the formula remains an excellent approximation elsewhere**, but it is an approximation.

**The immediate consequences:**

> **σ = My/I means stress varies LINEARLY with distance from the neutral axis** — **zero at the neutral axis, maximum at the extreme fibres.**

> **That is the exact opposite of transverse SHEAR stress**, which is **parabolic with its maximum at the neutral axis** — and the two are constantly confused.

**The SECTION MODULUS follows:**

> **Z = I/y_max**, so **σ_max = M/Z**

| Section | Z |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle b × h** | **bh²/6** |
| **Solid circle** | **πd³/32** |
| Hollow circle | π(D⁴ − d⁴)/(32D) |

> **Z is what actually sizes a beam**: compute M from statics, then choose a section with adequate Z.

**Why option (c), σ/2y, is a well-made distractor:**

> It has the **right form but a spurious factor of 2** — and dimensional analysis alone will not catch it, since the 2 is dimensionless. **Only knowing the formula settles it.**

**And why the section does NOT affect the moment:**

> **Bending moment comes from EQUILIBRIUM alone** — the section never enters the statics. **What the section changes is the STRESS: σ = M/Z.**

> A 200 mm and a 600 mm deep beam spanning the same distance under the same load carry **exactly the same moment** and quite different stresses.

> (**For an INDETERMINATE structure the section does matter indirectly**, through relative **EI** — moments redistribute toward stiffer members.)

examTip.trick: The full relation is **M/I = σ/y = E/R** — three terms, each pairing giving something useful: **σ = My/I** for stress, and **1/R = M/EI** for curvature and hence deflection.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) has the right form with a spurious factor of 2** — dimensional analysis cannot catch it, since 2 is dimensionless. Only knowing the formula settles it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bending stress is LINEAR, maximum at the extreme fibres; transverse SHEAR is PARABOLIC, maximum at the neutral axis.** Exact opposites, and constantly confused.

questions.stem: Which province of Nepal has the greatest number of engineering colleges recognised by the NEC?
questions.solution:
**Bagmati Province.**

> **Bagmati contains Kathmandu valley**, which concentrates the great majority of Nepal's higher education institutions — including the **Institute of Engineering (Pulchowk, Thapathali and Purwanchal campuses under TU)**, Kathmandu University's affiliates and numerous private colleges.

> **The concentration follows population, infrastructure and historical development**, and it is why the answer is not a matter of chance.

**Why the NEC's role here matters:**

> **Recognition of an institution is what makes its graduates ELIGIBLE FOR REGISTRATION.** A degree from an unrecognised programme does not lead to a license to practise.

> **That is the Council's real leverage over engineering education**: it cannot open or run colleges, but by controlling **whose graduates may register** it sets the floor for the whole system.

**What the Council assesses for recognition:**

| Area | Examples |
|---|---|
| **Faculty** | Numbers, qualifications, **student–teacher ratio**, permanence |
| **Physical infrastructure** | Classrooms, drawing halls, land and buildings |
| **Laboratories** | Equipment, capacity, adequacy for the programme |
| **Library** | Titles, volumes, journals, reading space |
| **Curriculum** | Conformity to the prescribed minimum standards |
| Student admission | Compliance with prescribed conditions |

> **The minimum average required for affiliation is 70%**, assessed across these areas — so an institution strong in one respect and weak in another can still fall short.

**The boundary of the Council's role:**

| The Council DOES | The Council does NOT |
|---|---|
| **Recognise** institutions and programmes | **Open or run** colleges |
| **Prescribe** minimum standards and admission conditions | **Award** degrees |
| **Register** engineers; issue the **license** | Fix fees or salaries |
| **Regulate conduct**; take disciplinary action | **Represent** engineers' interests |

> **The COUNCIL regulates; the ASSOCIATION (NEA) represents.** NEC registration is a **legal requirement** to practise; NEA membership is voluntary.

**The Council facts worth learning as one block:**

| Fact | Value |
|---|---|
| **NEC Act** | **2055 BS (1998 AD)** |
| **NEC Regulations** | **2057 BS** |
| **Total members** | **21** |
| **Chairman** | Bachelor's + **15 years**, nominated by GoN |
| **Vice-Chairman** | Bachelor's + **10 years**, nominated by GoN |
| **Registrar (Member Secretary)** | Bachelor's + **10 years** |
| **Nominated by the Council itself** | **2** |
| **Elected from the NEA** | **5** |
| **NEA President** | **Ex officio** |
| **Institutional affiliation** | **70%** |
| **Reconstitution after dissolution** | **3 months** |
| **Code of conduct articles** | **8**, raised to **11** in 2079 |
| First Registrar | Er. Bindeshwar Yadav |

> **These recall questions are the cheapest marks on the paper** for anyone who has read the Council's material once, and several appear in every sitting. **Learning the block is worth far more than the time it takes.**

**And the provincial dimension appears elsewhere in the Act:** **seven Council members are nominated one from each province, with at least three women** — a deliberate provision for geographical and gender representation on a body whose institutions are heavily concentrated in one province.

examTip.trick: **Bagmati contains Kathmandu valley**, which concentrates most of Nepal's higher education — the Institute of Engineering campuses plus numerous private colleges. Not a matter of chance.
examTip.trap: This is pure recall, but it sits inside the **Council block** that supplies several marks every sitting. Learn the block rather than the isolated fact.
examTip.mnemonic: **Recognition is the Council's real leverage** — an unrecognised degree leads to no license. It cannot run colleges, but it decides **whose graduates may register**, which sets the floor for the whole system.

questions.stem: Which water is used in cement concrete?
options: Water from sewer can also be used if drinking water is not available easily
questions.solution:
**Potable water** — water fit to drink.

> **The working rule is simple and practical: if water is fit to drink, it is fit for concrete.** That is why the specification is expressed this way rather than through a list of chemical limits.

> **The converse does not hold** — some water unfit to drink is acceptable for concrete — but the potability test is the one that can be applied on site without a laboratory.

**Why water quality matters:**

| Impurity | Effect |
|---|---|
| **CHLORIDES** | **Corrode the reinforcement** — the most serious |
| **SULPHATES** | **Expansive ETTRINGITE** formation; disruption |
| **Organic matter** | **Retards setting**; may prevent hardening altogether |
| **Acids** | Attack the cement paste |
| **Alkalis** | Alkali–aggregate reaction |
| Suspended solids, oil | Impair bond |
| Sugar | **A powerful retarder** — even traces delay setting markedly |

> **Chlorides are the gravest concern in reinforced concrete**, because they break down the **passive oxide film** that the concrete's alkalinity forms on the steel — causing **pitting corrosion** that is localised, rapid and hard to detect.

> **Once corrosion starts, rust occupies 2–4 times the volume of the steel and SPALLS the cover off**, exposing more steel and accelerating the process. **The failure is self-accelerating.**

**Why SEA WATER is specifically excluded** — the case option (d) gestures at:

> **Sea water contains about 3.5% dissolved salts, largely chlorides.** It may be used for **plain concrete** in some circumstances but **NEVER for reinforced or prestressed concrete.**

> **It also causes efflorescence and can reduce the 28-day strength by 10–15%.**

> **Option (d) — sewer water — is not merely poor practice but dangerous**: it carries organic matter that would retard or prevent setting, and pathogens that would endanger workers.

**The IS 456 limits for mixing water:**

| Parameter | Limit |
|---|---|
| **pH** | **NOT LESS than 6** |
| **Organic solids** | ≤ 200 mg/l |
| Inorganic solids | ≤ 3000 mg/l |
| **Sulphates (as SO₃)** | ≤ 400 mg/l |
| **Chlorides — PLAIN concrete** | **≤ 2000 mg/l** |
| **Chlorides — REINFORCED concrete** | **≤ 500 mg/l** |
| Suspended matter | ≤ 2000 mg/l |

> **Note the chloride limit is FOUR TIMES stricter for reinforced concrete** — which is the numerical expression of everything above.

**And CURING water matters as much as mixing water:**

> **Curing water must meet the same quality requirements**, because impurities are drawn into the surface where the cover — the very layer protecting the steel — is formed.

> **Sea water used for curing causes efflorescence and surface staining** even where the mixing water was sound.

**A practical field test**, where no laboratory is available: **compare the setting time and 7-day strength of mortar cubes made with the doubtful water against those made with distilled water.** IS 456 permits acceptance on that basis.

examTip.trick: **If it is fit to drink, it is fit for concrete** — a rule that can be applied on site without a laboratory. The converse does not hold, but the potability test is the practical one.
examTip.trap: **The chloride limit is FOUR TIMES stricter for REINFORCED concrete (500 mg/l) than plain (2000 mg/l)** — because chlorides break down the passive film on the steel and cause pitting corrosion.
examTip.mnemonic: **CURING water must meet the same standard as mixing water** — impurities are drawn into the surface, which is exactly the cover layer protecting the steel. Sea water stains and effloresces even sound concrete.

questions.stem: Find the maximum anchorage length for D = 20 mm.
questions.solution:
**320 mm.**

**Working.**

> **For a U-shaped hook (180° bend), the MAXIMUM anchorage length = 16 D**
> **= 16 × 20 = 320 mm** ✓

**The anchorage values for standard hooks and bends (IS 456):**

| Detail | Anchorage value |
|---|---|
| **U-bend (180° hook)** | **16 D — the MAXIMUM** |
| **90° bend** | **8 D** |
| **45° bend** | **4 D** |
| Each 45° of turn | **+4 D**, up to the 16 D ceiling |

> **The rule is 4D per 45° of turn, capped at 16D** — which makes the whole table one relation rather than four separate facts.

> **The word "MAXIMUM" in the question points to the 180° U-bend**, which is the largest value obtainable.

**What anchorage is FOR:**

> **A bar can only carry the force the calculation assumes if it is ANCHORED well enough to develop that force.**

> **Development length L_d = φ σ_s/(4 τ_bd)** is the **straight** length needed to transfer the bar's full force into the concrete by bond.

> **A hook provides an equivalent anchorage in a much shorter physical space**, which is why hooks exist at all: **at a support there is rarely room for a full straight development length.**

**How a bend anchors:**

| Mechanism | Note |
|---|---|
| **BEARING of the bend against the concrete inside it** | **The dominant mechanism** |
| Additional bond along the bent length | Secondary |
| Mechanical interlock | — |

> **Because the resistance comes mainly from BEARING, the concrete inside the bend must be sound** — and that is why **minimum bend radii** are specified.

> **Too tight a bend crushes the concrete inside it and splits the cover.**

**Minimum internal bend diameters (IS 2502):**

| Bar type | Minimum |
|---|---|
| **Mild steel** | **2 D** for hooks |
| **Deformed (HYSD)** | **4 D** for bends, larger for hooks |

> **HYSD bars need larger radii** because they are stronger and less ductile — bending them too tightly can **crack the bar itself.**

**Where anchorage is critical:**

| Location | Note |
|---|---|
| **At simple supports** | Bars must be anchored **beyond the face** — a common detailing failure |
| **Curtailment points** | A bar must extend a development length beyond where it is no longer needed |
| **Laps** | Lap length typically **L_d or greater** |
| **Beam–column joints** | Especially critical under seismic loading |

> **A bar that cannot develop its stress is not carrying the force the calculation assumed** — one of the commonest failures in reinforced concrete detailing, and **invisible once the concrete is poured.**

**And the seismic dimension:**

> **Anchorage into a joint must develop the bar's full YIELD strength**, because the design relies on the bar **yielding** rather than pulling out.

> **A pull-out failure is brittle and sudden; a yielding bar is ductile and gives warning.** The whole capacity-design philosophy depends on the anchorage being **stronger than the bar.**

> **The companion seismic rule: ties must have 135° hooks**, because a **90° hook opens out the moment the cover spalls** — which is precisely when the tie is needed.

examTip.trick: **4D per 45° of turn, capped at 16D.** So 90° gives 8D and a 180° U-bend gives the **maximum 16D** — and the word "maximum" in the question points straight to it.
examTip.trap: **8D (160 mm) is the 90° bend value.** Remembering "8D" without remembering which bend it belongs to is the standard error in this topic.
examTip.mnemonic: **A bend anchors mainly by BEARING, not bond** — so **minimum bend radii** matter: too tight and the concrete inside crushes and the cover splits. HYSD bars need larger radii still.

questions.stem: The following operations are required for tunnelling in rocky terrain: 1. Removing the foul gases  2. Marking the tunnel profile  3. Setting up and drilling  4. Checking misfire  5. Mucking. The correct sequence is:
questions.solution:
**2, 3, 1, 4, 5** — marking, drilling, removing foul gases, checking misfire, mucking.

> The source gives the sequence explicitly: **2. Marking the tunnel profile → 3. Setting up and drilling → 1. Removing the foul gases → 4. Checking misfire → 5. Mucking.**

**Why the order is what it is** — each step is a precondition for the next:

| Step | Why it comes there |
|---|---|
| **2. MARK the profile** | **You cannot drill until you know where** — the drill pattern is set out on the face |
| **3. Set up and DRILL** | Holes are drilled, charged and **blasted** |
| **1. Remove FOUL GASES** | **Blasting fumes must be cleared before anyone may approach the face** |
| **4. Check MISFIRE** | **Only once the air is safe can anyone go forward to look for unexploded charges** |
| **5. MUCK** | Remove the broken rock, once the face is confirmed safe |

> **The two safety steps — ventilation then misfire check — must come between the blast and any person returning to the face**, and in that order.

> **Ventilating BEFORE checking for misfires is not a preference but a necessity**: no one can safely enter to inspect until the fumes are gone.

**Why a MISFIRE is so dangerous:**

> **An unexploded charge buried in the muck pile can detonate during mucking** — struck by a loader bucket or a hammer.

> **That is why the check precedes mucking**, and why misfires are handled by trained personnel following a strict procedure rather than being dug out.

**The tunnel atmosphere requirements** that step 1 must achieve:

| Gas | Limit |
|---|---|
| **Oxygen** | **NOT LESS than 19.5%** |
| **Carbon dioxide** | Not more than **0.5%** |
| **Hydrogen sulphide** | Not more than **0.001% (10 ppm)** |
| Carbon monoxide | Not more than 50 ppm |

> **Blasting produces CO and CO₂ in quantity**, and **H₂S may be released from the strata itself.**

> **H₂S is the most treacherous**: it smells of rotten eggs at low concentration but **PARALYSES the sense of smell at higher ones** — the warning disappears exactly when the danger becomes lethal. **Hence instrument monitoring, never the nose.**

**The full excavation cycle:**

> **Mark → drill → charge → BLAST → ventilate → check misfire → SCALE → muck → SUPPORT → survey → repeat**

> **SCALING** — knocking down loose rock from the roof and walls — is the other safety step, performed before anyone works beneath.

**What governs the advance rate:**

> **The cycle time is set by the SLOWEST step**, and **MUCK REMOVAL and VENTILATION frequently control it.**

| Constraint | Note |
|---|---|
| **One working face** | Nothing proceeds in parallel |
| **Restricted space** | Single-track haulage |
| **Growing haul distance** | Worsens as the tunnel advances |
| Ventilation time | Fixed by the volume to be cleared |

> **A tunnel's progress is usually a LOGISTICS problem rather than an excavation one** — which is why long tunnels are driven from **multiple faces**, using adits and shafts to multiply the working points.

examTip.trick: Each step **enables** the next: you cannot drill before marking, cannot approach the face before ventilating, cannot check misfires before the air is safe, and must not muck before the misfire check.
examTip.trap: **Ventilating before checking misfires is a necessity, not a preference** — no one can enter to inspect until the fumes clear. Any sequence putting the misfire check first is unsafe as well as wrong.
examTip.mnemonic: **A misfire buried in the muck pile can detonate under a loader bucket** — which is exactly why the check precedes mucking. And **H₂S paralyses the sense of smell**, so monitor by instrument.

questions.stem: The formula for effective interest rate is:
questions.solution:
**i_eff = (1 + i/n)ⁿ − 1**, where **n is the number of compounding periods per year** and **i the nominal annual rate.**

**Where it comes from:**

> **i/n is the rate PER PERIOD**, and compounding it **n times** over the year gives the growth factor **(1 + i/n)ⁿ.**

> **Subtracting 1 converts a growth FACTOR into a RATE** — which is why the −1 is there and why options (a) and (b) fail immediately.

**The check that settles it — take n = 1** (annual compounding, where effective must equal nominal):

| Option | Value at n = 1, i = 0.12 |
|---|---|
| **(d) (1 + 0.12)¹ − 1** | **= 0.12** ✓ |
| (b) (1.12)¹ − 2 | = −0.88 ✗ |
| (c) (1 + 1/1)^{0.12} − 1 | = 0.087 ✗ |
| (a) (2 + 0.12)¹ − 1 | = 1.12 ✗ |

> **Only option (d) reduces correctly**, and the substitution takes a few seconds without recalling anything.

**Worked illustration** — 12% nominal, compounded at different frequencies:

| Compounding | n | Effective rate |
|---|---|---|
| **Annually** | 1 | **12.00%** |
| Semi-annually | 2 | 12.36% |
| **Quarterly** | 4 | **12.55%** |
| Monthly | 12 | 12.68% |
| **Daily** | 365 | **12.75%** |
| **Continuously** | ∞ | **e^{0.12} − 1 = 12.75%** |

> **The effective rate rises with compounding frequency but CONVERGES** — it does not grow without limit. **The continuous limit e^i − 1 is the ceiling**, and daily compounding is already almost there.

> **That convergence is the interesting part**: the difference between daily and continuous compounding is negligible, while the difference between annual and quarterly is material.

**Why it matters:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Comparing loans or investments** with different compounding | The only fair basis |
| **Consumer protection** | Many jurisdictions require the **effective** rate to be disclosed |
| **Project appraisal** | The discount rate must match the cash flow period |

> **A nominal rate is not comparable across different compounding frequencies** — quoting "12%" means different things monthly and annually. **The effective rate is what makes comparison possible.**

**The related distinction:**

| Rate | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **NOMINAL** | The **stated** annual rate, ignoring compounding within the year |
| **EFFECTIVE** | The **actual** annual rate, accounting for compounding |
| **Real** | **Adjusted for INFLATION** |

> **Real rate ≈ nominal rate − inflation rate** (exactly: **(1 + r_real) = (1 + r_nom)/(1 + inflation)**).

> **In project appraisal, a REAL discount rate must be used with REAL (constant-price) cash flows, and a NOMINAL rate with nominal cash flows.**

> **Mixing them is a genuine and common error** — discounting constant-price cash flows at a nominal rate understates the project's value substantially, and the error grows with the project's life.

examTip.trick: **Substitute n = 1** — with annual compounding the effective rate must equal the nominal. Only option (a) gives 0.12 for i = 0.12. A few seconds, no recall needed.
examTip.trap: **The −1 converts a growth FACTOR into a RATE.** Options (b) and (d) break that (−2 and 2 + i/n) and fail on inspection.
examTip.mnemonic: **The effective rate CONVERGES as compounding increases — the ceiling is e^i − 1.** Daily is already almost continuous. And use a **REAL rate with REAL cash flows**, never mixed.

questions.stem: Pick up the correct statement from the following during tunnel excavation:
options: Oxygen should not be less than 19.5%
Carbon dioxide should not be more than 0.5%
Hydrogen sulphide should not be more than 0.001%
questions.solution:
**All of the above** — all three are the standard tunnel atmosphere requirements.

**The limits:**

| Gas | Limit | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **OXYGEN** | **NOT LESS than 19.5%** | Below it, **impaired judgement, then unconsciousness** |
| **Carbon dioxide** | **Not more than 0.5%** | Asphyxiant; causes rapid breathing and headache |
| **Hydrogen sulphide** | **Not more than 0.001% (10 ppm)** | **Highly TOXIC** |
| Carbon monoxide | Not more than 50 ppm | Binds haemoglobin |
| Methane | Below the explosive limit | **Explosive at 5–15%** |

> **Normal air is about 20.9% oxygen**, so **19.5% is only a small reduction** — and the margin is deliberately tight because **oxygen deficiency impairs judgement BEFORE it is noticed.**

> **A person becoming hypoxic does not realise it**, which is why the limit is set so close to normal rather than at the point of obvious distress.

**Why HYDROGEN SULPHIDE is the most treacherous:**

> It smells strongly of **rotten eggs at low concentration** — but **at higher concentrations it PARALYSES the sense of smell.**

> **The warning disappears exactly when the danger becomes lethal.** A worker who notices the smell fading may believe the air has cleared when it has in fact become far more dangerous.

> **That is why H₂S is monitored by INSTRUMENT, never by nose**, and why its limit is expressed in **parts per million** rather than percent.

**Where the gases come from:**

| Gas | Source |
|---|---|
| **Oxygen depletion** | Consumed by workers, engines, **oxidation of rock and timber** |
| **CO and CO₂** | **Blasting fumes**, diesel plant, combustion |
| **H₂S and METHANE** | **Released from the STRATA** — particularly organic-rich or coal-bearing rock |
| Radon | Some geological formations |
| **Silica dust** | Drilling and blasting — **SILICOSIS is a long-term hazard** |

> **Methane and H₂S emerge from the ground itself and CANNOT be predicted from the surface** — which is why **CONTINUOUS monitoring**, not periodic testing, is the requirement.

**VENTILATION is the primary control:**

| System | Note |
|---|---|
| **BLOWING (forcing)** | Fresh air ducted to the face — **clears blasting fumes fastest** |
| **Exhausting** | Foul air drawn out — better for dust during mucking |
| **Reversible** | Blow to clear the face, exhaust during mucking — the usual arrangement |

> **Ventilation frequently CONTROLS the advance rate** of a tunnel, alongside muck removal: **the cycle cannot restart until the face is clear of fumes.**

**The other tunnelling hazards:**

| Hazard | Control |
|---|---|
| **Roof falls** | Prompt support — **rock bolts, shotcrete, mesh (NATM)**; and **SCALING** after each blast |
| **WATER inrush** | **PROBE DRILLING ahead of the face** |
| Squeezing / swelling ground | Flexible support, monitored convergence |
| Fire and explosion | Gas monitoring, non-sparking equipment |
| Dust | Wet drilling, ventilation, respirators |

> **Probe drilling ahead of the face is the single most valuable precaution in uncertain ground** — a water or gas inrush encountered without warning gives no time to react, **and in a tunnel there is only one way out.**

> **That last fact governs tunnel safety generally**: every hazard is magnified by the confinement and the single escape route, which is why the atmospheric limits are set so conservatively.

examTip.trick: Anchor on **normal air being 20.9% oxygen** — the 19.5% limit is a deliberately small reduction, because **hypoxia impairs judgement before it is noticed**.
examTip.trap: **H₂S paralyses the sense of smell at dangerous concentrations** — the warning vanishes exactly when the risk becomes lethal. Monitor by **instrument, never by nose**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Methane and H₂S come from the STRATA and cannot be predicted from the surface** — hence **continuous** monitoring. And **probe drill ahead of the face**: in a tunnel there is one way out.

questions.stem: Formula of shear strength of soil?
questions.solution:
**S = c + σ tan φ** — the **MOHR–COULOMB** failure criterion.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **S (or τ)** | **Shear strength** |
| **c** | **COHESION** — the strength at zero normal stress |
| **σ** | **Normal stress** on the failure plane |
| **φ (θ in the source)** | **Angle of internal FRICTION** |

**The structure of the equation is what makes it memorable:**

> **Shear strength has TWO components: a COHESIVE part independent of stress, and a FRICTIONAL part proportional to it.**

| Component | Depends on σ? | Analogy |
|---|---|---|
| **c — cohesion** | **NO — a constant intercept** | Glue between particles |
| **σ tan φ — friction** | **YES — proportional** | Friction between surfaces |

> **It is the equation of a STRAIGHT LINE**: intercept **c**, slope **tan φ**. **That is the Mohr failure envelope**, and every triaxial test is an exercise in finding those two numbers.

> **Option (a) rearranges it wrongly** (solving for c but keeping S on the right), and **option (d) attaches tan φ to the wrong term** — putting the friction coefficient on the cohesion rather than on the normal stress, which makes no physical sense.

> **Option (b) is not a strength equation at all** — **ki resembles Darcy's law (v = ki)**, a seepage relation.

**The two limiting cases:**

| Soil | Parameters | Strength |
|---|---|---|
| **Pure SAND (cohesionless)** | **c = 0** | **S = σ tan φ** — depends entirely on confinement |
| **Saturated CLAY, undrained** | **φ_u = 0** | **S = c_u** — independent of confinement |

> **A cohesionless soil has NO strength at zero normal stress** — which is why dry sand cannot stand in a vertical cut, and why **σ′ = 0 (the quick condition) means zero strength entirely.**

> **φ_u = 0 is a property of the TEST, not of the clay**: under undrained loading no volume change is possible, so added stress goes **entirely into pore pressure** and **σ′ is unchanged.** The same clay has a real **φ′ of 20–30°** in effective stress terms.

**The critical refinement — EFFECTIVE stress:**

> **S = c′ + σ′ tan φ′**, where **σ′ = σ − u**

> **Strength depends on EFFECTIVE stress alone.** Total stress governs nothing — which is Terzaghi's principle and the foundation of the whole subject.

> **That is why pore pressure measurement matters so much**, and why a **CU triaxial test with pore pressure measurement** is the standard route to c′ and φ′.

**Which parameters to use, and when:**

| Condition | Parameters |
|---|---|
| **Short term** (end of construction) | **c_u, φ_u = 0** — total stress |
| **Long term** | **c′, φ′** — effective stress |

**And which is critical depends on the problem:**

> **EMBANKMENT (loading): the SHORT term is worse** — the clay consolidates afterwards and gains strength.

> **CUTTING (unloading): the LONG term is worse** — pore pressures rise back to equilibrium and the clay softens.

> **Getting that pairing backwards is a genuine design error**, and it is among the most frequently examined points in soil mechanics.

**Typical values:**

| Soil | φ′ |
|---|---|
| Loose sand | 28 – 32° |
| **Dense sand** | **35 – 45°** |
| **Normally consolidated clay** | **20 – 30°** |

examTip.trick: It is the **equation of a straight line**: intercept **c**, slope **tan φ**. Two components — **cohesion independent of stress, friction proportional to it**. Every triaxial test finds those two numbers.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) attaches tan φ to the COHESION rather than the normal stress** — physically meaningless. And option (b) resembles **Darcy's v = ki**, a seepage relation, not a strength one.
examTip.mnemonic: **Strength depends on EFFECTIVE stress alone: S = c′ + σ′tanφ′.** And **embankment → SHORT term critical; CUTTING → LONG term critical** — reversing that pairing is a real design error.

questions.stem: When a train moves on a simply supported beam, the BM is maximum:
questions.solution:
**At (or near) the centre.**

> The source states it: **when a given load system moves from one end to the other of a simply supported beam, there will be a maximum bending moment for every section depending on the position of the load. The maximum of these bending moments will usually occur NEAR OR AT THE MID SPAN. The maximum of maximum bending moments is called the ABSOLUTE MAXIMUM bending moment.**

**The idea being tested — two different maxima:**

| Maximum | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Maximum BM at a GIVEN SECTION** | Found by positioning the load train to make **that section's** moment greatest |
| **ABSOLUTE maximum BM** | **The largest of all those section maxima** — the governing design moment |

> **Every section has its own worst load position**, and the absolute maximum is the largest value obtained across all sections.

> **For a simply supported span it occurs at or near midspan**, because the moment influence line's peak ordinate **ab/L** is greatest when **a = b = L/2**, giving **L/4.**

**Why "near" rather than exactly at the centre:**

> **For a SINGLE point load the absolute maximum is exactly at midspan.**

> **For a TRAIN of loads it is slightly off centre** — it occurs under one particular wheel, positioned so that **the midspan of the beam bisects the distance between that wheel and the resultant of all the loads on the span.**

> **That is the classical rule for absolute maximum moment under a moving load system**, and it explains the source's careful phrase "near or at".

**The influence line framework:**

| Quantity | Influence line for a simply supported span |
|---|---|
| **Reaction at A** | Linear, **1 at A → 0 at B** |
| **Moment at a section** (a from left) | **TRIANGULAR, all positive; peak ab/L** |
| **Shear at a section** | Two parallel lines with a **UNIT STEP** |

**Using them — two rules cover everything:**

| Load | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Point load W** | **W × ORDINATE** at its position |
| **UDL w** | **w × AREA** under the line over the loaded length |

> **Placement: point load → maximum ordinate; UDL → cover the whole region of ONE SIGN.**

**The essential contrast with SHEAR:**

> A **shear** influence line has a **unit step at the section — positive one side, NEGATIVE the other.**

> **Loading both sides therefore partly CANCELS**, so **maximum shear needs one side loaded only** — and the **maximum shear occurs at the SUPPORTS**, not at midspan.

> **Moment peaks at midspan; shear peaks at the supports.** The two design actions occur at different sections, which is the whole logic of beam detailing.

**Why this matters practically:**

> **Bridge design** is precisely this problem: a vehicle or train of axles must be positioned to produce the worst effect **at every section**, and the design envelope is the collection of those maxima.

> **Modern software does the search automatically**, moving the load train through every position — but the underlying concept is exactly what this question asks.

**And for an INDETERMINATE structure** the influence line is a **curve** that statics cannot produce — but **MÜLLER-BRESLAU's principle** gives its shape directly: **release the restraint, impose a unit displacement, and the deflected shape IS the influence line.**

examTip.trick: The moment influence line's peak ordinate is **ab/L**, greatest when **a = b = L/2** — so the **absolute maximum** across all sections falls at or near midspan.
examTip.trap: For a **TRAIN** of loads the absolute maximum is slightly **off centre** — under one wheel, positioned so midspan bisects the distance between that wheel and the **resultant** of the loads on the span.
examTip.mnemonic: **Moment peaks at MIDSPAN; shear peaks at the SUPPORTS.** A shear influence line changes sign at the section, so loading both sides cancels — maximum shear needs one side only.

questions.stem: Wall is considered smooth by ………
questions.solution:
**Rankine's theory.**

> The source lists the assumptions, and two are directly relevant: **"the face of the wall in contact with the backfill is considered VERTICAL AND SMOOTH"** and **"there is NO WALL FRICTION."**

**The full set of Rankine assumptions:**

| Assumption | Note |
|---|---|
| Soil is **homogeneous, isotropic, semi-infinite, elastic, dry and COHESIONLESS** | Valid for sand, **not for clay** |
| Ground surface is **planar** — horizontal or inclined | — |
| **Wall face VERTICAL and SMOOTH** | ← this question |
| Soil is in **plastic equilibrium** | Active or passive state fully mobilised |
| **Rupture surface is PLANAR** | — |
| **NO WALL FRICTION** | ← the same assumption stated again |
| Resultant acts **parallel to the ground surface** | Follows from zero wall friction |

**RANKINE versus COULOMB — the essential comparison:**

| | **RANKINE** | **COULOMB** |
|---|---|---|
| Based on | **Plastic equilibrium of the SOIL MASS** | **Equilibrium of a rigid WEDGE** |
| **Wall friction δ** | **NEGLECTED (zero)** | **INCLUDED** |
| Wall face | Assumed **vertical and smooth** | Any inclination and roughness |
| Result for ACTIVE pressure | **Higher — CONSERVATIVE** | Lower |
| Result for PASSIVE pressure | Lower — conservative | **OVERESTIMATES — dangerous** |

> **Ignoring wall friction OVERESTIMATES the active pressure**, which is **safe** — and that conservatism is why Rankine remains the everyday design method despite being less realistic.

> **But for PASSIVE pressure the position reverses and becomes dangerous**: Coulomb badly **overestimates** passive resistance at high friction angles, because the real failure surface is **curved**, not plane.

**The coefficients:**

> **K_a = (1 − sin φ)/(1 + sin φ) = tan²(45 − φ/2)** and **K_p = 1/K_a**

> **For φ = 30°: K_a = 1/3, K_p = 3** — a **ninefold ratio**, and the commonest examination values.

**And the movement required**, which explains why active is the design case:

| State | Wall movement needed |
|---|---|
| **ACTIVE** | **Very small — about 0.001 H** |
| **PASSIVE** | **Large — 0.02 to 0.05 H** |

> **The active state develops almost immediately**, so it is what a wall actually experiences. **Full passive resistance needs movement so large the structure may be unserviceable before it develops** — which is why passive resistance is discounted or ignored entirely.

**Why the other options are wrong:** **BLIGH's and KHOSLA's theories concern SEEPAGE beneath hydraulic structures**, not earth pressure — Bligh's creep theory and Khosla's potential-flow solution for barrage floors. **"Column theory" is not an earth pressure theory at all.**

examTip.trick: **Rankine NEGLECTS wall friction; Coulomb INCLUDES it.** That single difference generates every other contrast between the two theories.
examTip.trap: **Bligh and Khosla are SEEPAGE theories** for hydraulic structures, not earth pressure. Two of the four options belong to a different subject entirely.
examTip.mnemonic: **Ignoring wall friction is SAFE for active pressure (overestimates) but DANGEROUS for passive** — Coulomb badly overestimates passive resistance because the real failure surface curves.

questions.stem: Rough joint used to join concrete pipes is:
questions.solution:
**Bandage joint.**

> The source defines it: **this joint is mostly used for CONCRETE PIPES. The faces of the pipes at the ends are coated with a mortar and are BUTTED against each other.**

**The pipe joint family, as the source sets it out:**

| Joint | Used for |
|---|---|
| **BANDAGE joint** | **CONCRETE pipes** — ends coated with mortar and butted |
| **SPIGOT and SOCKET** | **CAST IRON pipes of all sizes**, and concrete pipes **below 60 cm diameter**. Filled with **bitumen, lead or sulphur mixed with sand** |
| **COLLAR joint** | **Hydraulic pipes** — pipes under **pressure** |
| **FLUSH joint** | **Sewers passing BELOW CULVERTS** |

> **Each joint suits a particular material, size or service condition** — which is what makes this a genuine four-way match.

**Why the joint type matters at all:**

> **A buried pipeline's joints are its weakest points.** They must accommodate:

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Watertightness** | Against **infiltration IN and exfiltration OUT** |
| **Some flexibility** | Ground movement, settlement, thermal effects |
| **Strength** | Against internal pressure and external load |
| Ease of laying | Field conditions, alignment tolerance |

> **INFILTRATION through defective joints is a serious operational problem in sewerage** — clean groundwater entering the sewer **overloads the treatment works** and can exceed the sewage flow itself in an old system.

> **Exfiltration is worse still**: sewage leaking out contaminates the groundwater, and it is invisible.

**The FLUSH joint's particular purpose:**

> Used **where the sewer passes below a culvert** — that is, where there is **no room for a projecting socket or collar.**

> **A flush joint keeps the external diameter constant**, so the pipe can be threaded through a tight opening. **It is a clearance solution, not a hydraulic one.**

**And the COLLAR joint for pressure pipes:**

> A **separate sleeve** placed over the butted ends and filled — giving a joint that can resist **internal pressure**, which a simple butted or socketed joint cannot.

> **Pressure is what distinguishes it**: a gravity sewer flows with a **free surface** and needs no pressure resistance, while a **rising main from a pumping station runs full and under pressure.**

**Note option (c) is a tautology** — "rough joint" simply restates the question's own words without naming a joint type, which is a tell in itself.

**Sewer materials**, for context:

| Material | Note |
|---|---|
| **Concrete / RCC** | The commonest for large sewers; **vulnerable to CROWN CORROSION** |
| **Stoneware (vitrified clay)** | **Impervious and acid-resistant** — excellent for sewage |
| Cast iron | Pressure mains, exposed lengths |
| PVC, HDPE | Increasingly common; flexible, light |

> **Stoneware's acid resistance matters** because **H₂S from septic sewage becomes SULPHURIC ACID on the moist crown**, destroying concrete sewers from the top down — the failure that ventilation and self-cleansing velocity exist to prevent.

examTip.trick: Each joint suits a **material, size or service condition**: bandage for **concrete**, spigot-and-socket for **cast iron and small concrete**, collar for **pressure**, flush for **tight clearance under a culvert**.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) merely restates the question's own words** without naming a joint type — a tell in itself. And spigot-and-socket does serve concrete pipes, but only **below 60 cm**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Joints are a pipeline's weakest points** — infiltration overloads the treatment works, exfiltration contaminates groundwater invisibly. And **stoneware resists the sulphuric acid** that destroys concrete sewer crowns.

questions.stem: Most accurate method to determine average precipitation:
questions.solution:
