**The isohyetal method.**

> The source describes it: **draw ISOHYETAL LINES (lines connecting points of equal rainfall) on a map; divide the area between these lines into polygons; calculate the average rainfall for each polygon; and determine the overall average by WEIGHTING each polygon's average by its AREA.**

**Why it is the most accurate:**

> **It is the only method that allows the analyst's JUDGEMENT and knowledge of the terrain to enter the interpolation.**

> **Isohyets are not drawn mechanically from the gauge values** — they are drawn taking account of **topography, known orographic effects, storm direction and the shape of the catchment.**

> **That is precisely what the other methods cannot do**, and it is why the isohyetal method is superior in mountainous terrain.

**The three methods compared:**

| Method | Basis | Suits |
|---|---|---|
| **ARITHMETIC average** | Simple mean of the gauges | **Flat terrain, EVENLY distributed gauges, small variation** |
| **THIESSEN polygon** | Each gauge weighted by its **AREA OF INFLUENCE** (perpendicular bisectors) | **Non-uniform gauge spacing**; assumes rainfall is uniform near each gauge |
| **ISOHYETAL** | **Contours of equal rainfall, drawn with judgement** | **MOUNTAINOUS terrain; the most accurate** |

**The decisive weakness of the Thiessen method:**

> **Thiessen polygons are PURELY GEOMETRIC — they take NO account of ELEVATION.**

> **In a mountainous catchment that is a serious defect**: the method can assign a valley gauge's low rainfall to a high ridge that actually receives several times as much, simply because the ridge falls inside that gauge's polygon.

> **The polygons are drawn on a plan; the rainfall varies with height.** The method cannot connect the two.

**Why this matters acutely in Nepal:**

> **Rainfall is dominated by OROGRAPHIC effects** — monsoon air forced up the Himalayan front.

| Location | Annual rainfall |
|---|---|
| **Lumle / Pokhara (windward)** | **Over 5000 mm** |
| **Manang, Mustang (RAIN SHADOW)** | **A few hundred mm** |

> **Those two are only tens of kilometres apart.** No purely geometric interpolation can represent such a gradient — **only isohyets drawn with knowledge of the terrain can.**

> **That extreme spatial variability is also why gauge network density matters so much**: WMO guidance suggests about **1 gauge per 250 km² in flat regions but 1 per 100 km² or denser in mountainous areas.**

**And the check on the records themselves:**

> The **DOUBLE MASS CURVE** — plotting one gauge's cumulative rainfall against the cumulative mean of surrounding gauges.

> **A CHANGE IN SLOPE reveals an inconsistency** — a gauge moved, a building erected nearby, an instrument changed — and the record can then be corrected before any averaging is attempted.

> **Averaging inconsistent records accurately is still averaging the wrong numbers**, which is why the consistency check precedes the choice of method.

examTip.trick: **Only the isohyetal method lets JUDGEMENT and terrain knowledge into the interpolation** — the contours are drawn accounting for topography, which no mechanical method can do.
examTip.trap: **THIESSEN polygons are purely GEOMETRIC and ignore ELEVATION entirely** — in mountains they can assign a valley gauge's rainfall to a high ridge receiving several times as much.
examTip.mnemonic: **Nepal is orographic: 5000 mm at Pokhara, a few hundred in Mustang's rain shadow, tens of kilometres apart.** No geometric method survives that gradient — and check records with a **DOUBLE MASS CURVE** first.

questions.stem: Cold frontal precipitation is formed due to:
options: When an advancing cold air mass meets warmer air; cold fronts move faster than warm fronts
When a large mass of air is forced to rise across landform barriers, such as high mountain ranges, plateaus and hills

Heating of the ground surface: the air warms, expands and is forced to rise to a great height, being replaced by colder air; as the air rises it cools, becomes saturated, condenses and clouds form, and by further cooling precipitation takes place
questions.solution:
**When an advancing cold air mass meets warmer air.**

> The source explains the mechanism: **cold fronts form when a mass of COLD air ADVANCES and DISPLACES a warmer air mass. This occurs due to differences in air DENSITY, with the DENSER COLD AIR PUSHING UNDERNEATH the warmer air. As the cold mass moves forward it LIFTS the warm air, creating a boundary known as a front.**

**Why the cold air goes underneath:**

> **Cold air is DENSER.** It behaves as a wedge, forcing itself beneath the warm air and lifting it — and **it is that forced lifting which produces the precipitation.**

> **All precipitation requires air to be LIFTED, cooled and its moisture condensed.** The types differ only in **what does the lifting.**

**The three mechanisms:**

| Type | Lifted by | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **CYCLONIC / FRONTAL** | **PRESSURE difference / air mass movement** | Widespread |
| **OROGRAPHIC** | **MOUNTAIN barrier** — option (b) | Heavy windward, **rain shadow** to lee |
| **CONVECTIVE** | **HEATING of the ground** — option (c) | **Localised, brief, VERY INTENSE** |

> **Options (b) and (c) are accurate descriptions of the OTHER two types** — which is what makes this a clean three-way discrimination rather than a guess.

**COLD front versus WARM front** — the distinction the question turns on:

| | **COLD front** | **WARM front** |
|---|---|---|
| Advancing air | **COLD, pushing UNDER** | **WARM, riding OVER** |
| Frontal slope | **STEEP** | **Gentle** |
| Lifting | **Rapid and violent** | Gradual |
| Cloud | **CUMULONIMBUS — towering** | Stratiform, layered |
| Precipitation | **SHORT, INTENSE, showery; thunderstorms** | **Prolonged, light to moderate, widespread** |
| Speed | **FASTER** — as the question notes | Slower |

> **The steep frontal slope is what makes a cold front violent**: the warm air is lifted rapidly rather than gliding gently upward, producing deep convective cloud and heavy showers.

> **A warm front's gentle slope produces the opposite** — hours of steady light rain from layered cloud.

> **And because cold fronts move faster, a cold front can OVERTAKE a warm one, forming an OCCLUDED front** — which is why the question's phrase about relative speed is part of the definition rather than an aside.

**Why the distinction matters hydrologically:**

| Precipitation type | Design consequence |
|---|---|
| **CONVECTIVE / cold frontal** | **High intensity, short duration** — governs **urban drainage and small catchments** |
| **Warm frontal / cyclonic** | **Long duration, moderate intensity** — governs **large catchment floods** |
| **OROGRAPHIC** | Sustained heavy rainfall — dominates **Nepal's monsoon** |

> **A small urban catchment has a short time of concentration and is worst hit by a brief intense storm; a large river basin needs prolonged rainfall over its whole area to flood.**

> **That is why the design storm duration is taken EQUAL TO THE TIME OF CONCENTRATION** — the duration at which the whole catchment contributes simultaneously and the peak is greatest.

**For Nepal specifically:** **OROGRAPHIC precipitation dominates**, with about **80% of annual rainfall in the four monsoon months** — a distribution that is the country's central water resources problem, and the whole argument for storage.

examTip.trick: **All precipitation needs air LIFTED** — the types differ only in what lifts it. Here **denser COLD air wedges UNDER the warm air** and lifts it. Options (b) and (c) describe orographic and convective lifting.
examTip.trap: **Options (b) and (c) are accurate descriptions of the OTHER two types** — a clean three-way discrimination, not a guess. Match the mechanism to the name.
examTip.mnemonic: **A cold front's STEEP slope lifts air violently — cumulonimbus, short intense showers. A warm front's gentle slope gives prolonged light rain.** And cold fronts move faster, so they can **occlude** a warm one.

questions.stem: What property of water makes it spherical?
questions.solution:
**Surface tension.**

> The source states it: **the surface tension of water provides the necessary WALL TENSION for the formation of bubbles with water. The tendency to MINIMISE that wall tension pulls the bubbles into SPHERICAL shapes.**

**The underlying principle:**

> **Surface tension arises because molecules at the surface have fewer neighbours than those in the bulk**, so the liquid behaves as though its surface were an elastic membrane under tension.

> **A system under tension minimises its ENERGY by minimising its AREA** — and **for a given VOLUME, the SPHERE is the shape with the LEAST surface area.**

> **That is the whole explanation**, and it is why raindrops, bubbles and droplets of mercury all take the same form.

**Surface tension of water:**

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **σ at 20 °C** | **0.073 N/m** |
| Units | **Force per unit LENGTH (N/m)**, or energy per unit area (J/m²) |
| With rising temperature | **DECREASES** |

> **The two unit forms are equivalent** — N/m and J/m² are dimensionally identical, which reflects the two ways of thinking about it: a **force pulling the surface together**, or an **energy cost per unit of surface created.**

**Where surface tension matters in civil engineering:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **CAPILLARY RISE** | **h = 4σcosθ/(γd)**, so **h ∝ 1/d** |
| **Apparent cohesion in moist sand** | Menisci bind the grains — the sandcastle effect |
| **Frost heave** | Capillary feeding of ice lenses — **SILT is worst affected** |
| Droplet formation | Sprinklers, spray |
| Manometer correction | Why tubes are specified at **≥ 6 mm bore** |

> **Apparent cohesion is the practically dangerous one**: **moist sand stands in a vertical cut because of the menisci between its grains — and that cohesion VANISHES the moment it is saturated or completely dried.**

> **That is why trench collapses in sand so often follow rain**, or the drying of a previously damp face.

**And why SILT is the most frost-susceptible soil:**

> It has **both a large capillary rise (1–10 m) AND enough permeability to feed water quickly to a growing ice lens.**

> **Clay has the rise but is too impermeable; sand is permeable but has too little rise.** Silt has both, which is why it heaves.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Viscosity** | Resistance to **shear** — governs flow rate, not shape |
| **Pressure** | Acts equally in all directions in a static fluid; does not create a surface |
| **CAVITATION** | **Vapour bubbles forming when pressure falls to the VAPOUR PRESSURE** — a destructive phenomenon, not a shape-determining property |

> **Cavitation is the most interesting distractor** because it does involve bubbles — but it explains **why bubbles FORM**, not **why they are SPHERICAL.** The shape is surface tension's doing in either case.

**Contact angle** determines the direction of capillary action:

| Liquid on glass | θ | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **Water** | **≈ 0° — wetting** | **RISES**; concave meniscus |
| **Mercury** | **≈ 130° — non-wetting** | **DEPRESSES**; convex meniscus |

> **cos 130° is negative**, so the formula returns a negative rise — a depression. **Mercury's cohesion exceeds its adhesion to glass.**

examTip.trick: **A surface under tension minimises its AREA, and for a given VOLUME the SPHERE has the least area.** That single geometric fact explains raindrops, bubbles and mercury droplets alike.
examTip.trap: **CAVITATION involves bubbles too** — but it explains why bubbles **FORM** (pressure falling to vapour pressure), not why they are **spherical**. The shape is surface tension's doing either way.
examTip.mnemonic: **h = 4σcosθ/(γd), so h ∝ 1/d.** Moist sand stands by **apparent cohesion** from its menisci — which **vanishes on saturation or full drying**, and is why trenches collapse after rain.

questions.stem: In which type of parking can the maximum number of vehicles be parked?
questions.solution:
**Perpendicular (90°) parking.**

> The source ranks them: **perpendicular parking MAXIMISES space efficiency — vehicles are parked perpendicular to the curb, allowing multiple vehicles side by side. 45-degree parking is more efficient than 75-degree but LESS SO than perpendicular. 75-degree requires MORE space per vehicle. Parallel parking accommodates ONE vehicle per space.**

**The efficiency ranking:**

| Type | Vehicles per unit kerb length | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **90° (perpendicular)** | **MOST** | Each vehicle occupies only its own **width** along the kerb |
| 60° | High | — |
| 45° | Moderate | Easier to enter than 90° |
| 30° | Lower | Easiest to enter |
| **PARALLEL** | **FEWEST** | Each vehicle occupies its own **LENGTH** along the kerb |

> **The principle is simple: the more nearly perpendicular the vehicle, the less kerb length it consumes.**

> **At 90° a car uses about 2.5 m of kerb (its width); parked parallel it uses about 6 m (its length plus manoeuvring space).** That is the whole difference — roughly **2.4 times more vehicles.**

**But the trade-off is real, and it runs the other way:**

| Angle | Kerb efficiency | **AISLE width needed** | Ease of manoeuvre |
|---|---|---|---|
| **90°** | **Best** | **WIDEST (~6 m)** | **Hardest — reversing required** |
| 45° | Moderate | Narrower | Easier |
| **Parallel** | **Worst** | **NARROWEST** | Hardest in traffic, but needs least width |

> **Perpendicular parking packs the most vehicles against the kerb but demands the widest aisle to manoeuvre in and out.**

> **So the best choice depends on the TOTAL area available, not the kerb length alone** — which is why angle parking at 45° or 60° is often chosen for a constrained site despite being less efficient per metre of kerb.

**Why PARALLEL parking survives despite being least efficient:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Needs the least ROAD WIDTH** | The vehicle sits within the kerb lane |
| **Least interference with through traffic** | A vehicle leaving moves parallel to the flow |
| Safest on a busy street | No reversing into moving traffic |

> **On a narrow urban street parallel parking is often the ONLY option**, and its inefficiency is the price of not obstructing the carriageway.

**The wider traffic engineering context:**

| Parking type | Note |
|---|---|
| **On-street** | Cheap but **reduces carriageway capacity** |
| **Off-street** | Surface lots, multi-storey, underground |

> **On-street parking consumes road capacity twice over** — the lane it occupies, and the disruption from vehicles entering and leaving.

> **Parking surveys** measure **accumulation** (vehicles present over time), **duration**, **turnover** (vehicles per space per day) and **parking index** (occupancy as a percentage of capacity).

> **High TURNOVER is desirable in a commercial area** — many short stays serve more people than a few all-day parkers, which is the entire rationale for time limits and metered charging.

examTip.trick: **The more perpendicular the vehicle, the less KERB LENGTH it consumes** — about 2.5 m (its width) at 90° against 6 m (its length) parallel. Roughly **2.4 times more vehicles**.
examTip.trap: **Perpendicular parking needs the WIDEST AISLE** to manoeuvre in and out — so the best choice depends on **total area**, not kerb length alone. Angle parking often wins on a constrained site.
examTip.mnemonic: **Parallel parking survives because it needs the least ROAD WIDTH** and least disturbs through traffic. And in commercial areas **high TURNOVER beats high capacity** — the rationale for time limits.

questions.stem: Future sum of present investing is called:
questions.solution:
**Compounding.**

> The source gives both directions: **finding the FUTURE SUM of a present investment is called COMPOUNDING; finding the PRESENT VALUE of a future cash flow is called DISCOUNTING.**

**The two directions of the same relationship:**

| Direction | Name | Formula |
|---|---|---|
| **PRESENT → FUTURE** | **COMPOUNDING** | **F = P(1 + i)ⁿ** |
| **FUTURE → PRESENT** | **DISCOUNTING** | **P = F/(1 + i)ⁿ** |

> **They are exact inverses** — the same equation solved for different unknowns, and the factors are reciprocals of each other.

> **Option (b), discounting, is therefore not merely wrong but precisely the opposite operation**, which is why it is the natural distractor.

**Why the distinction matters so much in engineering economics:**

> **Money has a TIME VALUE**: a rupee today is worth more than a rupee next year, because it can be invested in the meantime.

> **Cash flows occurring at different times CANNOT be compared or added directly.** They must first be brought to a common point in time — usually the present.

> **That is the entire basis of project appraisal.** NPV, IRR and the benefit–cost ratio all depend on discounting future flows to the present before any comparison is made.

**The standard compound interest factors:**

| Factor | Expression | Converts |
|---|---|---|
| **Single payment compound amount** | **(1 + i)ⁿ** | **P → F** |
| **Single payment present worth** | **1/(1 + i)ⁿ** | **F → P** |
| Uniform series compound amount | **[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]/i** | A → F |
| **SINKING FUND** | **i/[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]** | F → A |
| **Capital recovery** | **i(1 + i)ⁿ/[(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]** | P → A |
| Uniform series present worth | [(1 + i)ⁿ − 1]/[i(1 + i)ⁿ] | A → P |

> **Each is the RECIPROCAL of another**, so the six factors are really three pairs — and **the bracketed [(1 + i)ⁿ − 1] appears in four of them.**

**The power of compounding:**

> **F = P(1 + i)ⁿ is EXPONENTIAL in n**, which produces results that surprise:

| At 10% | Multiplier |
|---|---|
| 10 years | 2.6 × |
| 20 years | 6.7 × |
| **30 years** | **17.4 ×** |
| 50 years | 117 × |

> **The "rule of 72": money doubles in approximately 72/i years** — at 10%, about 7.2 years.

**And the same exponential works in reverse, which is the more consequential direction for infrastructure:**

> **Discounting shrinks distant benefits toward nothing.** At 12%, a benefit **50 years away is worth about 0.3% of its face value.**

> **That is why a HIGH discount rate makes long-lived infrastructure look poor** — a dam delivering benefits for a century is judged almost entirely on its first two decades.

> **The choice of discount rate for public projects is therefore genuinely contested**, and it often determines the answer more than any engineering input does. **Sensitivity analysis on it is essential.**

examTip.trick: **Compounding goes PRESENT → FUTURE; discounting goes FUTURE → PRESENT.** They are exact inverses, and the factors are reciprocals — so only one of each pair need be remembered.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is precisely the opposite operation**, which is what makes it the natural wrong answer. Fix the direction before anything else.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rule of 72: money doubles in about 72/i years.** And the same exponential in reverse means a benefit **50 years out is worth 0.3% at 12%** — which is why the discount rate decides infrastructure appraisals.

questions.stem: Expulsion of pore water from soil is called:
questions.solution:
**Consolidation.**

> The source states both halves of the pair: **expulsion of PORE WATER from soil is called CONSOLIDATION; expulsion of AIR from soil is called COMPACTION.**

**The distinction in full:**

| | **CONSOLIDATION** | **COMPACTION** |
|---|---|---|
| **Expels** | **WATER** | **AIR** |
| Applies to | **Fully SATURATED** soil | **Partially saturated** soil |
| Cause | **Sustained LOAD** | **MECHANICAL energy** — rolling, ramming, vibration |
| **Time** | **TIME-DEPENDENT — years** | **INSTANTANEOUS** |
| Nature | **NATURAL** — a response to loading | **ARTIFICIAL** — an engineering operation |
| Test | **OEDOMETER** | **PROCTOR** |

> **Compaction expels AIR in minutes by machine; consolidation expels WATER over years under load.** Those two sentences separate them completely, and the pair is examined in almost every paper.

**Why consolidation takes so long:**

> **Water must physically FLOW OUT of the soil**, and clay's permeability is extremely low — **below 10⁻⁹ m/s.**

> **The time depends on the DRAINAGE PATH LENGTH squared:**

> **t = T_v d²/c_v**

> **Doubling the layer thickness QUADRUPLES the time** — which is why thick clay layers settle for decades.

**And why VERTICAL DRAINS work:**

> **They do not change the total settlement at all** — they shorten the **drainage path**, converting long vertical drainage into short horizontal drainage.

> **Since t ∝ d², halving the path quarters the time.** A preload that would take twenty years can be completed in one or two.

> **That is the whole point of ground improvement by preloading with drains**: it does not reduce settlement, it **gets it over with before construction.**

**The three stages of consolidation:**

| Stage | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Immediate** | Expulsion of **air** and lateral distortion, if partly saturated |
| **PRIMARY** | **Expulsion of pore water** — the main settlement, governed by **c_v** |
| **SECONDARY (creep)** | **Gradual readjustment of clay particles** into a more stable configuration |

> **Secondary consolidation continues AFTER all excess pore pressure has dissipated** — so it cannot be predicted from pore pressure at all, and it **dominates the long-term settlement of ORGANIC soils and PEAT.**

**The parameters, and the question each answers:**

| Parameter | Question |
|---|---|
| **C_c, m_v** | **HOW MUCH** settlement |
| **c_v** | **HOW FAST** |
| **σ′_c** | Whether the clay is **normally or over-consolidated** |

> **A clay may be highly compressible yet drain quickly, or barely compressible yet take decades.** Keeping those two questions apart is the organising idea of the whole subject.

**Why option (d), "densification", is a reasonable-sounding trap:**

> **Both processes densify the soil** — that is their shared outcome. **But "densification" names the RESULT, not the MECHANISM**, and it does not distinguish which fluid is expelled.

> **The question asks specifically about pore WATER**, which identifies consolidation uniquely.

examTip.trick: **Compaction expels AIR in minutes by MACHINE; consolidation expels WATER over years under LOAD.** Two sentences separate them completely.
examTip.trap: **"Densification" names the RESULT, not the mechanism** — both processes densify the soil. The question specifies pore **WATER**, which identifies consolidation uniquely.
examTip.mnemonic: **t ∝ d², so halving the drainage path QUARTERS the time** — which is why **vertical drains** work. They do not reduce settlement; they get it over with before construction.

questions.stem: Bitumen is extracted from:
questions.solution:
**Petroleum products.**

> The source states it: **it is extracted from the FRACTIONAL DISTILLATION of crude oil — that is, petroleum products.**

**Where bitumen sits in the refining process:**

> **Crude oil is separated by fractional distillation into fractions of increasing boiling point:**

| Fraction | Boiling range |
|---|---|
| Gases, petrol (gasoline) | Lightest |
| Kerosene, diesel | Middle distillates |
| Lubricating oils | Heavy |
| **BITUMEN (residue)** | **The HEAVIEST — what remains at the bottom** |

> **Bitumen is the RESIDUE — the fraction that does not distil off.** That is why it is sometimes called "residual bitumen" or "straight-run bitumen".

> **Being the residue explains its properties**: it is composed of the largest, heaviest hydrocarbon molecules, which is why it is **semi-solid, viscous, thermoplastic and effectively involatile.**

**The important distinction — BITUMEN versus TAR:**

| | **BITUMEN** | **TAR** |
|---|---|---|
| **Source** | **PETROLEUM (crude oil)** | **Destructive distillation of COAL or wood** |
| Temperature susceptibility | Less | **More — hardens and cracks in cold** |
| Durability | Better | Poorer |
| **Health** | — | **CARCINOGENIC — largely banned for road use** |

> **The two are constantly confused, and they come from entirely different raw materials.** Tar has been largely abandoned for road work on both durability and health grounds.

**And ASPHALT is a third term worth pinning down:**

> **In British usage, ASPHALT means bitumen MIXED WITH AGGREGATE** — the finished paving material. **In American usage "asphalt" often means the binder itself.**

> **Natural asphalt** also occurs — as in the Trinidad Lake deposit — but nearly all bitumen used today is refinery-produced.

**The bitumen products family:**

| Product | Composition | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Paving grade bitumen** | Straight-run, graded by **penetration** (60/70, 80/100) | **Road pavement** |
| **CUTBACK** | Bitumen + **volatile SOLVENT** | Prime and tack coats; cold weather |
| **EMULSION** | Bitumen droplets **dispersed in WATER** | Cold application; **works on a DAMP surface** |
| **Blown (oxidised)** | Air blown through hot bitumen | Roofing, waterproofing |
| **Plastic bitumen** | Bitumen + thinner + **40–45% filler** | **Crack filling** |

> **Emulsions have largely displaced cutbacks** on environmental and safety grounds: a cutback releases its solvent into the atmosphere and is a fire risk, while an emulsion releases only water — **and it can be applied to a damp surface, which matters greatly in a monsoon climate.**

**The specification tests:** **penetration** (hardness, in tenths of a millimetre), **softening point** (ring and ball), **ductility (≥ 50 cm)**, flash and fire point, viscosity, **water content (≤ 0.2%)**, and **stripping value (retention > 95%)**.

> **No single test characterises bitumen** — a binder can pass penetration and still be unsuitable, which is why the specification lists them all.

examTip.trick: **Bitumen is the RESIDUE of crude oil distillation** — the heaviest fraction that does not distil off. That explains its properties: large molecules, semi-solid, thermoplastic, involatile.
examTip.trap: **BITUMEN comes from PETROLEUM; TAR from destructive distillation of COAL.** Entirely different raw materials, constantly confused — and tar is **carcinogenic and largely banned** for road use.
examTip.mnemonic: **EMULSIONS have displaced CUTBACKS** — water instead of solvent, no fire risk, and they work on a **damp surface**, which matters in a monsoon climate.

questions.stem: Moment of inertia through the centroid of a triangle parallel to the base is:
questions.solution:
**bd³/36.**

> The source gives the pair directly: **I_xx = bd³/36 (about the centroid) and I_base = bd³/12.**

**The three triangle values:**

| Axis | Distance from centroid | Second moment |
|---|---|---|
| **CENTROIDAL** (parallel to base) | 0 | **bd³/36** |
| **BASE** | **d/3** | **bd³/12** |
| **APEX (top)** | **2d/3** | **bd³/4** |

> **The denominators run 36, 12, 4**, and the ratios to the centroidal value are **1 : 3 : 9** — matching the **squares** of the distances (0, d/3, 2d/3).

> **That pattern is worth carrying**, because it converts three separate facts into one relation.

**Verification by the parallel axis theorem:**

> **I_base = I_c + A d² = bd³/36 + (½bd)(d/3)² = bd³/36 + bd³/18 = 3bd³/36 = bd³/12** ✓

> **The check takes ten seconds and removes any doubt about which value belongs to which axis.**

**The DIMENSIONAL check kills option (b) instantly:**

> **A second moment of area has dimensions of LENGTH⁴** — and **bd³ is already L⁴** (one length × one length cubed).

> **bd⁴ is L⁵** — dimensionally impossible, whatever the coefficient. **That eliminates option (b) with no recall at all.**

**Options (a) and (d) borrow from the rectangle:**

| Expression | Where it actually belongs |
|---|---|
| **bd³/3** | **RECTANGLE about its BASE** |
| **bd³/6** | Not a standard value; resembles the **section modulus bh²/6** |

> **And note the coincidence that traps candidates: bd³/12 is the RECTANGLE's CENTROIDAL value AND the TRIANGLE's BASE value.** The same expression means different things for different shapes.

**Standard second moments:**

| Shape | About the centroid | About the base |
|---|---|---|
| **Rectangle b × h** | **bh³/12** | **bh³/3** |
| **Triangle b × d** | **bd³/36** | **bd³/12** |
| **Circle diameter d** | **πd⁴/64** | — |
| **Semicircle** | **0.11 R⁴** | **πR⁴/8** |

**The parallel axis theorem and its consequence:**

> **I = I_centroid + A d²** — the added term is **ALWAYS positive.**

> **Therefore the CENTROIDAL axis always gives the MINIMUM second moment.** A computed value smaller than the centroidal one is arithmetically impossible — a useful self-check.

**Where these values are used:**

| Application | Relation |
|---|---|
| **Bending stress** | **σ = My/I** |
| **Section modulus** | **Z = I/y_max** |
| **Deflection** | **δ ∝ 1/EI** |
| **BUCKLING** | **P_cr = π²EI/L_e²**, using the **MINIMUM I** |

> **For buckling always take the LEAST second moment** — a column buckles about its **weak axis**, and using the strong-axis value is a serious error.

examTip.trick: **Dimensional check kills option (b) instantly** — a second moment is **L⁴**, and **bd³ is already L⁴** while **bd⁴ is L⁵**. No recall needed.
examTip.trap: **bd³/12 is the RECTANGLE's CENTROIDAL value AND the TRIANGLE's BASE value** — the same expression with two meanings. And **bd³/3** belongs to the rectangle about its base.
examTip.mnemonic: **Triangle: 36 centroid, 12 base, 4 apex** — ratios **1 : 3 : 9**, matching the squares of the distances (0, d/3, 2d/3). And **I = I_c + Ad² always ADDS**, so the centroidal value is the minimum.

questions.stem: Which of the following is not affected by chlorination?
questions.solution:
**Dissolved oxygen.**

> The source states it: **dissolved oxygen is NOT affected by chlorination. It is the amount of oxygen available to living aquatic plants and animals.**

**Why chlorination leaves DO unchanged:**

> **Chlorine's disinfecting action is on MICRO-ORGANISMS and reduced substances — not on dissolved oxygen.**

> **Chlorine does not react with O₂**, and it neither adds nor removes it from solution. **The two are chemically independent.**

> **What chlorine DOES consume is the CHLORINE DEMAND** — organic matter, ammonia, iron, manganese and hydrogen sulphide — all of which reduce the chlorine itself, not the oxygen.

**What chlorination DOES affect** — the other three options:

| Affected | How |
|---|---|
| **Dissolved bacteria** | **Killed — the entire purpose of chlorination** |
| **Dissolved CO₂** | Altered — hypochlorite raises pH, chlorine gas lowers it, shifting the carbonate equilibrium |
| **Initial oxygen demand** | **Reduced** — chlorine oxidises some of the demanding substances |

**The disinfection chemistry:**

> **Chlorine in water forms HOCl and OCl⁻:**

> **HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻**

| Species | Disinfecting power |
|---|---|
| **HOCl** | **Strong — about 80× more effective** |
| **OCl⁻** | Much weaker |

> **Raising the pH shifts the balance toward the weak OCl⁻**, so far more chlorine is needed for the same kill.

> **Hence the operating rule: chlorinate BELOW pH 7.5 where possible.**

> **And note the two agents pull the pH in opposite directions**: **bleaching powder (calcium hypochlorite) RAISES pH**, while **chlorine GAS LOWERS it** by forming HCl as well as HOCl.

**BREAKPOINT chlorination** — the concept that ties the demand together:

> As chlorine is added, it is **first consumed by the demand**; then it forms **CHLORAMINES with ammonia**; those are then **destroyed**; and only **beyond the BREAKPOINT does FREE residual chlorine appear.**

| Residual | Character |
|---|---|
| **COMBINED (chloramines)** | **Weaker but LONGER-LASTING** — persists through the network |
| **FREE (HOCl/OCl⁻)** | **Stronger but decays faster** |

> **The dose must exceed the breakpoint to leave a free residual**, which is why under-dosing can leave water *less* safe than a higher dose would — the chlorine is all consumed by the demand.

**The requirements for effective chlorination:**

| Factor | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Contact time** | At least **30 minutes** |
| **Residual** | **0.1 – 0.2 mg/l** free chlorine |
| **TURBIDITY** | **Must be LOW — particles SHIELD pathogens from the chlorine** |
| pH | Below 7.5 preferably |

> **Turbidity is the decisive one**: **chlorination of turbid water does not work reliably however large the dose**, because micro-organisms hide inside suspended particles. **Hence: clarify FIRST, disinfect LAST.**

**And the drawback worth knowing:** chlorine reacting with natural organic matter forms **TRIHALOMETHANES (THMs)**, which are themselves regulated — so the dose balances adequate residual against by-product formation.

examTip.trick: **Chlorine acts on micro-organisms and reduced substances — not on O₂.** The two are chemically independent, so DO passes through chlorination unchanged.
examTip.trap: Read the **NOT**. The other three are all genuinely affected — bacteria killed, CO₂ shifted by the pH change, oxygen demand reduced by oxidation.
examTip.mnemonic: **HOCl is ~80× stronger than OCl⁻, so chlorinate below pH 7.5.** And **turbidity SHIELDS pathogens** — clarify first, disinfect last, however large the dose.

questions.stem: Tensile strength of concrete is about:
questions.solution:
**About 10% of the compressive strength.**

> The source states it in the context of concrete's properties: **the major drawback of concrete is that it cannot resist significant tension. THE TENSILE STRENGTH OF CONCRETE IS ABOUT 10% OF ITS COMPRESSIVE STRENGTH. Thus the use of PLAIN concrete is limited to places where tensile stresses never develop — for example pedestals and mass concreting in dams.**

**The single most important fact about concrete as a material:**

> **It is strong in compression and very weak in tension** — and that asymmetry is the entire reason reinforcement exists.

> **Steel is placed exactly where the tension is**, and the composite works because the two materials have **almost identical coefficients of thermal expansion (≈ 12 × 10⁻⁶/°C)**, so they move together.

**The related IS 456 relations:**

| Property | Relation |
|---|---|
| **Flexural strength (modulus of rupture)** | **f_cr = 0.7√f_ck** |
| **Modulus of elasticity** | **E_c = 5000√f_ck** |
| Split tensile strength | ≈ 0.66 f_cr |
| Direct tensile strength | Lowest of the three |

> **Check for M25: f_cr = 0.7√25 = 3.5 MPa against f_ck = 25** — that is **14%**, and the direct tensile strength is lower still, giving the **~10%** figure.

> **Both main relations go as √f_ck** — flexural with 0.7 and elastic modulus with 5000. **Confusing the two coefficients is the commonest error in the topic.**

**Why the square root matters:**

> **Because strength enters as a SQUARE ROOT, doubling the compressive strength raises the tensile strength by only about 40%.**

> **Concrete's tensile weakness cannot be engineered away by using a richer mix.** That is why the answer is reinforcement rather than higher grade.

**Why three different "tensile" strengths exist:**

| Test | Gives |
|---|---|
| **Flexural (modulus of rupture)** — third-point loading | **HIGHEST** — assumes a linear stress block that does not really exist |
| **Split cylinder (Brazilian)** | Intermediate; the usual practical test |
| **Direct tension** | **LOWEST** and hardest to perform |

> **Each is measured differently and gives a different number**, which is why the code specifies which one applies to which calculation.

**The design consequence:**

> **Reinforced concrete design ASSUMES the concrete is CRACKED in tension and that the steel carries all of it.**

> **The design question is therefore not whether it cracks, but whether the CRACK WIDTH stays within limits** — **0.3 mm** normally, **0.2 mm** in aggressive exposure.

> **That is a genuinely different mental model from steel design**, and it is why minimum reinforcement, cover and crack control provisions matter so much.

**Where f_cr is the governing strength:**

> **In a RIGID PAVEMENT.** The slab bridges over the subgrade in **bending**, so **flexural strength — not compressive strength — is the design parameter** (Westergaard's analysis).

> **It also fixes the CRACKING MOMENT M_cr = f_cr I_gr/y_t**, which governs deflection calculations and the minimum reinforcement requirement.

examTip.trick: **~10% tensile is the single most important fact about concrete** — it is the entire reason reinforcement exists, and why plain concrete is limited to places where tension never develops.
examTip.trap: **Two IS 456 relations both go as √f_ck: f_cr = 0.7√f_ck and E_c = 5000√f_ck.** Confusing the coefficients is the commonest error in the topic.
examTip.mnemonic: **Because strength enters as a SQUARE ROOT, doubling f_ck raises tensile strength only ~40%** — it cannot be engineered away with a richer mix. RC design **assumes cracking** and controls **crack WIDTH** (0.3 mm).

questions.stem: Tensile strength of reinforcement in RCC is reduced by:
options: 15% as FOS for limit state method for steel is 1.15, design strength is σ/1.15
25% as FOS for limit state method for steel is 1.15, design strength is σ/1.15
35% as FOS for limit state method for steel is 1.15, design strength is σ/1.15
15% as FOS for limit state method for steel is 1.15, design strength is σ/2.25
questions.solution:
**15%, because the partial safety factor for steel is 1.15 and the design strength is σ/1.15.**

**Working:**

> **Design strength = f_y/1.15 = 0.87 f_y**
>
> **So the strength is reduced to 87% of characteristic — a reduction of about 13%**, which the source rounds to **15%** in describing the factor of 1.15.

> **The 0.87 f_y is the number that appears in every reinforced concrete calculation**, and it comes directly from **1/1.15.**

**Reading the options carefully:**

| Option | Percentage | Divisor | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **(a)** | **15%** | **1.15** | **✓ Consistent** |
| (b) | 25% | 1.15 | **Inconsistent** — 1.15 does not give 25% |
| (c) | 35% | 1.15 | Inconsistent |
| (d) | 15% | **2.25** | **Percentage right, divisor WRONG** |

> **Options (b) and (c) state a percentage that contradicts the divisor they themselves quote**, and **(d) keeps the right percentage but corrupts the divisor.**

> **Only (a) is internally consistent** — which means the question can be answered by checking each option against itself, without recalling the code.

**The two material partial safety factors:**

| Material | γ_m | Design strength |
|---|---|---|
| **Concrete** | **1.5** | **0.67 f_ck/1.5 = 0.447 f_ck** |
| **Steel** | **1.15** | **0.87 f_y** |

> **Concrete carries the LARGER factor because its strength is far more VARIABLE** — it is made on site, cured by whoever is there, and its strength depends on workmanship.

> **Steel is manufactured under factory control and arrives with a mill certificate**, so 1.15 suffices.

> **Each quantity is factored according to how well it is KNOWN** — that is the whole principle of limit state design, and it is more rational than working stress design's single global factor.

**Note the separate 0.67 applied to concrete:**

> **It accounts for the difference between the CUBE strength and the strength of concrete in a real flexural member under SUSTAINED load** — a distinct effect from variability, and worth keeping separate from the 1.5.

**Where 0.87 f_y appears:**

| Calculation | Use |
|---|---|
| **Tensile force in a beam** | **T = 0.87 f_y A_st** |
| **Moment capacity** | **M_u = 0.87 f_y A_st (d − 0.42 x_u)** |
| **Shear reinforcement** | V_us = 0.87 f_y A_sv d/s_v |
| **Development length** | **L_d = φ(0.87f_y)/(4τ_bd)** |

> **Together with 0.36 and 0.42 — the stress block's compressive force coefficient and centroid — the number 0.87 carries the whole of singly reinforced beam design.**

**And the load factors, for the other half of the picture:**

> **1.5 DL + 1.5 LL**; **1.2(DL + LL + WL)** for three loads; and **0.9 DL + 1.5 WL** where dead load **STABILISES.**

> **Loads are factored UP and strengths DOWN**, each by how well it is known — and **the 0.9 DL case is the one most often forgotten**, though it is what exposes overturning and uplift failures.

examTip.trick: **Check each option against ITSELF.** Options (b) and (c) quote a percentage that contradicts the divisor 1.15 they themselves state; (d) has the right percentage with a corrupted divisor. Only (a) is consistent.
examTip.trap: **Concrete's factor is 1.5, steel's is 1.15** — concrete is **site-made and variable**, steel is **factory-controlled**. And the separate **0.67** on concrete is a different effect (cube vs sustained in-member strength).
examTip.mnemonic: **0.87 f_y = f_y/1.15** appears in every RC calculation. With **0.36** (compressive force) and **0.42** (stress block centroid), those three numbers carry singly reinforced beam design.

questions.stem: Bitumen extraction test is done at:
questions.solution:
**3600 rpm at 110 °C.**

> The source describes the procedure: **the sample must be soft enough to be scraped off, or else placed on a flat pan and HEATED IN THE OVEN AT ABOUT 110 °C until it can be separated easily. The speed of revolution is gradually increased until it attains a MAXIMUM SPEED OF 3600 rev/min.**

**What the test does:**

> **It determines the BITUMEN CONTENT of a bituminous mix** — how much binder is actually present in a sample taken from the road or the plant.

> **The bitumen is dissolved in a SOLVENT** (commonly trichloroethylene or benzene), and the mixture is spun in a **CENTRIFUGE EXTRACTOR** so the solvent carrying the dissolved bitumen is thrown out through a filter ring, leaving the aggregate behind.

> **Bitumen content = (original weight − aggregate weight) ÷ original weight × 100**

**Why each condition is specified:**

| Condition | Reason |
|---|---|
| **110 °C** | **Softens the mix** so it can be broken up and the solvent can penetrate — **and drives off moisture**, which would otherwise be counted as binder |
| **3600 rpm** | **High enough centrifugal force** to drive the solvent out through the filter completely |
| **Gradual speed increase** | Prevents the sample being thrown out before the solvent has acted |

> **Option (c), 300 °C, is far too hot** — bitumen is handled at about **150 °C**, and 300 °C would **oxidise and degrade** the binder, altering the very thing being measured.

> **That reasoning eliminates it without recall**: a test temperature must not change the material being tested.

**Why bitumen content matters so much:**

> **It is a genuine OPTIMUM, not a maximum.**

| Binder content | Failure |
|---|---|
| **Too LITTLE** | **RAVELLING** — the mix lacks cohesion, sheds aggregate; water enters and **strips** the binder |
| **Too MUCH** | **BLEEDING and RUTTING** — excess binder acts as a lubricant; the mix loses stability and shoves |

> **Adding more binder past the optimum makes the pavement WORSE**, which is the point candidates most often get backwards.

**How the optimum is determined — the MARSHALL method:**

> Specimens are made at a **range of bitumen contents**, compacted with **75 blows per face** for heavy traffic, and five properties plotted:

| Property | Target (heavy traffic) |
|---|---|
| **Marshall STABILITY** | **≥ 9 kN** |
| **FLOW** | **2 – 4 mm** |
| **Air voids (Vv)** | **3 – 5%** |
| Voids filled with bitumen | 65 – 75% |
| Unit weight | Maximum |

> **The optimum is the average of the contents giving maximum stability, maximum density and 4% air voids**, then checked against every other criterion.

**And the air void target is deliberate, not a tolerance:**

> **Below 3%** the mix has no room for the binder to expand in hot weather and it **BLEEDS**; **above 5%** it is **permeable**, admitting water and air which **oxidise the binder and enable STRIPPING.**

> **The extraction test is therefore a quality-control check on the plant**, verifying that the mix being laid actually contains the binder content the Marshall design called for.

examTip.trick: **110 °C softens the mix and drives off moisture** (which would otherwise count as binder); **3600 rpm** gives enough centrifugal force to expel the solvent completely through the filter.
examTip.trap: **Option (c), 300 °C, is far hotter than bitumen's ~150 °C working temperature** — it would **oxidise and degrade** the binder, changing the very thing being measured. A test must not alter its subject.
examTip.mnemonic: **Binder content is an OPTIMUM, not a maximum: too little → RAVELLING, too much → BLEEDING and RUTTING.** The extraction test checks the plant is delivering what the **Marshall design** specified.

questions.stem: Carpet Area of a residential building is …………
questions.solution:
**50 to 65% of the plinth area.**

> The source gives both figures: **the carpet area of RESIDENTIAL buildings may be 50% to 65% of the plinth area, and that of an OFFICE building 60–75% of the plinth area.**

**The area definitions:**

| Area | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **PLINTH area** | The **built-up area measured at floor level, to the OUTER face of the external walls** |
| **CARPET area** | The **usable floor area** — literally, what you could lay carpet on |
| **CIRCULATION area** | **Corridors, staircases, lobbies, verandahs** |
| **Wall area** | The area occupied by the walls themselves |

> **Plinth area = carpet area + circulation area + wall area**

> **The three are NESTED**, and confusing which one a rate applies to is a common and expensive error.

**Typical proportions:**

| Component | Share of plinth area |
|---|---|
| **Carpet area (residential)** | **50 – 65%** |
| Carpet area (office) | 60 – 75% |
| Circulation area | 10 – 25% |
| Wall area | 10 – 15% |

> **An OFFICE has a HIGHER carpet ratio than a residence**, which is worth understanding rather than memorising: **a residence is divided into many small rooms**, each needing its own walls and access, while **an office has larger open floor plates** with proportionally less partitioning.

> **More rooms means more walls and more circulation** — hence the lower carpet ratio.

**Why the distinction matters commercially:**

> **Property is often SOLD on plinth or "super built-up" area but USED as carpet area.**

> **A buyer paying for 100 m² of plinth area receives only 50–65 m² of usable space** — which is precisely why several jurisdictions now require sale by **carpet area** and why the definitions are legally significant rather than merely technical.

**And why it matters in ESTIMATING:**

> **The plinth area method computes cost as plinth area × a rate**, so **the rate must come from a building of similar type, specification and locality.**

> **A rate derived from an office building applied to a residence would be wrong**, partly because the carpet ratios differ — the residence has more wall and more partition per square metre of plinth.

**The estimate types:**

| Estimate | Purpose | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| **Plinth area / cube rate** | **Preliminary; administrative approval** | **±15–20%** |
| **DETAILED** | Item by item from drawings; **technical sanction** | **±5%** |
| **REVISED** | Sanctioned amount exceeded by **>5%** | — |
| **SUPPLEMENTARY** | **ADDITIONAL work** not originally included | — |

> **REVISED = the SAME work costing more; SUPPLEMENTARY = ADDITIONAL work.** The discriminator is whether the **scope** changed or only the **cost**.

**And the approval sequence:** **administrative approval** (from the user department, on the preliminary estimate) → **TECHNICAL SANCTION** (from the competent engineering authority, on the detailed estimate) → expenditure sanction → tender.

> **Technical sanction is the ENGINEER's certification that the estimate is structurally and financially sound** — which is why the detailed estimate must be accurate to about 5%.

examTip.trick: **An OFFICE has a higher carpet ratio (60–75%) than a RESIDENCE (50–65%)** — because a residence is divided into many small rooms, each needing walls and access. More rooms, less carpet.
examTip.trap: **Carpet ⊂ carpet + circulation ⊂ plinth** — three nested areas, and confusing which one a rate applies to is a common and expensive error.
examTip.mnemonic: **Property is SOLD on plinth area but USED as carpet area** — a buyer paying for 100 m² receives 50–65 m² usable. That gap is why several jurisdictions now mandate sale by carpet area.

questions.stem: Which bacteria can function with and without oxygen?
questions.solution:
**Facultative bacteria.**

> The source explains: **facultative anaerobes CAN LIVE WITH OR WITHOUT OXYGEN. When oxygen is present they use aerobic cellular respiration to produce ATP; if oxygen becomes depleted they SWITCH to anaerobic respiration or fermentation. In contrast, OBLIGATE anaerobes must live WITHOUT oxygen.**

**The classification by OXYGEN requirement:**

| Type | Oxygen |
|---|---|
| **AEROBIC** | **REQUIRES** free oxygen |
| **ANAEROBIC (obligate)** | **Cannot tolerate** oxygen — it is toxic to them |
| **FACULTATIVE** | **Functions EITHER WAY** — switches according to availability |

**Why options (b) and (c) are wrong is a category error, and an instructive one:**

> **MESOPHILIC and THERMOPHILIC are TEMPERATURE classifications, not oxygen ones.**

| Class | Optimum temperature |
|---|---|
| **Psychrophilic** | **0 – 20 °C** |
| **MESOPHILIC** | **20 – 45 °C** — most common bacteria |
| **THERMOPHILIC** | **45 – 70 °C** |
| Hyperthermophilic | > 70 °C |

> **The two classifications are INDEPENDENT** — a bacterium is described by both, so an organism can be **mesophilic AND facultative** at the same time.

> **Recognising that the question asks about oxygen while two options answer about temperature settles it immediately.**

**Why facultative bacteria matter in wastewater treatment:**

> **They make the FACULTATIVE POND possible** — the most widely used waste stabilisation pond, and one particularly suited to Nepali conditions.

| Zone | Condition | Organisms |
|---|---|---|
| **Upper** | **AEROBIC** — oxygen from algae and surface reaeration | Aerobic bacteria |
| **Middle** | **FACULTATIVE** — variable oxygen | **FACULTATIVE bacteria** |
| **Bottom** | **ANAEROBIC** — sludge layer | Anaerobic bacteria |

> **A single pond therefore contains all three environments simultaneously**, and the facultative organisms in the middle layer function whichever way the oxygen happens to go.

> **That robustness is exactly why the pond works with minimal operation** — it does not need oxygen to be maintained at any particular level.

**The algae–bacteria symbiosis** that drives it:

> **ALGAE produce the oxygen that aerobic bacteria need; the bacteria produce the CO₂ and nutrients the algae need.**

> **The same organism that is a nuisance in a water supply reservoir is the working element of a stabilisation pond** — a good illustration that "pollution" is a matter of context.

**And why stabilisation ponds suit Nepal:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **No power required** | No aeration equipment |
| **Minimal operation and maintenance** | No skilled operators |
| **No imported spares** | — |
| Effective pathogen removal | Long detention time |
| **Low cost** | — |

> **Their cost is LAND and a long detention time (20–40 days)** — which is affordable where land is available and prohibitive where it is not.

**The anaerobic alternative — DIGESTION:** hydrolysis → acidogenesis → acetogenesis → **METHANOGENESIS**, producing **biogas (60–70% CH₄)**.

> **The METHANOGENS are the slowest and most sensitive organisms in the chain**, inhibited by low pH — so a digester that turns acidic **stalls**, and the standard operating check is the **volatile acids to alkalinity ratio**.

examTip.trick: **The question asks about OXYGEN, but two options answer about TEMPERATURE.** Mesophilic and thermophilic are temperature classes — a category error that settles the question instantly.
examTip.trap: **The two classifications are INDEPENDENT** — an organism can be mesophilic **and** facultative at once. They describe different properties, not alternatives.
examTip.mnemonic: **A FACULTATIVE POND holds all three zones at once** — aerobic top, facultative middle, anaerobic bottom. That robustness is why it works with no power and minimal operation, at the cost of **land**.

questions.stem: Minimum width of toilet door is:
questions.solution:
**750 mm** for a residential toilet.

> **The other three options can be discarded on physical grounds alone**: **450 mm, 350 mm and especially 100 mm are too narrow for a person to pass through.**

> **A 100 mm door is absurd** — narrower than a hand span — and its presence signals that the question rewards a sanity check rather than recall.

**Typical minimum door widths:**

| Door | Minimum width |
|---|---|
| **Main entrance** | **900 – 1200 mm** |
| Internal room | 750 – 900 mm |
| **Toilet / bathroom** | **750 mm** |
| **Wheelchair accessible** | **900 mm** |

> **And minimum heights: 2000–2100 mm** for all of them.

**Why the toilet door is the narrowest:**

> **It carries the least traffic and needs to admit only one person** — so it is the sensible place to economise on space in a constrained plan.

> **But it cannot go below about 750 mm**, because that is roughly the width required for a person to pass comfortably, and because **emergency access matters**: a person taken ill in a bathroom must be reachable.

> **That accessibility argument is why the dimension is a code minimum rather than a matter of preference**, and why **wheelchair access requires 900 mm.**

**The related room requirements** (NBC / typical building bye-laws):

| Space | Minimum |
|---|---|
| **Habitable room area** | **9.5 m²** (one room), 7.5 m² (others) |
| **Habitable room width** | **2.4 m** |
| **Ceiling height** | **2.4 m** |
| **Kitchen area** | **3.3 – 5.0 m²** |
| **Bathroom / WC area** | **1.1 – 2.8 m²** |
| **Staircase width** | **0.75 – 1.0 m** residential |
| **Riser / tread** | **≤ 190 mm / ≥ 250 mm** |

> **The riser-and-tread rule of thumb is worth carrying: 2R + T ≈ 600 mm**, which produces a comfortable stair — and a stair that violates it feels wrong to climb however correct each dimension is individually.

**Why these minima exist at all:**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **Health** | Light, ventilation, space per person |
| **SAFETY** | **Escape in an emergency** — the width of an exit determines how fast a building can be cleared |
| **Accessibility** | Wheelchair and mobility access |
| Amenity | Basic usability |

> **The escape argument is why door and stair widths are regulated more strictly than room sizes** — a narrow room is uncomfortable, but a narrow exit is dangerous.

**And the ventilation and lighting requirements** that accompany them: **openings of at least 10% of the floor area for light and 5% for ventilation** in a habitable room, with a **toilet requiring either a window or mechanical extraction.**

examTip.trick: **Sanity-check the physical dimension.** 450, 350 and especially **100 mm** are too narrow for a person to pass — the last is narrower than a hand span. Only 750 mm is plausible.
examTip.trap: The toilet door is the **narrowest** door in a house because it carries least traffic — but it cannot go below ~750 mm, because **emergency access** to someone taken ill inside must be possible.
examTip.mnemonic: **Stair rule of thumb: 2R + T ≈ 600 mm** gives a comfortable flight. And **escape width is regulated more strictly than room size** — a narrow room is uncomfortable, a narrow exit is dangerous.

questions.stem: The scour depth can be calculated using the formula:
questions.solution:
**R = 1.35 (q²/f)^{1/3}** — Lacey's normal scour depth.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **R** | **Normal scour depth** below the high flood level |
| **q** | **Discharge per unit width** (m³/s per m) |
| **f** | **Lacey's SILT FACTOR = 1.76√d**, with d in **millimetres** |

> **The exponent is ONE THIRD** — the same cube-root form that recurs throughout Lacey's regime relations, including **R = 0.473(Q/f)^{1/3}.**

> **Options (b) and (c) alter only the exponent**, which is exactly the detail this question tests.

**A dimensional sanity check settles it:**

> **q² has dimensions of L⁴/T², and dividing by f (dimensionless) leaves L⁴/T².** Taking the **cube root** gives **L^{4/3}/T^{2/3}** — which the empirical coefficient 1.35 converts to a length.

> **The 2/3 or 5/3 powers would give dimensionally different quantities**, and no single coefficient could reconcile them to a depth across the range of q. **The 1/3 is the only exponent consistent with a calibrated empirical constant.**

**How the scour depth is used — this is what makes it matter:**

> **The computed R is multiplied by a LOCATION FACTOR**, because scour is far deeper where the flow is concentrated or disturbed:

| Location | Multiplier |
|---|---|
| Straight reach | **1.25** |
| Moderate bend | 1.5 |
| Severe bend | 1.75 |
| **Bridge PIER NOSE** | **2.0** |
| **Right-angled bend / guide bank head** | **2.75** |

> **The guide bank head takes the most severe scour of any point** — which is why it carries the heaviest protection.

**And the consequence for foundations:**

> **Near a watercourse, SCOUR usually governs the foundation depth far more than bearing capacity does.**

> **A pier founded above the scour level will be UNDERMINED in a flood, however adequate its bearing pressure.**

> **SCOUR IS THE LEADING CAUSE OF BRIDGE FAILURE WORLDWIDE** — which is why this apparently minor empirical relation carries so much weight, and why foundation depths near rivers look excessive until the reason is understood.

**The LAUNCHING APRON** is the companion protection:

> **Loose stone laid horizontally at the toe. As the river scours a hole beside it, the stone at the edge FALLS (launches) into the hole, armouring the newly exposed slope.**

> **It is DESIGNED TO BE DESTROYED in a controlled way**, and its stone quantity is calculated to cover the **anticipated scour slope (usually 2:1)** down to the deepest expected scour — which is exactly what this formula provides.

**Lacey's regime relations, as a set:**

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Wetted perimeter** | **P = 4.75√Q** |
| **Hydraulic radius** | **R = 0.473(Q/f)^{1/3}** |
| **Velocity** | **V = [Qf²/140]^{1/6}** |
| **Bed slope** | **S = f^{5/3}/(3340 Q^{1/6})** |
| **Normal scour depth** | **R = 1.35(q²/f)^{1/3}** |

> **Note that 5/3 does appear in Lacey's work — in the SLOPE relation** — which is likely why it is offered as a distractor here. **Right exponent, wrong equation.**

examTip.trick: **The exponent is 1/3** — the same cube-root form as Lacey's **R = 0.473(Q/f)^{1/3}**. The regime relations use that power repeatedly.
examTip.trap: **5/3 DOES appear in Lacey's work — in the SLOPE relation S = f^{5/3}/(3340Q^{1/6}).** Right exponent, wrong equation, which is why it makes a convincing distractor.
examTip.mnemonic: **Multiply R by a LOCATION FACTOR: 2.0 at a pier nose, 2.75 at a guide bank head.** Near a river **scour governs foundation depth, not bearing capacity** — and scour is the leading cause of bridge failure worldwide.

questions.stem: The spherical shape of a raindrop after falling is due to:
questions.solution:
**Surface tension.**

> The source repeats the principle: **the surface tension of water provides the necessary WALL TENSION, and the tendency to MINIMISE that tension pulls the drop into a SPHERICAL shape.**

**The mechanism:**

> **Molecules at a liquid surface have fewer neighbours than those in the bulk**, so the surface behaves as an elastic membrane under tension.

> **A system under tension minimises its ENERGY by minimising its AREA — and for a given VOLUME, the SPHERE has the LEAST surface area.**

> **That single geometric fact explains raindrops, soap bubbles and mercury droplets alike.**

> **Note this question repeats the principle asked in Q25** — the same paper tests it twice, which is worth noticing in the examination itself.

**A caution about real raindrops** worth knowing:

> **A FALLING raindrop is not perfectly spherical.** Air resistance flattens its underside, and above about **2 mm** diameter it becomes distinctly **hamburger-shaped**; larger drops break up entirely.

> **The classic teardrop shape of illustration does not occur at all.** Surface tension pulls toward a sphere; **aerodynamic drag opposes it**, and the actual shape is the balance between them.

> **Small drops are nearly spherical because surface tension dominates at small scale** — which is the same reason capillary effects matter in fine pores and not in large pipes.

**Surface tension of water:**

| Property | Value |
|---|---|
| **σ at 20 °C** | **0.073 N/m** |
| Units | **N/m** (force per length) or **J/m²** (energy per area) — dimensionally identical |
| With rising temperature | **Decreases** |

**Where it matters in civil engineering:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **CAPILLARY RISE** | **h = 4σcosθ/(γd)**, so **h ∝ 1/d** |
| **Apparent cohesion** in moist sand | The sandcastle effect |
| **Frost heave** | Capillary feeding of ice lenses — **SILT is worst** |
| Manometer correction | Tubes specified at **≥ 6 mm bore** |

> **Apparent cohesion is the dangerous one**: **moist sand stands in a vertical cut because of menisci between its grains — and that cohesion VANISHES on saturation or complete drying.**

> **Which is why trench collapses in sand so often follow rain**, or the drying of a previously damp face.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | What it governs |
|---|---|
| **Viscosity** | Resistance to **shear** — determines the drop's **terminal velocity**, not its shape |
| **Density** | Determines its **weight**, not its shape |
| **Cavitation** | **Vapour bubbles forming when pressure falls to the VAPOUR PRESSURE** — a destructive phenomenon in pumps and turbines, unrelated to a falling drop |

> **Viscosity is the most interesting distractor** because it genuinely acts on a falling drop — through **Stokes' law, v_s = gd²(G−1)/18ν**, which governs how fast it falls.

> **But how fast it falls and what shape it takes are different questions**, and only surface tension answers the second.

examTip.trick: **A sphere has the least surface area for a given volume**, and a surface under tension minimises its area. One geometric fact explains raindrops, bubbles and mercury droplets alike.
examTip.trap: **VISCOSITY genuinely acts on a falling drop** — through Stokes' law it sets the **terminal velocity**. But how fast it falls and what shape it takes are different questions.
examTip.mnemonic: **A real falling raindrop is NOT spherical** — drag flattens it, and above ~2 mm it goes hamburger-shaped. The teardrop of illustration never occurs. And **this paper asks the same principle twice** (Q25).

questions.stem: Minimum width of road for a single lane in Nepal standard:
questions.solution:
**3.75 m.**

> The source gives the set: **single lane road 3.75 m; intermediate lane 5.5 m; multilane pavement width per lane 3.5 m.**

**The carriageway widths:**

| Configuration | Width |
|---|---|
| **SINGLE lane** | **3.75 m** |
| **INTERMEDIATE lane** | **5.5 m** |
| **TWO lanes** | **7.0 m** |
| **MULTI-lane — per lane** | **3.5 m** |

> **Notice the apparent paradox: a SINGLE lane (3.75 m) is WIDER than a lane within a multi-lane carriageway (3.5 m).**

> **The reason is that a single-lane road must accommodate a vehicle with clearance on BOTH sides**, since there is no adjacent lane to borrow from. **A lane in a multi-lane road has neighbouring lanes**, so it needs less individual margin.

> **That is worth understanding rather than memorising**, because it makes the numbers make sense rather than seeming arbitrary.

**And the intermediate lane (5.5 m)** is a genuine Nepali and Indian category:

> **Too narrow for two vehicles to pass freely, too wide for one** — used where traffic does not justify a full two-lane road but a single lane would be inadequate.

> **It is a deliberate compromise**, and it is why 5.5 m rather than 7.0 m appears on many hill roads.

**The wider road cross-section terms**, which are nested and frequently confused:

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **CARRIAGEWAY** | **The travelled way** — where vehicles run |
| **ROADWAY** | Carriageway **plus SHOULDERS** |
| **FORMATION width** | Roadway plus **side drains** — the earthwork width |
| **RIGHT OF WAY** | **ALL the land acquired** — formation, slopes, drains and reserve |

> **Each contains the one before it.** A national highway's **50 m right of way** may carry only a **7 m carriageway.**

**The Nepal Road Standard right-of-way widths:**

| Road class | Right of way |
|---|---|
| **National highway** | **50 m** |
| **Feeder road** | **30 m** |
| **District road** | **20 m** |
| **Village road** | **15 m** |

> **The reserve exists chiefly for FUTURE WIDENING** — acquiring land later, after development, is enormously more expensive.

> **Encroachment on the right of way is the single greatest obstacle to later road improvement in Nepal**: once buildings occupy the reserve, widening requires demolition and compensation, often costing more than the road itself.

> **The reserve is cheap to protect and ruinous to recover.**

**The associated geometric provisions:**

| Provision | Note |
|---|---|
| **Camber** | **2.5 – 3%** for bituminous, more for earth surfaces |
| **Shoulder width** | 0.9 – 2.5 m depending on class |
| **Extra widening on curves** | **nl²/2R + V/(9.5√R)** |
| Design speed | **Class I plain 120, steep 60 km/h** |

> **Extra widening is added ON TOP of these standard widths at curves**, because the rigid wheelbase makes rear wheels **track inside** the front ones (off-tracking), and drivers keep further apart on a bend.

examTip.trick: **A SINGLE lane (3.75 m) is WIDER than a lane in a multi-lane road (3.5 m)** — because it needs clearance on **both** sides with no adjacent lane to borrow from. The apparent paradox has a reason.
examTip.trap: **5.5 m is the INTERMEDIATE lane** — a real category, too narrow for free passing and too wide for one vehicle, used where a full two-lane road is not justified.
examTip.mnemonic: **Carriageway ⊂ roadway ⊂ formation ⊂ right of way.** A 50 m ROW may carry a 7 m carriageway — the reserve exists for **future widening**, and encroachment on it is the greatest obstacle to road improvement in Nepal.

questions.stem: For a simply supported beam, if the bending moment is constant, what will be the shear force?
questions.solution:
**Zero.**

> The source states it: **in a simply supported beam, if the bending moment is constant the shear force will be ZERO.**

**Why — it is calculus, not a rule to memorise:**

> **V = dM/dx**

> **If M is CONSTANT, then dM/dx = 0, so V = 0.** ✓

> **The shear force IS the slope of the bending moment diagram** — so a flat moment diagram means zero shear everywhere along it.

**This condition has a name — PURE BENDING:**

> **Constant moment with zero shear IS pure bending**, and it is not merely a curiosity:

> **It is exactly the condition assumed in the derivation of the flexure formula σ = My/I.**

> **The simple bending theory is STRICTLY valid only in pure bending**, which is why it is an approximation (a very good one for slender beams) everywhere else.

**Where pure bending is deliberately created:**

> **In the MIDDLE THIRD of a FOUR-POINT bending test.**

| Region | Condition |
|---|---|
| Between support and load point | Shear present, moment varying |
| **Between the two load points** | **CONSTANT moment, ZERO shear — PURE BENDING** |

> **That is why flexural strength (modulus of rupture) is measured with third-point loading** — the central region matches the theory's assumptions exactly, so the measured value belongs to the material rather than to the test arrangement.

> **A centre-point loading test would have shear everywhere except at one section**, and the result would be less clean.

**How constant moment arises in practice:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **Equal end COUPLES** with no transverse load | The purest case |
| **Between the two loads** of a symmetric two-point loading | The four-point test |
| A beam segment with no load and no shear | — |

**The governing relations, as a set:**

> **w = −dV/dx** and **V = dM/dx**

| Consequence | Statement |
|---|---|
| **Shear is the SLOPE of the moment diagram** | This question |
| **V = 0 marks a moment PEAK** | The turning point |
| **Change in M = AREA of the shear diagram** | The fastest hand method |
| Each integration raises the order by one | load → shear → moment |

**And the diagram features that follow:**

| Applied | SFD | BMD |
|---|---|---|
| **Point load W** | **JUMPS by W** | **KINK** |
| **COUPLE M** | **NO change** | **JUMPS by M** |
| **UDL w** | **LINEAR** | **PARABOLIC** |
| **No load** | **Constant** | **Linear** |

> **Note the last row**: with no load the shear is constant and the moment is **linear** — so a **constant** moment requires the shear to be not merely constant but **zero**, which is precisely what this question asks.

> **Option (b) is the trap for anyone who reasons "constant M → constant V"** without carrying the differentiation through.

examTip.trick: **V = dM/dx**, so a **constant** moment means **zero** shear. The shear force IS the slope of the moment diagram — calculus, not a rule to memorise.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) catches anyone reasoning "constant M → constant V"** without differentiating. A *linear* moment gives constant shear; a *constant* moment gives zero.
examTip.mnemonic: **Constant moment with zero shear IS PURE BENDING** — the condition σ = My/I assumes. Which is why flexural strength is measured in the **middle third of a four-point test**.

questions.stem: The mortar to sand ratio provided in brick masonry for frog filling is:
questions.solution:
**1 : 1** — cement to sand.

> The source states it: **the cement to sand ratio provided in brick masonry for FROG FILLING is 1:1, and the sand should be very fine clean sand, 3 mm and under.**

**Why the mix is so rich:**

> **1:1 is a very rich mortar** — far richer than the 1:4 to 1:6 used for laying masonry.

> **The reason is that the frog filling must be STRONGER THAN THE BRICK ITSELF.** If the filling were weaker, it would crush first and the test would measure the mortar rather than the brick.

> **The filling must not become the weak point**, which is the whole logic of specifying a rich mix for a job that carries no structural load in service.

**What the frog is, and why filling it matters:**

> **The FROG is the indentation on a brick's surface**, provided so that mortar keys into it and improves the bond between courses.

> **In a COMPRESSION TEST, however, that indentation is a VOID.** Tested as it comes, the platen would bear only on the **narrow rim** around the frog:

| Consequence | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Load concentrated on a small rim** | Very high local stress |
| **Stress distribution non-uniform** | Premature local crushing |
| **Measured "strength" reflects the rim** | **The number means nothing** |

> **Filling the frog restores a flat, full-area bearing surface**, so the result measures the brick's compressive strength rather than an artefact of its shape.

**The full test procedure:**

| Step | Detail |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Fill the frog with 1:1 cement mortar** |
| **2** | **Cure for 3 days** |
| **3** | **Immerse in water** before testing |
| **4** | Place between plywood sheets and load at a specified rate |
| **5** | **Strength = failure load ÷ GROSS area** |

> **The principle — eliminating specimen effects so the measured value belongs to the material — runs through all materials testing**: it is why concrete cubes are capped, why steel specimens have a defined gauge length, and why soil samples are trimmed to standard dimensions.

**The brick class ladder this test establishes:**

| Class | Compressive strength | Water absorption |
|---|---|---|
| **First class** | **≥ 10.5 N/mm²** | **≤ 15%** (12–15%) |
| **Second class** | **≥ 7.0 N/mm²** | ≤ 20% |
| **Third class** | **≥ 3.5 N/mm²** | ≤ 25% |

> **Strength falls and absorption rises together down the ladder**, because both measure the same underlying quality: **the degree of VITRIFICATION achieved in firing.**

**And the contrast with LAYING mortar:**

| Purpose | Mix |
|---|---|
| **FROG FILLING (test)** | **1:1 — must exceed the brick's strength** |
| **Brick masonry laying** | **1:4 to 1:6** |
| Plastering (internal) | 1:4 to 1:6 |
| Plastering (external) | 1:4 |

> **A richer laying mortar is NOT better**: mortar should be **weaker than the brick**, so that cracking from movement occurs in the **joints** — where it is cheap to rake out and repoint — rather than through the bricks themselves.

> **That is a genuinely important principle in masonry**, and it is the exact opposite of the requirement for frog filling.

examTip.trick: **The filling must be STRONGER than the brick**, or it crushes first and the test measures the mortar. That is why 1:1 — far richer than the 1:4 to 1:6 used for laying.
examTip.trap: **The frog is a VOID in a compression test.** Without filling, the platen bears on a narrow rim, the stress is wildly non-uniform, and the result measures **geometry, not material**.
examTip.mnemonic: **Laying mortar should be WEAKER than the brick** — so cracks form in the joints, cheap to rake out and repoint, rather than through the bricks. The exact opposite of the frog-filling requirement.

questions.stem: The extra width added to a road is:
questions.solution:
**Mechanical plus psychological widening.**

> The source gives both components: **extra widening consists of two components — the PSYCHOLOGICAL factor and the MECHANICAL factor.**

> **Extra widening = W_ps + W_m = V/(9.5√R) + nl²/(2R)**

**The two components:**

| Component | Formula | Cause |
|---|---|---|
| **MECHANICAL** | **n l²/(2R)** | The **rigid WHEELBASE** — rear wheels track **inside** the front ones |
| **PSYCHOLOGICAL** | **V/(9.5√R)** | Drivers keep **further from the edge and from each other** on a curve |

> where **n** = number of lanes, **l** = wheelbase (length of vehicle), **R** = radius, **V** = design speed in km/h.

**The distinguishing feature — worth noting because it makes both formulae memorable:**

> **MECHANICAL widening is pure GEOMETRY and contains NO SPEED.** It depends only on the wheelbase and the radius.

> **PSYCHOLOGICAL widening is BEHAVIOURAL and DOES contain speed.** The source confirms it: **"psychological widening is totally dependent on the design speed and the radius, and doesn't depend on the wheelbase of the vehicle."**

> **The presence or absence of V tells the two apart instantly.**

**Why mechanical widening exists — OFF-TRACKING:**

> **A vehicle's rear wheels do not follow the front wheels round a curve.** Because the wheelbase is rigid, **the rear wheels CUT THE CORNER**, tracking on a smaller radius.

> **The vehicle therefore sweeps a wider path than its own width**, and extra carriageway must be provided or the rear wheels run off the inside edge.

> **The effect worsens with a LONGER wheelbase and a SHARPER curve** — hence **l² in the numerator and R in the denominator.**

> **A long truck or articulated vehicle on a tight hairpin needs very substantial widening**, which is why hill-road hairpins are built so much wider than the straight sections.

**Why psychological widening exists:**

> Drivers instinctively **keep further from the pavement edge and from oncoming vehicles** on a curve, because the sight line is shorter and the vehicle feels less stable.

> **It is a real and measurable effect**, and providing for it prevents drivers crowding the centre line — which is the actual hazard.

**Where the widening is applied:**

> **Over the full circular curve, introduced GRADUALLY over the TRANSITION curve** — reaching its full value where the circular arc begins.

| Practice | Note |
|---|---|
| Usually on the **INSIDE** of the curve | Where the rear wheels track |
| Sometimes **half on each side** | Common where a transition is provided |
| **Not required for R > about 300 m** | The effect becomes negligible |

**The full set of curve provisions**, all designed together:

| Provision | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Superelevation** | **e = V²/(225R)**; e_max **7% plain, 10% hilly, 7% snow-bound** |
| **Minimum radius** | **R = V²/(127(e + f))**, f = 0.15 |
| **Extra widening** | **nl²/(2R) + V/(9.5√R)** |
| **Transition length** | **GREATEST of three criteria** |
| **Grade compensation** | **(30 + R)/R %, max 75/R**; not below 4% |

> **All five are needed together on a sharp curve.** Omitting any one produces a curve that is uncomfortable, unsafe, or unusable by heavy vehicles.

> **Failing to apply GRADE COMPENSATION is why trucks stall on tight hairpin bends** — the combination of sharp curve and steep grade exceeds what the vehicle can pull.

examTip.trick: **MECHANICAL widening is pure GEOMETRY — no speed appears (nl²/2R). PSYCHOLOGICAL is BEHAVIOURAL and does contain speed (V/9.5√R).** The presence of V tells them apart instantly.
examTip.trap: Options (b) and (c) add a third component — "shoulder" and "eye sight" — that does not exist. There are exactly **two** components, and no more.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rear wheels CUT THE CORNER (off-tracking) — hence l² on top, R beneath.** A long truck on a tight hairpin needs a great deal. And apply **grade compensation** too, or trucks stall.

questions.stem: Which should be considered while selecting consultancy?
questions.solution:
**Quality and cost** — the QCBS approach.

**Why not quality alone, and not cost alone:**

| Basis | Problem |
|---|---|
| **COST alone** | **Selects the cheapest proposal**, which for intellectual services usually means the **least experienced team and the fewest hours** — and a poor design costs far more in construction than it saves in fees |
| **QUALITY alone** | Ignores value for money entirely; there is always a better team available at a higher price |
| **QUALITY AND COST together** | **Balances technical merit against price** |

> **Consultancy is an INTELLECTUAL service, not a commodity**, which is exactly why selecting on price alone is inappropriate.

> **A contractor builds to a specification that already exists; a consultant CREATES the specification.** The quality of that creative work determines everything downstream, and it cannot be verified in advance the way delivered goods can.

**QCBS — Quality and Cost Based Selection:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Technical proposals evaluated** and scored | Against pre-declared criteria |
| **2. Only those above a minimum score** proceed | Below it, the proposal is rejected outright |
| **3. Financial proposals opened** for the qualified ones only | — |
| **4. Combined score** | Typically **70–80% technical weight, 20–30% financial** |

> **The technical weight is deliberately dominant**, which is the numerical expression of the principle above.

> **And the technical proposal is opened FIRST, before any price is seen** — so the technical evaluation cannot be influenced by knowing which firm is cheapest.

**The technical evaluation criteria:**

| Criterion | Note |
|---|---|
| **Firm's experience** on similar assignments | — |
| **KEY PERSONNEL** — qualifications and experience | Usually the **largest single weight** |
| **Methodology and work plan** | Understanding of the problem |
| Technology transfer / training | Where required |
| Local participation | — |

> **Key personnel usually carry the most weight**, because a consultancy's output depends on the individuals who actually do the work rather than on the firm's letterhead.

> **That is why substituting personnel after award is normally prohibited without approval** — it would defeat the basis on which the firm was selected.

**The other selection methods**, used where QCBS is not appropriate:

| Method | When |
