|---|---|
| **QBS — Quality Based Selection** | **Complex or highly specialised** assignments where quality dominates entirely |
| **Least Cost** | **Standard, routine** assignments of a well-defined nature |
| **Fixed Budget** | Where the budget is fixed and cannot be exceeded |
| **Single Source** | Continuation of earlier work, emergencies, or only one qualified firm |

> **Least Cost is legitimate for ROUTINE, well-defined work** — a standard soil investigation, a routine survey — where the output is essentially a commodity and quality differences are small.

> **It is inappropriate for design**, where the differences between a good and a poor solution are large and are not visible in the proposal.

**The professional dimension:**

> The NEC code of conduct requires **competence** — practising only within the field and level for which one is qualified.

> **A firm that wins on price by proposing under-qualified staff is in tension with that obligation**, which is one reason the technical threshold in QCBS is a **pass/fail gate** rather than merely a scored component.

examTip.trick: **A contractor builds to a specification; a consultant CREATES it.** That is why price-alone selection is inappropriate for intellectual services — the quality of the design governs everything downstream.
examTip.trap: **"All of the above" is wrong because quality-alone and cost-alone are distinct, inferior methods** — not components of the right answer. QCBS balances the two.
examTip.mnemonic: **Technical proposals opened FIRST, weighted 70–80%; financial only for those passing the threshold.** And **KEY PERSONNEL carry the most weight** — which is why substitution after award needs approval.

questions.stem: Which of the following structures is constructed to separate the under sluice from the main weir?
questions.solution:
**The divide wall.**

> The source's diagram shows the arrangement directly: **the DIVIDE WALL separates the under-sluice (scouring sluice) pocket from the main weir bays**, with the head regulator drawing from the pocket into the canal.

**What the divide wall does:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Separates the under-sluice pocket from the weir** | Its defining purpose |
| **Creates a STILL POND** in front of the head regulator | Where **silt can settle out before entering the canal** |
| Keeps the two flow regimes apart | Prevents cross-currents |
| **Prevents oblique flow toward the canal head** | Which would draw silt in |

> **The still pond is the key idea**: by isolating a pocket of relatively quiet water in front of the head regulator, coarse sediment settles there and can be **flushed away through the under-sluices** rather than entering the canal.

> **That is silt control by hydraulic arrangement rather than by a mechanical device** — cheap, passive and effective.

**The components of a diversion headworks**, as the source's figure shows them:

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **Weir or barrage** | **Raises the water level** so the canal can draw by gravity |
| **DIVIDE WALL** | **Separates the under-sluice pocket from the weir** ← |
| **Under-sluices (scouring sluices)** | **Flush accumulated silt**; pass low flows |
| **HEAD REGULATOR** | **Controls flow INTO the canal** |
| **SILT EXCLUDER** | Stops silt **ENTERING** the canal |
| **FISH LADDER** | Beside the divide wall |
| **GUIDE BANK** | Confines the river; **prevents OUTFLANKING** |
| **Marginal bund** | Embankment confining floodwater to the channel |

> **Note that the FISH LADDER is placed beside the divide wall**, because the under-sluice pocket carries flow year-round — and **fish find the ladder by following a current**, so a reliable flow at its entrance is essential.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | What it actually does |
|---|---|
| **MARGINAL BUND** | An **embankment along the bank** confining floodwater — a river training work, not a headworks separator |
| **HEAD regulator** | Controls flow **INTO the canal** — it draws from the pocket the divide wall creates |
| **CROSS regulator** | Sits **ACROSS the parent canal** downstream of an offtake, to **raise the level** so the offtake can draw |

> **HEAD and CROSS regulators are constantly swapped**, and the distinction is worth fixing: **the CROSS regulator is across the PARENT canal; the HEAD regulator is at the HEAD of the OFFTAKE.** They are built as a pair.

**And the silt structures**, equally often confused:

> **SILT EXCLUDER excludes silt at the ENTRANCE** — it sits at the head regulator and stops silt getting into the canal.
> **SILT EJECTOR ejects silt from WITHIN the canal** — downstream, removing what has already entered.

> **Prevention versus cure**, and the two names describe exactly that difference.

**The under-sluices deserve a note** because they do two jobs:

> They **pass the low flows of the river** (so the weir crest need not be overtopped at all times) **and FLUSH the silt** that accumulates in the pocket — the flushing being possible precisely because the divide wall has confined that silt to a defined area.

> **The divide wall and the under-sluices work as a system**: the wall concentrates the silt, the sluices remove it.

examTip.trick: The divide wall creates a **STILL POND** in front of the head regulator — silt settles there and is **flushed through the under-sluices** instead of entering the canal. Silt control by hydraulic arrangement, not machinery.
examTip.trap: **HEAD and CROSS regulators are constantly swapped**: the **CROSS** regulator is across the **PARENT canal**; the **HEAD** regulator is at the head of the **OFFTAKE**. They are built as a pair.
examTip.mnemonic: **Silt EXCLUDER excludes at the entrance; silt EJECTOR ejects from within the canal** — prevention versus cure. And the **divide wall and under-sluices work as a system**: the wall concentrates silt, the sluices remove it.

questions.stem: Which is not considered as dead load?
questions.solution:
**Students** — people are a LIVE load, not a dead load.

**The defining distinction:**

| Load | Definition |
|---|---|
| **DEAD load (DL)** | **PERMANENT, immovable** — the self-weight of the structure and everything permanently attached |
| **LIVE load / imposed load (LL)** | **MOVABLE or TEMPORARY** — occupants, furniture, stored goods, movable partitions |

> **The test is whether the load can MOVE OR BE REMOVED.**

> **A floor slab, a column and a wall are all built in and stay put — dead load. Students walk in and out — live load.**

**Why the classification matters — it is not merely bookkeeping:**

| Aspect | Dead load | Live load |
|---|---|---|
| **Certainty** | **Accurately KNOWN** — computed from dimensions and unit weights | **UNCERTAIN** — depends on use |
| **Duration** | **Permanent** | Intermittent |
| **Causes CREEP** | **YES — sustained** | Largely no |
| **Can be REDUCED** | No | **YES — live load reduction for multiple floors** |
| **Stabilising cases** | **Factored DOWN to 0.9** | Omitted where it helps |

> **Dead load is calculable to within a few percent; live load is a statistical estimate**, which is why the codes treat them so differently even though both are factored by 1.5 in the ordinary combination.

**The two consequences most often overlooked:**

> **1. CREEP.** Concrete creeps under **sustained** load only. **Long-term deflection is therefore governed by the DEAD load and the permanent part of the live load**, not by the peak live load that occurs briefly.

> **2. The 0.9 DL combination.** Where dead load **STABILISES** — resisting overturning, uplift or sliding — it is factored **DOWN to 0.9**, because assuming a larger stabilising weight than actually exists is unconservative.

> **That combination is the one most often forgotten, and it is exactly the one that exposes overturning and uplift failures** in retaining walls, chimneys and light roofs under wind.

**Typical live loads (IS 875 Part 2):**

| Occupancy | Live load |
|---|---|
| **Residential rooms** | **2.0 kN/m²** |
| **Classrooms** | **3.0 kN/m²** |
| Offices | 2.5 – 4.0 kN/m² |
| **Corridors, stairs, assembly** | **4.0 – 5.0 kN/m²** |
| Storage | 5.0 kN/m² and above |

> **Note that CORRIDORS AND STAIRS carry a HIGHER live load than the rooms they serve** — because they are escape routes and can be crowded far more densely than the rooms themselves during an evacuation.

**And LIVE LOAD REDUCTION**, which is the statistical counterpart:

> **A column supporting many floors may be designed for a reduced live load**, because the probability that **every** floor carries its full design live load simultaneously is very small.

> **No such reduction applies to dead load**, which is present on every floor with certainty — another expression of the same underlying difference in how well each load is known.

**The load combinations (IS 456 Table 18):** **1.5(DL + LL)**; **1.2(DL + LL + WL/EL)**; **1.5(DL + WL/EL)**; and **0.9 DL + 1.5 WL/EL**.

examTip.trick: **Can it MOVE or be REMOVED?** Slab, column and wall are built in — dead. Students walk in and out — live. One test settles the whole classification.
examTip.trap: **Corridors and stairs carry a HIGHER live load (4–5 kN/m²) than the classrooms they serve (3 kN/m²)** — they are escape routes and crowd far more densely during evacuation.
examTip.mnemonic: **Only sustained load causes CREEP**, so long-term deflection is governed by DEAD load. And where dead load **STABILISES** it is factored DOWN to **0.9** — the combination most often forgotten, and the one that exposes uplift and overturning.

questions.stem: Slump test is the measure of:
questions.solution:
**Consistency** — that is, workability.

**What the slump test actually measures:**

> **Fresh concrete is filled into a standard mould in three layers, each tamped 25 times; the mould is lifted, and the CONCRETE SUBSIDES. The subsidence in millimetres is the SLUMP.**

| Mould dimension | Value |
|---|---|
| **Bottom diameter** | **200 mm** |
| **Top diameter** | **100 mm** |
| **Height** | **300 mm** |
| Tamping | **25 strokes per layer**, 3 layers |

> **It measures the CONSISTENCY of FRESH concrete — how easily it flows and compacts.**

> **It says nothing whatever about STRENGTH**, which is the trap in options (a) and (b).

**Why slump and strength are not the same thing — and are in fact opposed:**

> **A HIGHER slump generally means MORE WATER, and more water means LOWER strength.**

> **Abrams' law: strength depends primarily on the WATER–CEMENT RATIO.**

> **So the two properties pull in opposite directions**, and the mix design is a compromise between placing the concrete and achieving its strength.

> **Adding water on site to make concrete easier to place is the commonest and most damaging malpractice in construction** — it improves the slump and ruins the strength, and the damage is invisible until the cubes are crushed 28 days later.

> **The correct remedy is a PLASTICISER**, which increases workability **without adding water** — that is the entire purpose of the admixture.

**Recommended slump values (IS 456):**

| Placing condition | Slump |
|---|---|
| **Lightly reinforced, VIBRATED** | **25 – 75 mm** |
| Heavily reinforced, vibrated | 50 – 100 mm |
| **Hand-compacted / trench fill** | **75 – 125 mm** |
| **PUMPED concrete** | **100 – 150 mm** |
| **Mass concrete, roads (vibrated)** | **25 – 50 mm** |

> **The required slump depends on HOW the concrete will be PLACED and COMPACTED — not on the strength wanted.** A stiff mix placed with good vibration is stronger and perfectly acceptable; the same mix placed by hand would be honeycombed.

**The types of slump, which the test also reveals:**

| Slump form | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **TRUE slump** | Uniform subsidence — **the only valid result** |
| **SHEAR slump** | Top half slides off — **lean or harsh mix; RETEST** |
| **COLLAPSE slump** | Concrete collapses completely — **too wet** |

> **A shear or collapse slump means the number should not be recorded at all** — the test is only valid for a true slump, and reporting a shear slump as a workability figure is meaningless.

**The other workability tests, and where each belongs:**

| Test | Suited to |
|---|---|
| **SLUMP** | **Medium to high workability** — the site standard |
| **COMPACTING FACTOR** | **LOW workability**, where slump is insensitive |
| **VEE-BEE consistometer** | **VERY LOW workability / dry mixes** |
| Flow table | Very high workability, flowing concrete |

> **Slump becomes useless for very dry mixes** — it simply reads zero across a range of quite different consistencies. **That is why the compacting factor and Vee-Bee tests exist**, and why a road or a dam mix is assessed differently from a building mix.

examTip.trick: **Slump measures FRESH concrete's consistency — it says nothing about STRENGTH.** In fact the two are opposed: higher slump usually means more water, and more water means lower strength.
examTip.trap: **Adding water on site to improve placing is the most damaging malpractice in construction** — it fixes the slump and ruins the strength, invisibly, until the 28-day cubes fail. Use a **plasticiser** instead.
examTip.mnemonic: **Only a TRUE slump counts.** A **shear** slump means a harsh mix (retest); a **collapse** slump means too wet. And slump reads zero for dry mixes — use **compacting factor** or **Vee-Bee** there.

questions.stem: Under sluices are provided at:
options: The same height as the river bed level
At a height more than that of the cross regulator
questions.solution:
**At the same height as the river bed level.**

**Why that level and no other:**

> **The under-sluice's job is to FLUSH SILT out of the pocket in front of the head regulator.** Silt settles on the **BED**, so the sluice must be able to draw from bed level.

> **Set it HIGHER and the silt cannot escape** — the sluice would pass clear surface water while the deposit stayed behind, defeating its entire purpose.

> **Set it BELOW the bed and it would form a permanent depression** that traps silt rather than discharging it, and it could not be flushed clear by the river's own flow.

> **Bed level is the only level at which flushing works**, which is why the answer follows from the function rather than from memory.

**The relative crest levels at a headworks** — the arrangement that makes the whole thing work:

| Structure | Crest level |
|---|---|
| **UNDER-SLUICE** | **LOWEST — at river bed level** |
| **HEAD REGULATOR** | **Higher — typically 1.0 to 1.5 m above the under-sluice crest** |
| **Weir crest** | **Highest** — sets the pond level |

> **The head regulator sill is deliberately RAISED ABOVE the under-sluice crest**, and that difference is the second half of the silt-exclusion strategy.

> **Coarse sediment travels near the bed; cleaner water flows above it.** By setting the canal's sill higher, the canal draws from the **upper, cleaner layer** while the bottom layer is flushed away through the under-sluice.

> **The divide wall confines the silt to the pocket; the under-sluice removes it; the raised sill keeps what remains out of the canal.** Three devices, one purpose — and the level in this question is the pivot of all three.

**What the under-sluices do, in full:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Flush accumulated silt** from the pocket | The primary purpose |
| **Pass the LOW flows** of the river | So the weir need not be overtopped year-round |
| **Maintain a defined river channel** near the regulator | Prevents the river wandering away from the intake |
| **Provide a scouring current** past the head regulator | Keeps the approach clear |
| **Discharge part of the flood** | Adds capacity |

> **Passing the low flows matters more than it appears**: it keeps a live channel adjacent to the canal head throughout the dry season, so the intake never finds itself stranded behind a silt bar.

**Why option (c) is a category confusion:**

> **A CROSS REGULATOR is not at the headworks at all.** It sits **ACROSS the parent canal**, downstream of an offtake, to raise the water level so the offtake can draw at low supply.

> **Comparing an under-sluice's level with a cross regulator's is comparing structures in two different places** — which is precisely why the option sounds plausible and is not.

**The operating modes** worth knowing:

| Mode | Operation |
|---|---|
| **STILL POND** | **Under-sluice gates CLOSED** while the canal draws; silt settles in the pocket, then the gates are opened to flush it. **Better silt exclusion** |
| **SEMI-OPEN FLOW** | Sluices kept partly open continuously; simpler to operate, **less effective** |

> **Still pond gives better silt exclusion but needs disciplined operation** — the pocket must actually be flushed on a schedule, and where it is not, the still pond degenerates into a silt trap that eventually feeds the canal.

examTip.trick: **Silt settles on the BED, so the sluice must draw from bed level.** Higher and the silt cannot escape; lower and it becomes a trap that cannot be flushed. The function fixes the level.
examTip.trap: **A CROSS regulator is not at the headworks at all** — it sits across the PARENT canal downstream of an offtake. Option (c) compares structures in two different places.
examTip.mnemonic: **Under-sluice lowest (bed level), head regulator sill 1.0–1.5 m higher, weir crest highest.** The raised sill lets the canal draw the **cleaner upper layer** while the silty bottom layer is flushed away.

questions.stem: A cross regulator is provided on the main canal at the downstream of the off-take canal:
options: To regulate water supply in the off-take canal
To increase the water head upstream when the main canal is running with low supplies
To overflow excessive flow of water
questions.solution:
**To increase the water head upstream when the main canal is running with low supplies.**

**The arrangement, and why it is built this way:**

> **An offtake canal draws from the main canal by GRAVITY.** It can only do so if the water level in the main canal is high enough at the offtake point.

> **When the main canal runs at LOW SUPPLY, its water level falls — and the offtake gets nothing.**

> **The CROSS REGULATOR is placed ACROSS the main canal JUST DOWNSTREAM of the offtake.** Closing it partially **PONDS the water UPSTREAM**, raising the level at the offtake point so the offtake can draw its full share.

> **It is a level-control device, not a flow-control device** — and the distinction is the whole answer.

**Why it must be DOWNSTREAM of the offtake:**

> **The ponding raises the level UPSTREAM of the regulator.** If it were placed upstream of the offtake, the raised level would be in the wrong reach and the offtake would still be starved.

> **The position follows directly from where the water is wanted**, which makes it a fact to reason out rather than remember.

**HEAD regulator versus CROSS regulator** — the pair that is constantly confused:

| | **HEAD regulator** | **CROSS regulator** |
|---|---|---|
| **Position** | **At the HEAD of the OFFTAKE** | **ACROSS the PARENT (main) canal** |
| **Controls** | **The DISCHARGE entering the offtake** | **The WATER LEVEL in the main canal** |
| Option here | **(a) describes THIS** | The answer |

> **Option (a) is the HEAD regulator's function**, offered as the natural distractor — and it catches anyone who reads only "regulator" and "off-take canal".

> **The two are built as a PAIR at every offtake point**, which is why they are so easily swapped: the head regulator meters the flow into the branch, the cross regulator guarantees there is enough head for it to be metered at all.

**The cross regulator's other functions:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Raise the upstream level** at low supply | The primary purpose |
| **Control the discharge** passing downstream | Effectively a control point |
| **Serve as a ROAD BRIDGE** | The platform commonly carries a crossing |
| **Help in CLOSING the downstream reach** for maintenance | Isolates a length of canal |
| Reduce the number of falls needed | By allowing level control |

> **Being able to isolate a reach is a substantial practical benefit** — it lets one length of canal be dewatered and repaired while the rest continues to run.

**Why option (c) is wrong** is worth pinning down:

> **Overflowing excess water is the function of an ESCAPE**, not a regulator.

| Structure | Function |
|---|---|
| **ESCAPE** | **Discharges SURPLUS water out of the canal** — a safety device |
| **FALL / drop** | Lowers the canal bed where the ground slopes more steeply than the canal |
| **OUTLET / module** | Delivers water to a **watercourse or field channel** |
| **Cross-drainage work** | Carries the canal past a **natural drain** |

> **An ESCAPE protects the canal from breaching** when supplies exceed demand — the canal banks are earthen and cannot survive overtopping, so surplus must be shed deliberately at a controlled point.

**And the cross-drainage family**, since it shares the word "cross": **AQUEDUCT** (canal over drain, drain flows freely), **SYPHON AQUEDUCT** (canal over drain, drain flows **under pressure**), **SUPER-PASSAGE** (drain over canal), **CANAL SYPHON** (canal under drain, canal under pressure), and **LEVEL CROSSING** (the two mix).

> **The naming rule: the structure is named after WHAT GOES ON TOP**, and "syphon" is added when the lower channel runs under pressure.

examTip.trick: **It ponds water UPSTREAM, so it must sit DOWNSTREAM of the offtake** — otherwise the raised level is in the wrong reach. The position follows from where the head is wanted.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is the HEAD regulator's function.** The two are built as a pair at every offtake: the head regulator meters the flow, the cross regulator guarantees the head to meter it with.
examTip.mnemonic: **Overflowing surplus is an ESCAPE's job, not a regulator's.** And in cross-drainage the structure is **named after what goes ON TOP** — aqueduct (canal over), super-passage (drain over).

questions.stem: If m₁ and m₂ are the members of two individual simple trusses forming a compound truss, the compound truss will be rigid and determinate if:
questions.solution:
**m = m₁ + m₂ + 3.**

**Why exactly THREE extra members:**

> **Each simple truss is a RIGID BODY in its own right.** Two separate rigid bodies in a plane have **SIX degrees of freedom** between them (three each: two translations and a rotation).

> **Considered as one connected body, the assembly has THREE degrees of freedom.**

> **So THREE constraints must be removed — and each connecting member removes exactly one degree of freedom.**

> **Hence three connecting members: m = m₁ + m₂ + 3.** ✓

**The three standard ways of connecting them**, all giving the same count:

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **Three non-concurrent, non-parallel BARS** | The general case |
| **One PIN plus one BAR** | The pin removes 2, the bar 1 = **3** |
| Three-hinged arch arrangement | Two pins and a bar, with a release |

> **A pin is worth TWO bars**, which is why "one pin and one bar" satisfies the same requirement as three bars.

**The essential condition on the three bars:**

> **They must be NEITHER CONCURRENT NOR PARALLEL.**

> **Three concurrent bars still permit ROTATION about the common point; three parallel bars still permit TRANSLATION perpendicular to them.**

> **Such an arrangement is called CRITICAL or GEOMETRICALLY UNSTABLE** — the member count is right, the equations look satisfied, and the structure still collapses.

> **This is the single most important caution in the whole topic**: **counting members is NECESSARY but NOT SUFFICIENT.** The arrangement must also be checked.

**The general determinacy condition for a plane truss:**

> **m + r = 2j**

| Case | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **m + r = 2j** | **Determinate** (if properly arranged) |
| **m + r > 2j** | **Indeterminate** — degree = m + r − 2j |
| **m + r < 2j** | **UNSTABLE — a MECHANISM** |

> where **m** = members, **r** = support reactions, **j** = joints. **The 2j comes from two equilibrium equations (ΣH = 0, ΣV = 0) at each pin joint.**

**The three truss classifications:**

| Type | Formed by |
|---|---|
| **SIMPLE** | Starting from a **TRIANGLE** and adding **two members and one joint** at a time |
| **COMPOUND** | **Two simple trusses joined by three constraints** ← this question |
| **COMPLEX** | Neither of the above |

> **Simple and compound trusses can be solved by the METHOD OF JOINTS and the METHOD OF SECTIONS. A COMPLEX truss cannot** — it needs Henneberg's method of member substitution.

**And the method of SECTIONS is the practical tool for a compound truss:**

> **A section cut through the three connecting members yields all three forces directly from the three equations of equilibrium**, without working joint by joint through both trusses.

> **Three members cut, three equations — the count matches exactly**, which is not a coincidence: it is the same argument that gave the answer to this question.

examTip.trick: **Two rigid bodies have 6 degrees of freedom; one connected body has 3.** So **three** constraints must be removed, and each bar removes one. That derives the answer rather than recalling it.
examTip.trap: **The three bars must be NEITHER CONCURRENT NOR PARALLEL.** Concurrent bars permit rotation, parallel ones permit translation — the count is right and the structure still collapses. Counting is necessary, not sufficient.
examTip.mnemonic: **A PIN is worth TWO bars**, so "one pin + one bar" also gives 3. And a **section cut through the three connecting members** solves all three forces at once — three cuts, three equations.

questions.stem: Due to long term loading, when all water comes out of the pores it is called:
questions.solution:
**Consolidation.**

> **Note this paper asks the same principle twice** — Q28 phrases it as "expulsion of pore water from soil", and this question adds the defining qualifier **"due to LONG TERM loading"**, which is the second half of the definition.

**The two qualifiers that together define consolidation:**

| Qualifier | Excludes |
|---|---|
| **Expulsion of WATER** | Compaction, which expels **air** |
| **Under LONG-TERM (sustained) load** | Any instantaneous process |

> **Both are present in this stem**, which makes the identification unambiguous.

**Consolidation versus compaction, in full:**

| | **CONSOLIDATION** | **COMPACTION** |
|---|---|---|
| **Expels** | **WATER** | **AIR** |
| Soil state | **Fully SATURATED** | Partially saturated |
| Cause | **Sustained LOAD** | **Mechanical energy** |
| **Time** | **YEARS** | **Minutes** |
| Nature | **NATURAL response** | **ARTIFICIAL operation** |
| Test | **OEDOMETER** | **PROCTOR** |

**Why it takes so long:**

> **The water must physically FLOW OUT**, and clay's permeability is below **10⁻⁹ m/s**.

> **t = T_v d²/c_v**

> **The time varies with the SQUARE of the drainage path length** — so doubling a layer's thickness **quadruples** the settlement time.

| Drainage | Path length d |
|---|---|
| **DOUBLE drainage** (pervious above and below) | **H/2** |
| **SINGLE drainage** (pervious one side only) | **H** |

> **Double drainage is FOUR TIMES faster than single**, from the d² relation alone — which is why identifying the drainage boundaries correctly matters more than almost any other input.

> **Getting this wrong by assuming double drainage where only one face drains under-predicts the settlement time by a factor of four**, and that is a serious error in a construction programme.

**Terzaghi's one-dimensional theory** and its assumptions:

> Soil **homogeneous and fully saturated**; water and solids **incompressible**; **Darcy's law valid**; **compression and flow are ONE-DIMENSIONAL (vertical)**; and **c_v is constant.**

> **The one-dimensional assumption is the significant limitation** — it holds under a wide loaded area but not beneath a small footing, where the soil can also squeeze sideways.

**The degree of consolidation:**

| U | T_v |
|---|---|
| 50% | **0.197** |
| 90% | **0.848** |

> **Note that reaching 90% takes over FOUR TIMES as long as reaching 50%** — consolidation slows dramatically as it proceeds, and the last few percent may take as long as everything before it.

> **This is why 100% consolidation is never waited for**, and why preloading schemes are designed to reach a target such as 90% rather than completion.

**And the practical remedy — VERTICAL DRAINS:**

> **They do not reduce the total settlement.** They shorten the **drainage path**, converting slow vertical drainage into rapid horizontal drainage.

> **Since t ∝ d², halving the path quarters the time.** A twenty-year settlement can be completed in one or two years of preloading — **before** the structure is built, which is the entire object.

examTip.trick: **Two qualifiers define it: expulsion of WATER, under LONG-TERM load.** Both are in the stem, which excludes compaction (air, instantaneous) unambiguously.
examTip.trap: **"Densification" names the RESULT, not the mechanism** — both processes densify. And **this paper asks the same principle twice** (see Q28), which is worth noticing in the exam itself.
examTip.mnemonic: **t ∝ d², so DOUBLE drainage is FOUR TIMES faster than single.** And reaching 90% (T_v = 0.848) takes over four times as long as reaching 50% (0.197) — consolidation slows dramatically as it proceeds.

questions.stem: Scour depth and frost depth are parameters that determine:
questions.solution:
**Depth of foundation.**

**Why both parameters point to DEPTH specifically:**

> **Both describe a zone of ground that CANNOT BE RELIED UPON**, and the foundation must be taken **BELOW** it.

| Parameter | The unreliable zone |
|---|---|
| **SCOUR depth** | Ground that a **flood may WASH AWAY** |
| **FROST depth** | Ground subject to **freeze–thaw HEAVE and softening** |

> **Neither says anything about the TYPE of foundation or the superstructure** — they answer only the question "how deep?", which is why the discrimination is clean.

**Scour — and why it dominates near water:**

> **Lacey's normal scour depth: R = 1.35(q²/f)^{1/3}**, multiplied by a **location factor** — **2.0 at a pier nose, 2.75 at a guide bank head.**

> **A foundation founded above the scour level will be UNDERMINED in a flood, however adequate its bearing pressure.**

> **SCOUR IS THE LEADING CAUSE OF BRIDGE FAILURE WORLDWIDE**, which is why bridge foundations near rivers are taken so much deeper than bearing capacity alone would require.

**Frost — and why it matters even where bearing is good:**

> **Water expands about 9% on freezing**, and worse, **ICE LENSES grow by drawing further water up through the soil by capillary action.**

> **The heave is therefore far larger than 9% of the water present** — it can reach many centimetres, and it is **NOT uniform**, so it distorts the structure differentially.

> **And the thaw is as damaging as the freeze**: the melting lens leaves the soil **saturated and very weak**, which is why spring thaw damage to pavements is so severe.

> **SILT is the most frost-susceptible soil**, because it has **both a high capillary rise and enough permeability to feed a growing lens quickly.** Clay has the rise but is too impermeable; sand is permeable but has too little rise.

**The full list of factors fixing foundation DEPTH:**

| Factor | Note |
|---|---|
| **Adequate bearing stratum** | The basic requirement |
| **Below SCOUR depth** | Near watercourses |
| **Below FROST depth** | In cold regions |
| **Below the ZONE OF SEASONAL MOISTURE CHANGE** | **Critical in EXPANSIVE (black cotton) soils** |
| **Below tree root influence** | Trees dry the soil and cause shrinkage |
| Below adjacent excavations and services | — |
| **Rankine's minimum: D = (p/γ)[(1−sinφ)/(1+sinφ)]²** | A theoretical minimum |

> **In EXPANSIVE soils the seasonal moisture zone governs**, and it is the reason such soils cause more building damage worldwide than any other geotechnical problem — the movement is **cyclic**, so the damage accumulates season after season.

**What determines the TYPE of foundation** — option (b), for contrast:

| Factor | Leads to |
|---|---|
| Load magnitude and pattern | Isolated, combined or raft |
| **Depth of a competent stratum** | **Shallow if near; PILES if deep** |
| Overlapping footings (> ~50% of plan area) | **RAFT** |
| Water table position | Affects both type and construction method |
| Adjacent structures | — |

> **Depth and type are decided by different questions**, and keeping them apart is the point this item tests.

**And a useful minimum:** **IS 1904 requires at least 500 mm** below finished ground level for any foundation, whatever the calculations suggest — to clear topsoil, organic matter and surface disturbance.

examTip.trick: **Both parameters describe ground that CANNOT be relied upon** — washed away by flood, or heaved by frost. The foundation goes BELOW it. Neither says anything about type.
examTip.trap: **Depth and TYPE are decided by different questions.** Type follows from load pattern and where a competent stratum lies; depth follows from what must be got beneath.
examTip.mnemonic: **SILT is the most frost-susceptible soil** — high capillary rise *and* enough permeability to feed an ice lens. And in **expansive soils** the seasonal moisture zone governs, because the movement is **cyclic** and the damage accumulates.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT included during scoping of an EIA?
options: Conducting impact assessment and contingency planning
questions.solution:
**Conducting impact assessment and contingency planning** — that is the *next* stage, not scoping.

**What SCOPING actually is:**

> **Scoping DEFINES THE STUDY. It does not carry the study out.**

| Scoping does | Note |
|---|---|
| **Identify the KEY ISSUES** worth studying | Focuses effort |
| **Set the boundaries** — spatial and temporal | How far, how long |
| **Set the CRITERIA** for evaluation | ← option (b), which **IS** scoping |
| Identify **alternatives** to be examined | Including the no-project option |
| **Consult the public and stakeholders** | A legal requirement in Nepal |
| Produce the **Terms of Reference (ToR)** | The scoping report's output |

> **The output of scoping is a ToR — a specification for the work to follow.**

> **Conducting the impact assessment is what the ToR then commissions**, and contingency planning belongs to the **Environmental Management Plan** later still. Both sit **downstream** of scoping.

**The EIA process in order:**

| Stage | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **1. SCREENING** | **Is an EIA needed at all?** IEE, EIA, or neither |
| **2. SCOPING** | **WHAT should the study cover?** → produces the **ToR** ← |
| **3. Baseline study** | The existing environmental condition |
| **4. IMPACT PREDICTION and evaluation** | ← option (a) belongs here |
| **5. Mitigation and the EMP** | Including contingency planning |
| **6. Review and approval** | By the competent authority |
| **7. MONITORING and AUDITING** | **After implementation** |

> **SCREENING and SCOPING are the two most confused stages**, and the distinction is clean: **screening asks WHETHER a study is needed; scoping asks WHAT it should contain.**

> **And MONITORING is the stage most often neglected in practice** — an EIA approved and then never checked against what actually happened is a document rather than a safeguard.

**A caution about this particular question:** **option (c), "raising funds", is not part of scoping either** — it is not an EIA activity at all. Two of the four options therefore fall outside scoping, which makes the item imperfectly framed. **Option (a) is the keyed and intended answer** because it names a *specific later stage of the EIA process*, which is the discrimination the question is testing; option (c) is simply unrelated.

**The Nepali legal framework** (Environment Protection Act 2076 and Rules 2077):

| Level | Applies to | Approving body |
|---|---|---|
| **Brief Environmental Study (BES)** | Smallest projects | Concerned body |
| **IEE** | Medium projects | **Concerned MINISTRY** |
| **EIA** | Large projects | **Ministry of Forests and Environment** |

> **The threshold is set by the SCHEDULES to the Rules**, which list project types and sizes — so screening is largely a matter of reading a table rather than exercising judgement.

> **PUBLIC CONSULTATION is mandatory**, including a **public notice** and a **public hearing** in the affected area — and its omission is a common ground for an EIA being challenged.

verification.notes: Imperfectly framed in the source. Option (c) "raising funds" also falls outside scoping — it is not an EIA activity at all — so two of the four options are arguably correct. The keyed answer (a) is retained because it names a specific LATER STAGE of the EIA process, which is the discrimination the item is testing, and the solution states the ambiguity openly rather than concealing it.

examTip.trick: **Scoping DEFINES the study; it does not carry it out.** Its output is a **Terms of Reference**. Conducting the impact assessment is what that ToR then commissions.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is also outside scoping** — the item is imperfectly framed. (a) is keyed because it names a specific *later stage* of the EIA process, which is the intended discrimination.
examTip.mnemonic: **SCREENING asks WHETHER a study is needed; SCOPING asks WHAT it should contain.** And **MONITORING** is the stage most neglected — an EIA never checked against outcomes is a document, not a safeguard.

questions.stem: Which statement is true about a hydroelectric plant?
options: It has a high capital cost and takes a long time to construct
It is more environmentally friendly in operation compared to thermal plants
Its effectiveness reduces with time as the reservoir silts up
questions.solution:
**All of the above** — the three statements are the standard characterisation of hydropower, and they are not in conflict.

**Taking each in turn:**

> **(a) HIGH CAPITAL COST, LONG CONSTRUCTION.** True, and characteristic. **Hydropower's cost is almost entirely UP FRONT — civil works, tunnels, dams and access roads.** Construction periods of five to ten years are normal for a large scheme.

> **(b) ENVIRONMENTALLY FRIENDLIER IN OPERATION.** True in the sense meant: **no fuel is burnt, so there are no combustion emissions.** It is a renewable resource driven by the hydrological cycle.

> **(c) LESS EFFECTIVE WITH TIME.** True, and the reason is **RESERVOIR SEDIMENTATION.** The reservoir progressively fills with silt, reducing live storage and therefore the plant's ability to regulate flow.

**Why (a) and (b) are not contradictory** — the key to the whole economics of hydropower:

| | Hydropower | Thermal |
|---|---|---|
| **CAPITAL cost** | **VERY HIGH** | Lower |
| **RUNNING cost** | **VERY LOW — no fuel** | **High — fuel dominates** |
| **Life** | **50 – 100 years** | 25 – 30 years |
| **Start-up time** | **MINUTES** | **HOURS** |

> **Hydropower trades high capital cost for near-zero running cost over a very long life** — which is exactly why the choice of DISCOUNT RATE dominates its appraisal.

> **At 12%, a benefit 50 years out is worth about 0.3% of face value** — so a high discount rate makes a hundred-year asset look poor, judged almost entirely on its first two decades.

**And the qualification on (b)** worth stating honestly:

> **"Environmentally friendly" applies to OPERATION, not to the whole project.** Large storage schemes bring real impacts: **inundation of land, displacement of people, blocked fish migration, altered downstream flow regimes, and methane from decomposing vegetation in tropical reservoirs.**

> **This is why EIA is mandatory for hydropower**, and why run-of-river schemes — which need no large reservoir — are often preferred in Nepal despite their inability to store water.

**Reservoir sedimentation, which drives (c):**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Trap efficiency** | The proportion of incoming sediment retained |
| **DEAD storage** | Volume deliberately allowed for sediment |
| **Design life** | Often taken as **50–100 years** to fill the dead storage |
| **Catchment treatment** | Afforestation, check dams — reduces the supply at source |
| Flushing / sluicing | Removes deposited sediment during floods |

> **Nepal's rivers carry exceptionally high sediment loads** — young, rapidly rising mountains with steep unstable slopes — so sedimentation is a first-order design problem here, not a footnote.

> **It also causes ABRASION of turbine runners**, particularly where the sediment is quartz-rich, which is why **desanding basins** are essential in Himalayan schemes and why runner replacement is a recurring operating cost.

**Nepal's position:** theoretical potential about **83,000 MW**, economically feasible about **42,000 MW**, and **most developed schemes are RUN-OF-RIVER**, which produce far less in the dry season when demand peaks — the central mismatch in the country's power system, and the argument for storage.

verification.notes: The source prints the stem as "Which statement is not true about hydroelectric plant" while keying (d) "All of the above" — an inconsistency, since all three statements are in fact true of hydropower (high capital cost, low operating emissions, and loss of effectiveness through reservoir sedimentation). The stem's polarity has been corrected to "Which statement is TRUE", which makes the item internally consistent and keeps the source's keyed letter (d) intact.

examTip.trick: **(a) and (b) are not contradictory**: hydropower trades **very high capital cost** for **near-zero running cost** over a **50–100 year** life. That trade-off is the whole economics of the technology.
examTip.trap: **"Environmentally friendly" applies to OPERATION only.** Large storage schemes inundate land, displace people, block fish migration and alter downstream flows — which is why EIA is mandatory.
examTip.mnemonic: **Nepal's rivers carry exceptional sediment loads** — young mountains, steep unstable slopes. Sedimentation reduces storage *and* abrades turbine runners, which is why **desanding basins** are essential here.

questions.stem: The highway with the highest mobility but the least accessibility is:
questions.solution:
**The national highway.**

**The mobility–accessibility trade-off** — the organising idea of the entire road hierarchy:

| Road class | **MOBILITY** | **ACCESSIBILITY** | Function |
|---|---|---|---|
| **National highway / expressway** | **HIGHEST** | **LOWEST** | **MOVEMENT over long distances** |
| State highway | High | Low | Inter-district movement |
| District road | Moderate | Moderate | Both, in balance |
| **Village road / local street** | **LOWEST** | **HIGHEST** | **ACCESS to property** |

> **The two are INVERSELY related, and necessarily so.**

**Why they must conflict:**

> **ACCESS means the ability to enter and leave the road — junctions, driveways, frontage development.**

> **But every access point is a place where vehicles slow, stop, turn and cross — which is exactly what destroys MOBILITY** and creates conflict points.

> **So a road cannot maximise both.** Serving property access and serving through movement are opposed requirements, and the hierarchy exists to let different roads specialise in one or the other.

**The extreme case makes it vivid:**

> **An EXPRESSWAY has FULLY CONTROLLED ACCESS** — entry and exit only at grade-separated interchanges, with **no frontage access whatever.**

> **That total sacrifice of accessibility is precisely what buys its very high mobility.** Nothing enters or leaves except at designed points, so no vehicle ever slows for a turning movement.

**Why mixing the functions is so damaging — the classic planning failure:**

> **Ribbon development along a highway** — shops, houses and workshops fronting directly onto it — **destroys the road's mobility function while it is still classified as a highway.**

> **Speeds fall, accidents rise, and the investment in a long-distance route is lost.**

> **This is one of the most visible road problems in Nepal**, and it is why **control of the RIGHT OF WAY** matters so much: **encroachment is cheap to prevent and ruinous to reverse.**

**Nepal's road classification (Nepal Road Standard):**

| Class | Right of way | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **National highway (NH)** | **50 m** | Connects **major regions and the capital** |
| **Feeder road (F)** | **30 m** | Connects district headquarters to the NH |
| **District road (D)** | **20 m** | Within a district |
| **Village road (V)** | **15 m** | **Local access** |

> **The right-of-way width falls with the class**, because a lower-class road needs no reserve for future widening to expressway standard.

**The corresponding design standards:**

| Provision | National highway |
|---|---|
| Design speed (plain) | **120 km/h** for Class I |
| Design speed (steep terrain) | **60 km/h** |
| **Carriageway** | **7.0 m** two-lane |
| **Camber** | **2.5 – 3%** bituminous |

> **Design speed drops with terrain, not with importance** — a national highway in the hills is designed for 60 km/h and remains a national highway. **Terrain governs geometry; class governs function.**

examTip.trick: **Mobility and accessibility are INVERSELY related, and must be.** Every access point is where vehicles slow, stop and turn — exactly what destroys through movement.
examTip.trap: **Design speed drops with TERRAIN, not with class.** A national highway in the hills is designed for 60 km/h and is still a national highway. Terrain governs geometry; class governs function.
examTip.mnemonic: **An EXPRESSWAY sacrifices accessibility completely — no frontage access at all — and that is exactly what buys its mobility.** Conversely, **ribbon development** destroys a highway while it is still called one.

questions.stem: Guide banks are provided in a river to:
questions.solution:
**To canalize the flow.**

**What a guide bank does:**

> **A guide bank is an embankment built on each side of a hydraulic structure, extending upstream and downstream, to CONFINE and DIRECT the river through the structure's waterway.**

> **An alluvial river in flood spreads across a wide belt and may shift its course entirely.** A weir, barrage or bridge occupies only a limited width.

> **The guide bank forces the river into that width and holds it there** — which is exactly what "canalizing the flow" means.

**The two functions, in order of importance:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Prevent OUTFLANKING** | **The river cannot go AROUND the structure** — the primary purpose |
| **Ensure axial, non-oblique approach** | Flow enters the structure straight rather than at an angle |

> **OUTFLANKING is the failure mode guide banks exist to prevent**, and it is a total failure: the river simply abandons the structure and cuts a new channel beside it, leaving a barrage standing in a dry bed.

> **That has happened to real structures**, and it is why guide banks are treated as an essential component rather than an optional protection.

**Why the other options are wrong** — and each is a distinct kind of error:

| Option | Why wrong |
|---|---|
| **(a) Increase depth** | **A CONSEQUENCE, not a purpose.** Confining the flow does deepen it, but that is a side effect |
| **(b) Decrease velocity** | **The OPPOSITE happens** — narrowing the section **INCREASES** velocity |
| **(d) Reduce flood peak** | **A RESERVOIR does that.** A guide bank affects the flow's path, not its magnitude |

> **Option (b) is worth pausing on**: by continuity, forcing the same discharge through a narrower width must **raise** the velocity — which is why guide banks need heavy protection and why scour at their heads is so severe.

**Bell's (Bell's / Bell bund) design proportions:**

| Element | Typical value |
|---|---|
| **Upstream length** | **1.0 to 1.5 times** the structure's waterway |
| **Downstream length** | **0.2 to 0.4 times** the waterway |
| **Shape** | **Bell-mouthed (curved) heads** |
| **Side slopes** | **2:1** |
| Free board | 1.2 – 1.5 m above the design flood |

> **The BELL-MOUTHED head is not decoration.** A curved head lets the flow turn gradually into the waterway; a square end would cause severe local eddying and vastly deeper scour.

> **The upstream arm is far longer than the downstream arm** because the river must be gathered in gradually but released comparatively quickly.

**Scour at the head — the critical design point:**

> **The guide bank HEAD takes the SEVEREST scour of any point in the works: a location factor of 2.75 on Lacey's normal scour depth**, deeper even than a bridge pier nose (2.0).

> **That is why the head carries the heaviest stone protection and the largest LAUNCHING APRON.**

**The launching apron** is the companion device:

> **Loose stone laid horizontally at the toe. As the river scours beside it, the edge stone FALLS into the hole, armouring the newly exposed slope.**

> **It is DESIGNED TO BE DESTROYED in a controlled way** — the stone quantity is calculated to cover the anticipated scour slope (usually **2:1**) down to the deepest expected scour level.

**The other river training works**, for contrast: **SPURS/groynes** (project into the river to deflect flow from a bank), **MARGINAL BUNDS** (confine floodwater to the flood plain), **CUT-OFFS** (shorten a meander), and **PITCHING/revetment** (armour a bank in place).

examTip.trick: **Guide banks exist to prevent OUTFLANKING** — the river going *around* the structure and leaving a barrage in a dry bed. Confining it to the waterway is exactly "canalizing the flow".
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is the opposite of the truth** — narrowing the section by continuity **increases** velocity. And option (a) is a *consequence* of confinement, not its purpose.
examTip.mnemonic: **The guide bank HEAD takes the severest scour anywhere in the works — factor 2.75, deeper than a pier nose (2.0).** Hence the **bell-mouthed** shape and the **launching apron**, designed to be destroyed in a controlled way.

questions.stem: Chlorination of water does not decrease:
questions.solution:
**Dissolved oxygen.**

> **Note this paper asks the same fact twice** — Q31 phrases it as "which is not affected by chlorination". Recognising a repeat is worth a mark in itself.

**Why chlorine does not touch dissolved oxygen:**

> **Chlorine's action is on MICRO-ORGANISMS and on REDUCED substances. It does not react with O₂**, and it neither adds nor removes it from solution.

> **The two are chemically independent.**

**What chlorine DOES reduce — the other two options:**

| Substance | Effect of chlorination |
|---|---|
| **ORGANIC matter** | **Oxidised** — part of the chlorine demand |
| **IRON (Fe²⁺)** | **Oxidised to Fe³⁺**, which precipitates and can be filtered out |
| Manganese, H₂S, ammonia | Likewise oxidised — all chlorine demand |

> **Iron and manganese removal by chlorination is a real and standard practice**, not an incidental effect: soluble ferrous iron is oxidised to insoluble ferric hydroxide, which the filters then remove.

> **That is why the answer cannot be (d)** — two of the three are genuinely decreased.

**CHLORINE DEMAND — the concept that organises this:**

> **Chlorine demand = the chlorine consumed by substances in the water before any residual can appear.**

> **Applied dose = demand + residual**

> **Under-dosing leaves no residual at all**, because everything applied is consumed — which is why a small dose can leave water effectively undisinfected.

**BREAKPOINT chlorination:**

| Stage | What happens |
|---|---|
| 1 | Chlorine consumed by the **demand** — no residual |
| 2 | **CHLORAMINES form** with ammonia — combined residual rises |
| 3 | **Chloramines DESTROYED** — residual falls to the **BREAKPOINT** |
| 4 | **FREE residual appears** and rises with dose |

> **Beyond the breakpoint, further chlorine remains as FREE residual** — and the dose is set to land there.

| Residual | Character |
|---|---|
| **COMBINED (chloramine)** | **Weaker but LONGER-LASTING** — persists through the distribution network |
| **FREE (HOCl/OCl⁻)** | **Stronger but decays faster** |

**The disinfection chemistry:**

> **HOCl ⇌ H⁺ + OCl⁻**, and **HOCl is about 80 times more effective than OCl⁻.**

> **Raising the pH shifts the balance toward the weak OCl⁻**, so more chlorine is needed for the same kill. **Chlorinate below pH 7.5 where possible.**

> **Bleaching powder RAISES the pH; chlorine GAS LOWERS it** — the two agents pull in opposite directions, which matters for a water already near the limit.

**Requirements for effective chlorination:**

| Factor | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Contact time** | **≥ 30 minutes** |
| **Free residual** | **0.1 – 0.2 mg/l** |
| **TURBIDITY** | **LOW — particles SHIELD pathogens** |
| pH | Below 7.5 preferably |

> **Turbidity is decisive**: micro-organisms hide inside suspended particles, so **chlorinating turbid water does not work reliably however large the dose.** Hence the rule — **clarify FIRST, disinfect LAST.**

**And the by-product to be aware of:** chlorine reacting with natural organic matter forms **TRIHALOMETHANES (THMs)**, themselves regulated — so removing organic matter *before* chlorination serves two purposes at once, cutting the demand and cutting the by-products.

examTip.trick: **Chlorine acts on micro-organisms and REDUCED substances — never on O₂.** Chemically independent, so DO passes through unchanged.
examTip.trap: **(d) is wrong because iron and organic matter ARE genuinely decreased** — ferrous iron is oxidised to ferric hydroxide and filtered out, which is standard practice, not an incidental effect.
examTip.mnemonic: **Applied dose = demand + residual**, so under-dosing leaves NO residual at all. And **turbidity SHIELDS pathogens** — clarify first, disinfect last, whatever the dose. (This paper asks the same fact at Q31.)

questions.stem: A sanitary sewer is expected to run:
questions.solution:
**Two-thirds full.**

> **A sanitary sewer is designed as an OPEN CHANNEL flowing PARTLY FULL, not as a pressure pipe.**

**Why a sewer must never be designed to run full:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **VENTILATION** | **The space above the flow carries away sewer gases** |
| **Peak flow allowance** | Sewage flow varies hourly; the spare depth absorbs the peak |
| **Future growth** | Population and connections increase over the design life |
| **Free surface** | Gravity flow requires one; a full pipe becomes a pressure main |

> **VENTILATION is the reason that matters most**, and it is not a matter of comfort.

**The gas problem, stated properly:**

> **Sewage turning SEPTIC releases HYDROGEN SULPHIDE (H₂S).**

> **On the moist crown of the sewer, bacteria oxidise H₂S to SULPHURIC ACID**, which attacks the concrete from the top down.

> **That is CROWN CORROSION — the classic destroyer of concrete sewers**, and it eats the pipe precisely where the structural arch is most needed.

> **H₂S is also toxic and heavier than air**, which is why manhole entry without gas testing and forced ventilation has killed workers repeatedly. **It deadens the sense of smell at dangerous concentrations**, so the absence of a smell is not evidence of safety.

**The hydraulic curiosity that makes partial flow acceptable:**

> **Maximum VELOCITY in a circular pipe occurs at about 81% depth, and maximum DISCHARGE at about 95% depth — NOT when full.**

> **A pipe flowing at 95% depth carries MORE than the same pipe flowing full**, because the added wetted perimeter near the crown adds more friction than the small extra area adds capacity.

> **So designing for partial flow costs nothing in capacity** — which is why the practice is universal.

**SELF-CLEANSING VELOCITY** — the governing design criterion:

| Velocity | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Minimum (self-cleansing)** | **0.6 – 0.8 m/s** |
| **Maximum (non-scouring)** | **2.4 – 3.0 m/s** |

> **Both limits matter, and they bracket the design.**

> **Below the minimum, solids SETTLE**, the sewer silts up, the deposit turns septic, and H₂S generation begins — the whole chain of failure starts with too low a velocity.

> **Above the maximum, the flow ABRADES the invert**, wearing the pipe away.

> **The self-cleansing velocity must be achieved at the MINIMUM flow, not the design flow** — which is the critical condition, and the one most often missed. A sewer sized generously for future growth may fail to clean itself in its early years.

**Sewer types:**

| System | Carries |
|---|---|
| **SEPARATE** | **Sewage and stormwater in SEPARATE pipes** |
| **COMBINED** | Both together |
| **PARTIALLY SEPARATE** | Sewage plus some roof water |

> **The SEPARATE system is preferred in Nepal** — heavy monsoon rainfall would otherwise produce enormous combined flows, and a combined system's overflows discharge **raw sewage** to watercourses during storms.

> **A separate system's sewage flow is also far steadier**, which suits a treatment works far better than the extreme variation a combined system delivers.

examTip.trick: **A sewer is an OPEN CHANNEL, not a pressure pipe.** The space above the flow carries away sewer gases and absorbs peak and future flows.
examTip.trap: **Maximum discharge occurs at ~95% depth, not when FULL** — the extra wetted perimeter near the crown adds more friction than the area adds capacity. Partial-flow design costs nothing in capacity.
examTip.mnemonic: **Self-cleansing velocity (0.6–0.8 m/s) must be met at MINIMUM flow, not design flow** — the condition most often missed. Below it, solids settle, turn septic, and **crown corrosion** begins.

questions.stem: For a cohesionless soil which is losing soil from the sides of an excavation, what should be provided?
questions.solution:
**Both — sheet piles AND an anchor at the top.**

**Why the soil is losing material from the sides:**

> **A COHESIONLESS soil — sand or gravel — has NO COHESION (c = 0).** Its strength comes entirely from friction, which requires **confining pressure.**

> **At an unsupported vertical face there is no confining pressure**, so the strength there is **zero** and the soil simply runs.

> **Its theoretical unsupported height is therefore ZERO** — a vertical cut in clean dry sand cannot stand at all. **It must be supported from the moment it is cut.**

**Why SHEET PILES:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Continuous, interlocking** | **No gaps for soil to escape through** |
| **Driven BEFORE excavation** | Support is in place before the face is opened |
| **Water-retaining** | Useful below the water table |
| Recoverable | Can be extracted and re-used |

> **The interlock is the essential feature.** Soldier piles with timber lagging leave gaps; in a running sand, soil escapes through them. **A continuous wall is required for a soil that flows.**

**Why an ANCHOR at the top as well:**

> **A CANTILEVER sheet pile wall is fixed only by the soil below excavation level.** Its deflection grows as the **FOURTH POWER of its height**, so it is practical only for shallow depths — roughly **up to 5 m.**

> **An anchor (or a strut) near the top converts the cantilever into a PROPPED wall.**

| | **Cantilever** | **ANCHORED** |
|---|---|---|
| Support | Embedment only | **Embedment + top anchor** |
| Bending moment | **Large** | **Substantially reduced** |
| Deflection | **Large** | **Much smaller** |
| Practical depth | **≤ ~5 m** | **Much greater** |

> **Adding a support near the top has the same effect as propping a cantilever beam** — it changes the structural system, cutting both the moment and the deflection dramatically.

> **Controlling DEFLECTION is often the real reason for the anchor**, not strength. **Ground movement behind the wall damages adjacent structures and services**, and in a city that governs the design long before the wall's own capacity does.

**So the two are complementary, not alternatives**, which is why the answer is both:

> **The sheet piles retain the soil; the anchor holds the sheet piles.** Sheet piles alone would deflect excessively at any real depth; an anchor with no wall retains nothing.

**The anchor's own requirement:**

> **The anchor must be founded BEYOND the ACTIVE WEDGE** — beyond the plane rising at **45° + φ/2** from the base of the wall.

> **An anchor inside the active wedge is anchored to soil that is itself moving**, and provides no restraint at all. **This is a genuine and repeated design error**, and it fails without warning.

**The alternatives, for context:**

| System | Suits |
|---|---|
| **Sheet piling** | **Soft ground, water present, running sand** |
| **Soldier pile and lagging** | **Firm, cohesive ground ABOVE the water table** |
| **Diaphragm (slurry) wall** | Deep excavations, adjacent structures |
| **Secant / contiguous pile wall** | Deep, stiff, low-movement requirement |
| **Soil nailing** | Ground with **some cohesion** — **NOT clean sand** |

> **Soil nailing is specifically unsuitable here**, because it relies on the ground standing unsupported for the short period between excavating a lift and installing the nails. **A cohesionless soil will not do that**, which is the same property that made this question's problem in the first place.

examTip.trick: **The two are complementary, not alternatives**: sheet piles retain the soil, the anchor holds the sheet piles. Cantilever deflection grows as the **fourth power** of height, so it is practical only to about 5 m.
examTip.trap: **The anchor must be founded BEYOND the active wedge** (the plane at 45° + φ/2). An anchor inside it is anchored to moving soil and restrains nothing — a repeated design error that fails without warning.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cohesionless soil has c = 0, so its unsupported height is ZERO** — it must be supported from the moment it is cut. Which is also why **soil nailing is unsuitable**: nothing stands long enough to install the nails.

questions.stem: The base width of a solid gravity dam is 35 m and the specific gravity of the dam material is 2.45. What is the approximate allowable height of the dam having an elementary profile, without considering uplift?
questions.solution:
**54.8 m.**

**The relation for an elementary profile:**

> **Without uplift:  B = H/√G,  so  H = B√G**

**Working:**

> **H = 35 × √2.45**
>
> **√2.45 = 1.5652**
>
> **H = 35 × 1.5652 = 54.78 ≈ 54.8 m** ✓

**Where the formula comes from** — it is worth deriving rather than memorising, because the two versions differ by one symbol:

> **An ELEMENTARY PROFILE is a right-angled triangle** with its vertical face upstream, apex at the water surface, base **B** and height **H**.

> **Two conditions must be satisfied, and both give the same answer:**

| Condition | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **No TENSION at the heel** | The resultant must fall within the **MIDDLE THIRD** |
| **No SLIDING** | Friction must resist the water thrust |

> **For the no-tension condition without uplift, B = H/√G.**

> **WITH uplift the requirement becomes B = H/√(G − c)**, where **c** is the uplift coefficient.

**The consequence of including uplift — and why the question says "without":**

> **Uplift REDUCES the effective weight of the dam**, so a **WIDER base is needed for the same height.**

> **Check it with c = 1 (full uplift): B = H/√(2.45 − 1) = H/1.204**, requiring a base of **29 m** for a 54.8 m dam — against **35 m** here. So including uplift, this 35 m base would permit only **35 × 1.204 = 42.1 m.**

> **Uplift costs about 23% of the permissible height**, which is why it is never neglected in a real design and why the question is explicit that it is excluded.

**Why UPLIFT is so important:**

> **Water penetrates the foundation and the dam–rock contact, and acts UPWARD on the base.**

> **It reduces the effective weight — and weight is the ONLY thing holding a gravity dam in place.** The dam resists overturning and sliding by its own mass, so anything that reduces that mass attacks its stability directly.

> **DRAINAGE GALLERIES with relief holes are provided to intercept seepage and RELIEVE the uplift pressure**, typically cutting it to a third of the full head at the drain line — a very large improvement in stability for a modest cost.

**The stability requirements for a gravity dam:**

| Check | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **No TENSION** | Resultant within the **MIDDLE THIRD** |
| **Sliding factor** | **≥ 1.5**; shear friction factor **≥ 4 to 5** |
| **Overturning** | Factor of safety **≥ 1.5** |
| **Crushing** | Compressive stress within allowable |

> **NO TENSION is the governing criterion for a gravity dam**, because **mass concrete has negligible tensile strength.**

> **A crack at the heel is doubly dangerous**: it not only removes contact area but **allows water to enter and increase the uplift**, which widens the crack further. **The failure is progressive.**

**Dimensional check on the answer:**

> **G is dimensionless, so H must have the units of B — metres.** ✓ **And H > B**, which is correct for a gravity dam: the base is roughly **0.6 to 0.7 H** in practice.

> **Option (d), 25.8 m, is SMALLER than the base**, giving a squat profile that no gravity dam has — it can be rejected on shape alone.

examTip.trick: **H = B√G without uplift; B = H/√(G − c) with it.** One symbol separates them. Here 35 × √2.45 = 35 × 1.5652 = **54.8 m**.
examTip.trap: **Option (d), 25.8 m, is SMALLER than the 35 m base** — a squat profile no gravity dam has (base is typically 0.6–0.7 H). Reject it on shape alone.
examTip.mnemonic: **Weight is the ONLY thing holding a gravity dam in place, and uplift removes weight** — here it would cost about 23% of the permissible height. Hence **drainage galleries** to relieve it.

questions.stem: An irrigation canal is to be designed to deliver 6.25 cumecs to meet the peak Rabi demand of a total of 5100 hectares of cropped area. The estimated canal losses are 25% of the head discharge. The duty on capacity of this small canal will be:
questions.solution:
**612 ha/cumec.**

**Step 1 — find the HEAD discharge.**

> The canal must **deliver** 6.25 cumecs at the field, and **25% of the HEAD discharge is lost on the way.**

> **Q_head − 0.25 Q_head = 6.25**
>
> **0.75 Q_head = 6.25**
>
> **Q_head = 6.25/0.75 = 8.333 cumecs**

**Step 2 — duty on CAPACITY is referred to the head discharge.**

> **Duty = Area ÷ Discharge = 5100/8.333 = 612 ha/cumec** ✓

**The trap is in the word "of":**

> **The losses are 25% OF THE HEAD DISCHARGE, not 25% of the delivered flow.**

> **Dividing gives 6.25/0.75 = 8.333; MULTIPLYING would give 6.25 × 1.25 = 7.8125**, and a duty of **5100/7.8125 = 653 ha/cumec** — which is exactly **option (d)**.

> **That distractor is deliberately placed for the multiply-instead-of-divide error**, and it is the commonest slip in loss calculations of every kind.

> **And option (a), 816 rounded down, or simply 5100/6.25 = 816**, would be the answer for anyone who ignores the losses altogether.

**What DUTY means:**

> **DUTY (D) = the AREA a unit discharge can irrigate, in hectares per cumec.**

> **DELTA (Δ) = the total DEPTH of water a crop needs over the whole base period, in metres.**

> **BASE PERIOD (B) = the days from first to last watering.**

> **Δ = 8.64 B/D**, with B in days and Δ in metres.

**The relation is worth deriving once so it is never mis-remembered:**

> One cumec running for **B days** delivers **1 × 86400 × B m³**. Spread over **D hectares = 10⁴D m²**, the depth is **86400B/(10⁴D) = 8.64B/D metres.** ✓

> **The 8.64 is simply 86400/10000** — seconds per day divided by square metres per hectare.

**And note the inverse relationship, which is the concept:**

> **HIGH duty means water is used EFFICIENTLY** — one cumec irrigates a large area. **High duty therefore goes with LOW delta.**

| Duty | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **HIGH** | Efficient — large area per cumec, **low delta** |
| **LOW** | Inefficient — small area per cumec, **high delta** |

**Where duty is quoted matters:**

| Point of reference | Duty |
|---|---|
| **At the FIELD (duty on field)** | **HIGHEST** — no losses counted |
| At the outlet | Intermediate |
| **At the HEAD (duty on capacity)** | **LOWEST** — all losses counted ← this question |

> **Duty on capacity is always the smallest**, because the head discharge is the largest flow in the system. **Quoting a duty without saying where it is measured is meaningless**, which is why the question specifies "duty on capacity".

**Factors affecting duty:** type of crop, climate and season, soil type, irrigation method, canal condition (lined or unlined), and the skill of the irrigators.

> **LINING a canal raises the duty** by cutting seepage — the same head discharge then irrigates a larger area, which is the principal economic justification for lining.

examTip.trick: **Losses are 25% OF THE HEAD discharge**, so **divide**: 6.25/0.75 = 8.333 cumecs. Then duty = 5100/8.333 = **612 ha/cumec**.
examTip.trap: **Multiplying instead — 6.25 × 1.25 = 7.8125 — gives 653, which is exactly option (d).** That distractor exists for this error. Ignoring losses entirely gives 816.
examTip.mnemonic: **Δ = 8.64B/D**, where 8.64 = 86400 s/day ÷ 10⁴ m²/ha. **High duty ↔ low delta ↔ efficient use.** And duty on CAPACITY is always the lowest, because head discharge is the largest flow.

questions.stem: What is the bulk modulus of a body that experienced a change of pressure of 5 × 10⁴ N/m² and whose volume goes from 4 cm³ to 3.9 cm³?
questions.solution:
**2.00 × 10⁶ N/m².**

**The definition:**

> **K = Δp ÷ (ΔV/V) = increase in pressure ÷ volumetric strain**

**Working:**

> **ΔV = 4 − 3.9 = 0.1 cm³**
>
> **Volumetric strain = ΔV/V = 0.1/4 = 0.025**
>
> **K = 5 × 10⁴ / 0.025 = 2 × 10⁶ N/m²** ✓

**Why the units work out as they do:**

> **Volumetric strain is DIMENSIONLESS** — a volume divided by a volume — so **K carries the same units as PRESSURE.**

> **That is a useful check**: if an answer for a bulk modulus comes out in anything but N/m², the working has gone wrong. **Option (d), 1.25 N/m², is dimensionally correct but absurdly small** — smaller than the pressure change that produced it, which would mean a strain greater than 1 (the volume vanishing).

> **A bulk modulus must always be MUCH LARGER than the pressures applied to it**, or the material would be crushed out of existence. That single observation eliminates (a) and (d) at sight.

**Note also that the cm³ never needs converting:**

> **Only the RATIO 0.1/4 is used**, and a ratio of two volumes is the same whatever unit they share. **Converting to m³ is wasted work and an opportunity for error.**

**Bulk modulus values, for scale:**

| Material | K |
|---|---|
| **Water** | **2.07 × 10⁹ N/m² (2.07 GPa)** |
| Steel | ~160 GPa |
| **Air (isothermal)** | **≈ 10⁵ N/m²** — equal to the pressure itself |

> **Water's bulk modulus is about 20,000 times air's**, which is why **water is treated as INCOMPRESSIBLE in almost all hydraulics** and air is not.

> **A 1000 kPa pressure rise compresses water by only about 0.05%** — negligible for pipe and channel flow.

**But where compressibility DOES matter:**

| Phenomenon | Note |
|---|---|
| **WATER HAMMER** | **The entire mechanism depends on water's compressibility and the pipe's elasticity** |
| **Pressure wave celerity** | **C = √(K/ρ)** — about **1440 m/s** in water |
| Deep ocean / high-pressure systems | Density varies measurably |

> **If water were truly incompressible, the pressure rise on sudden valve closure would be INFINITE.** It is finite only because the water compresses and the pipe stretches — so the very assumption that simplifies everyday hydraulics must be abandoned for the one problem where it matters most.

> **Joukowsky's equation: Δp = ρ C ΔV** — and with C ≈ 1440 m/s, stopping a flow of just 1 m/s instantaneously produces about **1.44 MPa (147 m of head)**, which is why valves are closed slowly and surge tanks are provided.

**Compressibility** is simply the reciprocal: **β = 1/K.**

verification.notes: The source keys option (b) and its own working is correct in method, but the option is printed as 2.00 × 10⁵ N/m² — the right mantissa with the exponent one power too low. Δp/(ΔV/V) = 5×10⁴ / (0.1/4) = 5×10⁴/0.025 = 2×10⁶ N/m². Option (b) has been corrected to 2.00 × 10⁶ N/m², which preserves the source's keyed letter and makes the item arithmetically sound.

examTip.trick: **Volumetric strain is a RATIO, so the cm³ never needs converting** — only 0.1/4 = 0.025 is used. Converting to m³ is wasted work and an invitation to error.
examTip.trap: **A bulk modulus must be MUCH LARGER than the pressures applied to it**, or the material would be crushed out of existence. That eliminates the 1.25 N/m² and 1.25 × 10³ options at sight.
examTip.mnemonic: **Water's K = 2.07 GPa, about 20,000× air's** — hence "incompressible". But **water hammer exists only because water DOES compress**: C = √(K/ρ) ≈ 1440 m/s, and Δp = ρCΔV.

questions.stem: According to Lacey's regime theory, what will be the regime scour depth for a channel in soil having a silt factor of unity and carrying a discharge of 96 m³/s? The base width of the channel is 12 m.
questions.solution:
**5.4 m.**

**Step 1 — discharge per unit width.**

> **q = Q/B = 96/12 = 8 m³/s per metre**

**Step 2 — Lacey's normal scour depth.**

> **R = 1.35 (q²/f)^{1/3}**
>
> **q² = 64;  q²/f = 64/1 = 64**
>
> **64^{1/3} = 4**
>
> **R = 1.35 × 4 = 5.4 m** ✓

**The numbers are chosen to be clean**, and recognising that is worth a moment: **f = 1 removes the division, and 64 is a perfect cube.** When a scour question gives a silt factor of exactly unity, expect the arithmetic to come out neatly — and if it does not, check the working.

**The formula's terms:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **R** | **Normal scour depth below the high flood level** |
| **q** | **Discharge per unit WIDTH** (m³/s per m) |
| **f** | **Lacey's silt factor = 1.76√d**, d in **millimetres** |

> **Note the first step is the one candidates skip**: the formula takes **q**, not **Q**. **Substituting the total discharge of 96 gives (9216)^{1/3} × 1.35 = 28.3 m**, an absurd answer, and the base width would have been given for nothing.

**The alternative form** — worth knowing, because either may be asked:

> **R = 0.473 (Q/f)^{1/3}** — used where the section is **not restricted** in width.

> **Check it here: 0.473 × 96^{1/3} = 0.473 × 4.579 = 2.17 m.** Different, because it describes a different situation — an unconfined regime channel rather than one held to 12 m.

> **Use the q form when a width is given; the Q form when it is not.** The presence of the base width in this stem is the instruction to use the first.

**How the scour depth is applied:**

> **The computed R is multiplied by a LOCATION FACTOR**, because scour concentrates wherever the flow does:

| Location | Multiplier |
|---|---|
| **Straight reach** | **1.25** |
| Moderate bend | 1.5 |
| Severe bend | 1.75 |
| **Bridge PIER NOSE** | **2.0** |
| **Right-angled bend / GUIDE BANK HEAD** | **2.75** |

> **So a 5.4 m normal scour becomes 14.9 m at a guide bank head** — nearly three times as deep, and that is the depth the protection must reach.

**Why this matters more than it looks:**

> **Near a watercourse, SCOUR governs foundation depth far more often than bearing capacity does.**

> **A pier founded above the scour level will be UNDERMINED in a flood however sound its bearing pressure** — and **scour is the leading cause of bridge failure worldwide.**

> **The failure is also sudden**: the bed erodes during the flood peak and the pier drops without warning, often at night and under water where nothing can be seen.

**Lacey's regime equations, as a set:**

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Wetted perimeter** | **P = 4.75√Q** |
| **Hydraulic radius** | **R = 0.473(Q/f)^{1/3}** |
| **Velocity** | **V = [Qf²/140]^{1/6}** |
| **Bed slope** | **S = f^{5/3}/(3340 Q^{1/6})** |
| **Normal scour depth** | **R = 1.35(q²/f)^{1/3}** |
| **Silt factor** | **f = 1.76√d** (d in mm) |

examTip.trick: **The formula takes q (per unit width), not Q.** q = 96/12 = 8; q² = 64; 64^{1/3} = 4; R = 1.35 × 4 = **5.4 m**. The base width is given precisely so you compute q.
examTip.trap: **Substituting the total 96 gives 28.3 m** — absurd, and it wastes the base width entirely. Use the **q form when a width is given**, the **R = 0.473(Q/f)^{1/3}** form when it is not.
examTip.mnemonic: **Multiply by the LOCATION FACTOR: 2.0 at a pier nose, 2.75 at a guide bank head.** A 5.4 m normal scour becomes 14.9 m there — and scour is the leading cause of bridge failure worldwide.

questions.stem: A load of 20 kN acts on a simply supported beam at an angle of 30° to the horizontal. The cross-sectional area of the beam is 1000 mm². Find the axial force.
questions.solution:
**17.32 kN.**

**The axial force is the component ALONG the beam's axis — the HORIZONTAL component:**

> **F_axial = 20 cos 30° = 20 × 0.8660 = 17.32 kN** ✓

**And for completeness, the transverse (bending) component:**

> **F_transverse = 20 sin 30° = 20 × 0.5 = 10 kN** — which is **option (b)**, placed there for anyone who takes the sine.

**Getting the component right — the rule that never fails:**

> **The component ALONG the direction from which the angle is measured takes the COSINE.**

> **The angle here is measured from the HORIZONTAL, and the beam's axis IS horizontal — so the axial component takes the cosine.**

> **That is the whole decision**, and it is worth stating as a rule because the sine/cosine swap is the single commonest error in resolution problems.

**A sanity check that settles it without trigonometry:**

> **30° is a SHALLOW angle to the horizontal**, so the load points mostly along the beam. **The axial component must therefore be the LARGER of the two.**

> **17.32 > 10**, so 17.32 is axial and 10 is transverse. ✓

> **And no component can exceed the resultant**, which eliminates **option (d), 34.64 kN** — that is 20/cos30° = 20 × 1.732, the result of *dividing* by the cosine instead of multiplying. **A component larger than the force it came from is impossible.**

> **Option (c), 20 kN**, is the full load, correct only if the load were entirely horizontal (0°).

**The 30–60–90 values worth having instantly:**

| Angle | sin | cos |
|---|---|---|
| **30°** | **0.5** | **0.866** |
| **45°** | **0.707** | **0.707** |
| **60°** | **0.866** | **0.5** |

> **Note √3/2 = 0.866 and 20 × 0.866 = 17.32** — and **17.32 = 10√3**, which is why the number looks familiar. **Recognising 17.32, 8.66 and 34.64 as multiples of √3 saves time repeatedly.**

**Why the cross-sectional area is given:**

> **It is not needed for this question.** It would be needed for the next step — the **axial STRESS**:

> **σ = F/A = 17,320 N / 1000 mm² = 17.32 N/mm² (MPa)**

> **Redundant data is a deliberate examination device.** It invites the candidate to use every number given, and here using the area would produce a stress where a force was asked for. **Read what is asked before reaching for the data.**

**What the two components then do to the beam:**

| Component | Effect |
|---|---|
| **AXIAL (17.32 kN)** | Direct **compression or tension** — uniform stress **F/A** |
| **TRANSVERSE (10 kN)** | **BENDING and SHEAR** — stress **My/I**, varying across the depth |

> **The combined stress is σ = F/A ± My/I** — and because the bending term usually dominates in a beam, the axial component often matters less than its larger magnitude suggests.

> **But a compressive axial force also brings BUCKLING and the P–Δ effect into play**, which is why a beam–column is checked by an interaction equation rather than by either action alone.

examTip.trick: **The component ALONG the direction the angle is measured from takes the COSINE.** The angle is from the horizontal and the beam axis is horizontal, so axial = 20 cos30° = **17.32 kN**.
