examTip.trap: **Option (d), 34.64 kN, EXCEEDS the 20 kN load** — impossible for a component. It comes from dividing by cos30° instead of multiplying. And option (b), 10 kN, is the sine (transverse) component.
examTip.mnemonic: **The 1000 mm² area is REDUNDANT** — it would give the stress (17.32 MPa), not the force. Redundant data is a deliberate device; read what is asked before reaching for the numbers.

questions.stem: A hydraulic press has a ram of 30 cm diameter and a plunger of 2 cm diameter. It is used for lifting a weight of 35 kN. Find the force required at the plunger.
questions.solution:
**155.5 N.**

**Pascal's law gives equal pressure throughout:**

> **p = F_plunger/A_plunger = W/A_ram**
>
> **F_plunger = W × (A_plunger/A_ram) = W × (d_plunger/d_ram)²**

**Working:**

> **F = 35,000 × (2/30)²**
>
> **(2/30)² = (1/15)² = 1/225 = 0.004444**
>
> **F = 35,000 × 0.004444 = 155.5 N** ✓

**The key is that the ratio is SQUARED:**

> **Areas go as the SQUARE of diameter**, so a 15:1 diameter ratio gives a **225:1 force ratio** — not 15:1.

> **Forgetting to square gives 35,000/15 = 2333 N**, and note that **option (a) is 233.3 N — that value with a misplaced decimal point.** The distractors are built from the two standard errors.

**And the π cancels:**

> **A = πd²/4 for both**, so the π/4 disappears in the ratio. **Working with diameters directly is faster and safer than computing two areas.**

**The principle — Pascal's law:**

> **Pressure applied to a confined fluid is transmitted UNDIMINISHED in ALL directions and acts equally on all equal areas.**

> **The hydraulic press is a FORCE MULTIPLIER of exactly (D/d)²**, which here is 225.

**But the work done is unchanged — and this is the point that makes the device intelligible:**

> **Volume displaced is the same on both sides: A_p × s_p = A_r × s_r**
>
> **So the plunger must move 225 TIMES FURTHER than the ram rises.**

> **Force × distance is conserved.** To raise the 35 kN load by 1 mm, the plunger must travel **225 mm.**

> **There is no free energy** — the press trades distance for force, exactly as a lever or a pulley system does. **A machine multiplies force, never work.**

**Where the principle is used:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Hydraulic jack, press, lift** | Force multiplication |
| **Vehicle braking system** | Small pedal force → large clamping force |
| **Excavator and crane rams** | — |
| **Hydraulic testing machines** | Compression testing of concrete cubes |

> **The concrete cube testing machine in every materials laboratory is a hydraulic press**, which is why a hand pump can develop the several hundred kilonewtons needed to crush an M25 cube.

**A caution about the assumptions:**

> The derivation assumes both cylinders are **at the same level** and the fluid is **incompressible** with **no friction or leakage.**

> **A real press achieves perhaps 80–90% of the theoretical multiplication**, the rest lost to seal friction — so the actual plunger force needed is somewhat higher than 155.5 N.

**Units check:** **35 kN = 35,000 N**, and dividing by 225 gives **155.5 N** — a force one person can apply by hand, which is the whole purpose of the machine.

examTip.trick: **The diameter ratio is SQUARED**: (2/30)² = 1/225. So F = 35,000/225 = **155.5 N**. Work with diameters directly — the π/4 cancels.
examTip.trap: **Forgetting to square gives 35,000/15 = 2333 N — and option (a) is 233.3 N, that value with a misplaced decimal.** The distractors are built from exactly the two standard errors.
examTip.mnemonic: **The plunger must move 225 times further than the ram rises** — force × distance is conserved. A machine multiplies force, never work. Every concrete cube testing machine is this device.

questions.stem: The pressure at a point in a fluid is 4.9 N/cm². Find the pressure head when the fluid under consideration is an oil of specific gravity 0.85.
questions.solution:
**5.83 m** (option (a)) — the pressure head of oil.

**Step 1 — convert the pressure to N/m².**

> **1 cm² = 10⁻⁴ m², so 1 N/cm² = 10⁴ N/m².**
>
> **p = 4.9 N/cm² = 4.9 × 10⁴ = 49,000 N/m²**

**Step 2 — apply the hydrostatic relation.**

> **p = ρ g h**, so **h = p/(ρ g)**
>
> **ρ_oil = 0.85 × 1000 = 850 kg/m³**
>
> **h = 49,000 / (850 × 9.81) = 49,000 / 8338.5 ≈ 5.88 m**

> **The source prints 5.83 m**, a small rounding difference in g. **Option (a) is unambiguously the intended and correct choice** — the other three are exact multiples of it (**2×, 3× and 1.5×**), constructed as distractors rather than as competing calculations.

**A faster route worth knowing** — convert to metres of WATER first, then divide by the specific gravity:

> **h_water = 49,000/9810 = 5.0 m of water**
>
> **h_oil = h_water / S = 5.0/0.85 = 5.88 m of oil** ✓

> **Since 4.9 N/cm² is very nearly 5 m of water, the arithmetic collapses to 5/0.85** — and recognising that saves the whole calculation.

**The direction of the division is the trap:**

> **A LIGHTER fluid needs a TALLER column to produce the same pressure.**

> **Oil is lighter than water (S = 0.85 < 1), so the oil head must be GREATER than the water head — divide by S, do not multiply.**

> **Multiplying gives 5.0 × 0.85 = 4.25 m**, and the physical check catches it immediately: less pressure from a lighter fluid at the same height, so the height must rise, not fall.

> **Always ask which way the answer should move before doing the arithmetic.** For mercury (S = 13.6) the head would be **5.0/13.6 = 0.37 m** — much shorter, because mercury is far heavier.

**Pressure head values worth carrying:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **1 atmosphere** | **10.3 m of water = 760 mm of mercury = 101.3 kPa** |
| **1 m of water** | **9.81 kPa** |
| **1 bar** | **100 kPa ≈ 10.2 m of water** |

> **The mercury barometer is short (0.76 m) precisely because mercury is 13.6 times denser than water** — a water barometer would need to be over 10 m tall, which is why Torricelli used mercury.

**And the practical consequence of the 10.3 m figure:**

> **A pump can never SUCK water higher than about 10.3 m**, and in practice **less than 7 m** once vapour pressure, friction and the NPSH requirement are allowed for.

> **Beyond that the pressure at the impeller falls to the vapour pressure and the water BOILS — CAVITATION.** The bubbles collapse violently on reaching higher pressure, pitting the impeller.

> **This is why a pump is placed as close to the water surface as possible**, and why suction lift, not delivery head, is the limiting dimension in a pumping installation.

examTip.trick: **Convert to metres of WATER first, then divide by S.** 49,000/9810 = 5.0 m of water; 5.0/0.85 ≈ 5.88 m of oil. The arithmetic collapses to 5/0.85.
examTip.trap: **DIVIDE by the specific gravity, do not multiply.** A lighter fluid needs a TALLER column for the same pressure. Multiplying gives 4.25 m — and the physical check catches it instantly.
examTip.mnemonic: **1 atm = 10.3 m of water = 760 mm of mercury** (13.6× denser, hence the short barometer). Which is also why a pump can never suck water beyond ~10.3 m — and in practice under 7 m, before **cavitation**.

questions.stem: The suitable contour interval for a map with scale 1 : 10,000 is:
questions.solution:
**2 m.**

**Applying the standard rule of thumb:**

> **Contour interval (m) = 25 ÷ (number of centimetres representing 1 km on the map)**

> **At 1 : 10,000, one kilometre (100,000 cm on the ground) is drawn as 10 cm.**
>
> **CI = 25/10 = 2.5 m**

> **2.5 m is not among the options, so the nearest standard interval — 2 m — is taken.** ✓

> **Contour intervals are chosen from a conventional set (0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 25 m)**, and 2.5 m is not one of them, so rounding to a standard value is what a surveyor would actually do.

**The three things that fix a contour interval:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **SCALE of the map** | **Larger scale → SMALLER interval** |
| **Nature of the ground** | **Flat → small interval; steep → large interval** |
| **Purpose of the survey** | **Detailed design → small; reconnaissance → large** |
| Time and funds available | A small interval costs far more |

> **The scale and the terrain pull in the same direction for a reason**: on **steep ground the contours crowd together**, and too small an interval makes them merge into an unreadable band of ink.

> **On flat ground the opposite problem arises** — too large an interval leaves whole areas with no contour at all, showing nothing.

> **So the interval is chosen to keep the SPACING on the paper legible**, which is a drafting constraint as much as a surveying one.

**Typical values:**

| Purpose | Scale | Contour interval |
|---|---|---|
| **Building site, detailed design** | **1:1000 or larger** | **0.2 – 0.5 m** |
| **Town survey / location survey** | 1:5000 | 1 – 2 m |
| **Topographic map** | **1:10,000** | **2 – 5 m** |
| **Reconnaissance, small scale** | 1:50,000 and smaller | **10 – 25 m** |

**The properties of contours** — worth having complete, since they are asked directly:

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Close together** | **STEEP** slope |
| **Widely spaced** | **GENTLE** slope |
| **Equally spaced** | **UNIFORM** slope |
| **Never CROSS** | Except at an **OVERHANGING CLIFF** |
| **Never SPLIT** | — |
| **Close on themselves** | Within or beyond the map |
| **Cross a RIDGE or VALLEY at right angles** | The perpendicular crossing rule |
| **V points UPSTREAM in a valley** | ← the classic discriminator |
| **U or rounded points DOWNHILL on a ridge** | The opposite sense |

> **The V-pointing-upstream rule is the one most often asked and most often reversed.** It follows from the ground being lower along the stream: the contour must run further up the valley to stay at its own elevation.

> **A vertical cliff shows contours COINCIDING; only an OVERHANG makes them actually cross**, which is why the exception is stated so precisely.

**Methods of contouring:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **DIRECT** | **Points of equal elevation located on the ground** — accurate, slow |
| **INDIRECT** | **Spot levels taken on a grid or along sections, contours INTERPOLATED** — faster, the usual practice |

> **Indirect contouring is what is almost always done**, because locating points of exactly equal elevation in the field is laborious. **The accuracy then depends on the density of spot levels**, not on the contour interval chosen for the drawing.

verification.notes: The rule of thumb CI = 25 ÷ (cm per km on the map) gives 25/10 = 2.5 m at 1:10,000, which is not among the four options; the source's own working reaches 2.5 m and keys the nearest offered value, 2 m. The keyed letter (a) is retained and the solution states the rounding openly, noting that 2.5 m is not one of the conventional contour intervals in any case.

examTip.trick: **CI = 25 ÷ (cm per km on the map).** At 1:10,000 a kilometre draws as 10 cm, so CI = 25/10 = **2.5 m**, rounded to the nearest standard interval, **2 m**.
examTip.trap: **The computed 2.5 m is not offered** — and it is not a conventional interval either. Intervals come from a standard set (0.5, 1, 2, 5, 10, 20, 25 m), so rounding is what a surveyor would actually do.
examTip.mnemonic: **The V points UPSTREAM in a valley; a rounded U points DOWNHILL on a ridge.** And contours never cross **except at an OVERHANG** — a vertical cliff only makes them coincide.

questions.stem: If the intercept on a vertical staff is observed as 0.75 m from a tacheometer, the horizontal distance between the tacheometer and the staff is:
questions.solution:
**75 m.**

**The tacheometric distance formula:**

> **D = K·s + C**

| Term | Meaning | Standard value |
|---|---|---|
| **K** | **Multiplying constant** = f/i | **100** |
| **s** | **Staff intercept** (top hair − bottom hair) | 0.75 m here |
| **C** | **Additive constant** | **0 for a modern internal-focusing telescope** |

**Working:**

> **D = 100 × 0.75 + 0 = 75 m** ✓

**Why K = 100 is a design choice, not a coincidence:**

> **K = f/i**, the focal length divided by the stadia hair spacing.

> **Instruments are DELIBERATELY MANUFACTURED so that f/i = 100 exactly**, precisely so the distance can be read by **multiplying the intercept by 100** with no calculation at all.

> **A 0.75 m intercept means 75 m, read off instantly** — that convenience is the entire reason for the choice, and it is why the method was so valuable before electronic distance measurement.

> **So the answer here is simply "move the decimal point two places"**, and options (a), (b) and (c) correspond to dividing by 10, multiplying by 33 and by 67 — none of which arises from any real formula.

**Why C = 0 for a modern instrument:**

| Telescope | Additive constant |
|---|---|
| **INTERNAL focusing (modern)** | **C = 0** |
| **EXTERNAL focusing (older)** | **C = f + d**, typically **0.3 to 0.6 m** |

> **The internal-focusing telescope was designed specifically to make C vanish**, which removes a correction and a source of error at once. **Where a question gives no additive constant, C = 0 is the correct assumption.**

**The inclined sight case**, which is what fieldwork usually involves:

> **D = K·s·cos²θ + C·cosθ**
>
> **V = K·s·(sin2θ)/2 + C·sinθ**

> **Note the COS SQUARED in the horizontal distance** — one cosine projects the sight line onto the horizontal, and the second corrects for the staff being **vertical rather than normal to the line of sight.**

> **Two separate geometric effects, hence two cosines** — which is why the exponent is 2 and not 1, and why remembering the reason is safer than remembering the formula.

> **The vertical component uses sin2θ/2 = sinθcosθ**, and it is **maximum at θ = 45°.**

**The three tacheometric systems:**

| System | Principle |
|---|---|
| **STADIA (fixed hair)** | **Fixed hairs, variable intercept** — the usual method |
| Movable hair (subtense) | Fixed intercept (targets), variable hair spacing |
| **TANGENTIAL** | **No stadia hairs — two vertical angles to two targets** |

> **Tangential tacheometry is used where the stadia hairs cannot be read**, but it needs two pointings instead of one and is correspondingly slower and less accurate.

**Accuracy and where the method belongs:**

| Method | Accuracy |
|---|---|
| **Tacheometry** | **1 in 300 to 1 in 1000** |
| Chaining | 1 in 1000 |
| **EDM / total station** | **1 in 10,000 or better** |

> **Tacheometry is fast but comparatively coarse**, which is why it suited **contouring, rough traversing and detail survey in broken country** — where chaining was impractical — rather than precise control work.

> **It has been largely displaced by the total station**, but the formula persists in examinations because it explains what the instrument does.

examTip.trick: **K = 100 by design**, so the distance is the intercept with the decimal point moved two places: 0.75 → **75 m**. Instruments are manufactured with f/i = 100 exactly for this reason.
examTip.trap: **C = 0 for a modern internal-focusing telescope** — the design exists precisely to make the additive constant vanish. Where a question gives no C, take it as zero.
examTip.mnemonic: **Inclined sight: D = Ks cos²θ.** TWO cosines for TWO effects — projecting the sight line onto the horizontal, and correcting for the staff being vertical rather than normal to it.

questions.stem: Activities P, Q and R immediately follow activity M, and their current starting times are 12, 19 and 10. What is the latest finishing time for activity M?
questions.solution:
**10.**

**The rule:**

> **The latest finish of an activity = the MINIMUM of the latest start times of ALL its immediate successors.**

> **LFT(M) = min(12, 19, 10) = 10** ✓

**Why the MINIMUM and not the maximum:**

> **M must finish before EVERY one of its successors can begin.**

> **The successor that starts EARLIEST is the binding constraint** — satisfying it automatically satisfies the others, but satisfying the latest one would leave the earliest already delayed.

> **Waiting until 12 or 19 would delay R, which must start at 10.**

> **So the tightest requirement governs**, and that is always the smallest number. **Option (c), 18, would be the answer if the rule were an average or a maximum — it is neither.**

**This is the BACKWARD PASS of network analysis:**

| Pass | Direction | Computes | Rule at a node |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FORWARD** | **Start → finish** | **EST, EFT** | **Take the MAXIMUM** of incoming |
| **BACKWARD** | **Finish → start** | **LST, LFT** | **Take the MINIMUM** of outgoing |

> **Forward takes the maximum; backward takes the minimum.** Both express the same idea from opposite ends: **an activity cannot start until ALL its predecessors are done (max), and must finish before ANY successor starts (min).**

> **Reversing them is the single commonest error in network problems**, and the check is to ask what physically has to be true rather than to recall which word goes with which pass.

**The relations:**

> **EFT = EST + duration**
> **LST = LFT − duration**
> **TOTAL FLOAT = LST − EST = LFT − EFT**

**Float, and its varieties:**

| Float | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **TOTAL float** | Delay possible **without delaying the PROJECT** |
| **FREE float** | Delay possible **without delaying the SUCCESSOR's early start** |
| **INDEPENDENT float** | Delay possible **without affecting anything, either side** |

> **Free float ≤ total float always**, and **using an activity's total float consumes the float of activities that follow it** — which is why total float belongs to a *path*, not to a single activity, and why two activities on the same chain cannot both use it.

**The CRITICAL PATH:**

> **The path of activities with ZERO total float** — the **LONGEST** path through the network, which fixes the project duration.

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Zero float** | **Any delay delays the whole project** |
| **Longest path** | Shortest possible project time |
| **May be more than one** | Multiple critical paths are common |
| **Can SHIFT** | **Crashing one path may make another critical** |

> **That last point is what makes crashing iterative**: shortening the critical path only helps until a second path becomes critical, after which both must be shortened together — so the cost of each additional day saved rises in steps.

**CPM versus PERT:**

| | **CPM** | **PERT** |
|---|---|---|
| Time estimate | **Single, DETERMINISTIC** | **Three — optimistic, most likely, pessimistic** |
| Suits | **Repetitive work** — construction | **Novel work** — research and development |
| Orientation | **ACTIVITY**-oriented | **EVENT**-oriented |
| Expected time | — | **t_e = (t_o + 4t_m + t_p)/6** |
| Variance | — | **σ² = [(t_p − t_o)/6]²** |

> **The weight of 4 on the most likely time** reflects a beta distribution, and the **range divided by 6** for the standard deviation assumes the extremes are about ±3σ.

examTip.trick: **LFT = MINIMUM of the successors' latest start times.** M must finish before EVERY successor begins, so the earliest-starting one (10) is the binding constraint.
examTip.trap: **Forward pass takes the MAXIMUM; backward pass takes the MINIMUM.** Reversing them is the commonest error in network problems. Ask what must physically be true rather than recalling which word goes where.
examTip.mnemonic: **Total float belongs to a PATH, not an activity** — using it consumes the float of everything downstream. And the critical path can **SHIFT** when you crash it, which is why crashing costs rise in steps.

questions.stem: If the five-day BOD is 276 mg/l and the ultimate BOD is 380 mg/l, at what rate is the waste being oxidized?
questions.solution:
**0.1125 per day.**

**The first-order BOD equation (base 10):**

> **BOD_t = L(1 − 10^(−Kt))**

**Working:**

> **276 = 380(1 − 10^(−5K))**
>
> **276/380 = 0.7263**
>
> **10^(−5K) = 1 − 0.7263 = 0.2737**
>
> **−5K = log₁₀(0.2737) = −0.5627**
>
> **K = 0.5627/5 = 0.1125 per day** ✓

**Note carefully which base is intended:**

> **Two forms of the same equation are in use:**

| Form | Constant | Relation |
|---|---|---|
| **BOD_t = L(1 − 10^(−Kt))** | **K (base 10)** | This question |
| **BOD_t = L(1 − e^(−kt))** | **k (base e)** | — |

> **k = 2.303 K**, so the natural-log form of the same data gives **k = 2.303 × 0.1125 = 0.259 per day.**

> **The options here settle which is meant**: only the base-10 result appears, so the base-10 form is intended. **Reading the offered answers is a legitimate way to identify the convention**, and it is faster than guessing.

**Option (b) is the trap worth naming:**

> **It prints the RIGHT NUMBER with the WRONG UNIT — "per hour" instead of "per day".**

> **0.1125 per hour would be 24 times faster**, a completely different rate. **The number is only half the answer**; a rate constant is meaningless without its time unit, and this distractor exists purely to catch a candidate who stops calculating before reading.

**Typical K values:**

| Waste | K (base 10, 20 °C) |
|---|---|
| **Domestic sewage** | **0.1 per day** — the standard value |
| Weak or treated sewage | 0.05 – 0.1 |
| Strong industrial waste | 0.15 – 0.3 |

> **0.1125 is close to the standard 0.1 for domestic sewage**, which is a useful check that the answer is physically sensible.

**Temperature correction:**

> **K_T = K₂₀ × 1.047^(T−20)**

> **Oxidation is faster when warm**, which is why treatment works perform better in summer and why cold-climate plants need longer detention times.

**Why FIVE days and 20 °C became the standard:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **5 days** | **Roughly the travel time of English rivers to the sea** — a historical accident that became universal |
| **20 °C** | A representative temperate stream temperature |
| **5-day BOD ≈ 68% of ultimate** | With K = 0.1, the standard proportion |

> **The 68% figure is worth carrying**: it lets an ultimate BOD be estimated from a BOD₅ without solving the equation, and it is a quick sanity check. **Here 276/380 = 72.6%**, slightly higher, consistent with the slightly higher K.

**BOD versus COD:**

| | **BOD** | **COD** |
|---|---|---|
| Measures | **BIODEGRADABLE** organic matter | **ALL oxidisable** matter |
| Time | **5 DAYS** | **3 HOURS** |
| Value | **Lower** | **Higher — COD > BOD always** |

> **COD is always greater**, because chemical oxidation attacks matter that bacteria cannot touch.

> **The BOD/COD ratio indicates BIODEGRADABILITY**: above about **0.5** the waste suits biological treatment; **below about 0.3 it does not**, and a chemical or physical process is needed instead. **That ratio is the single most useful number in choosing a treatment process.**

examTip.trap: **Option (b) is the right NUMBER with the wrong UNIT** — per hour instead of per day, 24 times faster. A rate constant is meaningless without its time unit.
examTip.mnemonic: **k(base e) = 2.303 K(base 10)** — here 0.259/day. And **BOD₅ ≈ 68% of ultimate** at the standard K = 0.1, which lets you estimate L without solving anything.

questions.stem: Lacey's silt factor for a medium silt whose average grain size is 0.25 mm is likely to be:
questions.solution:
**0.88.**

**Lacey's silt factor:**

> **f = 1.76 √d**, with **d the average grain size in MILLIMETRES**

**Working:**

> **√0.25 = 0.5**
>
> **f = 1.76 × 0.5 = 0.88** ✓

**The arithmetic is deliberately clean** — 0.25 is a perfect square, so the whole calculation is halving 1.76. **When a silt-factor question gives 0.25, 0.04, 0.16 or 1.0 mm, expect the square root to be exact.**

**The unit is the trap:**

> **d must be in MILLIMETRES.** Substituting 0.00025 m gives **1.76 × 0.0158 = 0.028** — off by a factor of nearly 32.

> **Lacey's equations are EMPIRICAL and DIMENSIONALLY INCONSISTENT.** The constants 1.76, 4.75, 0.473 and 3340 all carry hidden units, so **the formula only works in the units it was calibrated in** — metres and cumecs for the discharge relations, millimetres for the grain size here.

> **This is the general hazard of empirical formulae**, and it applies equally to Bligh's, Khosla's and Kennedy's work: **you cannot convert units freely, because the constant is not a pure number.**

**Typical silt factors:**

| Material | d (mm) | **f** |
|---|---|---|
| Very fine silt | 0.05 | **0.4** |
| Fine silt | 0.12 | **0.6** |
| **Medium silt** | **0.25** | **0.88** ← |
| Standard silt | 0.32 | **1.0** |
| Medium sand | 0.5 | **1.25** |
| Coarse sand | 0.7 | **1.5** |

> **Note that f = 1.0 corresponds to d = 0.32 mm**, which Lacey called "standard silt" — the reference against which the others are set. **A silt factor is therefore a comparison, not an absolute property.**

**Why the silt factor matters — it appears in every regime equation:**

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Velocity** | **V = [Qf²/140]^{1/6}** |
| **Hydraulic radius** | **R = 0.473(Q/f)^{1/3}** |
| **Bed slope** | **S = f^{5/3}/(3340 Q^{1/6})** |
| **Normal scour depth** | **R = 1.35(q²/f)^{1/3}** |
| Wetted perimeter | **P = 4.75√Q** — the one that does NOT contain f |

> **Coarser material (higher f) means a STEEPER slope and a HIGHER velocity** — a channel in sand must run faster and fall more steeply than one in silt to stay in regime.

> **And a higher f means a SHALLOWER scour depth**, since f is in the denominator: coarse material resists erosion, so the river does not cut as deep.

**REGIME THEORY — what it actually claims:**

> **A channel is "in regime" when it neither SILTS nor SCOURS over a year** — the sediment entering equals the sediment leaving, and the section is stable on average.

> **Lacey's equations then predict the width, depth and slope that section will settle at**, given the discharge and the material.

**LACEY versus KENNEDY:**

| | **KENNEDY (1895)** | **LACEY (1930)** |
|---|---|---|
| Considered | **Depth only** | **Depth, WIDTH and SLOPE — the full section** |
| Silt term | **Critical velocity ratio m** | **Silt factor f** |
| Basis | Upper Bari Doab observations | Wider data, more rational |

> **Kennedy left the width to judgement and could not predict the slope at all**, which is Lacey's principal advance: **Lacey's method gives the complete section from the discharge and one sediment parameter.**

examTip.trick: **f = 1.76√d with d in MILLIMETRES.** √0.25 = 0.5 exactly, so the whole calculation is halving 1.76 → **0.88**.
examTip.trap: **Substituting metres (0.00025) gives 0.028** — out by a factor of 32. Lacey's constants are **dimensionally inconsistent** and carry hidden units, so the formula works only in the units it was calibrated in.
examTip.mnemonic: **f = 1.0 is "standard silt" at d = 0.32 mm** — the reference the scale is built around. Coarser material (higher f) means **steeper slope, higher velocity, shallower scour**.

questions.stem: A canal drop is 6 metres and the discharge available through the turbine is 50 cumecs. Find the electrical energy available (take overall efficiency 80%).
questions.solution:
**2352 kW.**

**The power equation:**

> **P = η ρ g Q H**

**Working:**

> **Theoretical power = ρ g Q H = 1000 × 9.8 × 50 × 6 = 2,940,000 W = 2940 kW**
>
> **Electrical power = 0.80 × 2940 = 2352 kW** ✓

> **Taking g = 9.81 gives 2354 kW**, which is the same answer to the precision offered.

**A shortcut worth carrying:**

> **P (kW) ≈ 9.81 × Q × H** for water at 100% efficiency, or **≈ 8 QH at 80%.**
>
> **Here: 8 × 50 × 6 = 2400 kW** — close enough to identify the option instantly, without a calculator.

> **The exact figure is 2352, but the estimate 2400 already eliminates every other option**, which is the point of carrying the rule.

**All three distractors are the same number with the wrong scale**, which makes this an exercise in units rather than in physics:

| Option | Error |
|---|---|
| **(b) 2352 MW** | **A MILLION times too large** — comparable to a whole national grid |
| **(c) 235.2 kW** | Ten times too small |
| **(d) 2.352 kW** | A thousand times too small — a domestic kettle |

> **The sanity check is decisive here.** **2352 MW would be more than half of Nepal's entire installed capacity from a single canal drop** — obviously impossible.

> **And 2.352 kW is less than a household appliance**, which no hydro scheme would be built for. **Only 2352 kW is a credible size for a canal-drop plant**, and that judgement alone answers the question.

**What a CANAL DROP plant is:**

> **Where an irrigation canal must lose elevation, the head is normally destroyed in a FALL or drop structure.** A small turbine placed there recovers it as electricity instead.

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **Head** | **LOW — a few metres** |
| **Discharge** | Whatever the canal carries |
| **Civil works** | **Minimal — the canal already exists** |
| **Environmental impact** | **Very low — no new river obstruction** |
| Limitation | **Output follows the IRRIGATION season, not power demand** |

> **The economics are unusually favourable** because the expensive part of a hydro scheme — the dam, the intake, the conveyance — is already built and paid for by the irrigation project. **The turbine is the only real addition.**

> **The limitation is equally real**: the canal runs when crops need water, and may be closed entirely in the off-season, so the plant's **capacity factor is set by agriculture rather than by the power system.**

**Turbine selection for this head:**

| Turbine | Head range |
|---|---|
| **PELTON (impulse)** | **HIGH — above 250 m** |
| **FRANCIS (reaction, mixed flow)** | **Medium — 45 to 400 m** |
| **KAPLAN / propeller (reaction, axial)** | **LOW — below 60 m** ← 6 m |
| Cross-flow (Banki) | Low head, small schemes — common in Nepal |

> **A 6 m head calls for a KAPLAN or a cross-flow turbine.** Kaplan's **adjustable blades** maintain good efficiency over a wide flow range, which suits a canal whose discharge varies through the season.

**And the units, stated plainly:**

> **ρ in kg/m³, g in m/s², Q in m³/s and H in m give POWER in WATTS.** **Divide by 1000 for kW.** Getting that division wrong is exactly what options (c) and (d) are built from.

examTip.trick: **P (kW) ≈ 8QH at 80% efficiency** — here 8 × 50 × 6 = 2400 kW, close enough to pick the option without a calculator. The exact value is 2352 kW.
examTip.trap: **All three distractors are the same number at the wrong scale.** 2352 MW would exceed half of Nepal's installed capacity from one canal drop; 2.352 kW is less than a kettle. Sanity alone answers it.
examTip.mnemonic: **A 6 m head means KAPLAN or cross-flow, never Pelton.** And a canal-drop plant's economics are excellent — the civil works already exist — but its **capacity factor follows the irrigation season**, not power demand.

questions.stem: The bending moment at 2 m from the left support of a simply supported beam of length 8 m carrying a UDL of 1 kN/m over the entire span is:
questions.solution:
**6 kNm.**

**Step 1 — reactions.**

> **Symmetrical loading, so each reaction carries half the total load:**
>
> **R_A = R_B = wL/2 = 1 × 8/2 = 4 kN**

**Step 2 — bending moment at x = 2 m.**

> **M(x) = R_A·x − w·x²/2**
>
> **M(2) = 4 × 2 − 1 × 2²/2 = 8 − 2 = 6 kNm** ✓

**The general formula, if preferred:**

> **M(x) = wx(L − x)/2 = 1 × 2 × 6/2 = 6 kNm** ✓

> **This form is faster and harder to get wrong**, because it needs no reaction calculation — and it shows the parabola directly: **M is proportional to x(L − x)**, zero at both ends and maximum at mid-span.

**The distractors, each from a specific error:**

| Option | Where it comes from |
|---|---|
| **(c) 8 kNm** | **R_A × x = 4 × 2**, forgetting to subtract the UDL's own moment |
| **(d) 16 kNm** | **wL²/8 = 1 × 64/8** — the maximum moment at **MID-SPAN**, not at 2 m |
| (a) 4.5 kNm | Miscellaneous |

> **Option (d) is the most tempting**, because **wL²/8 = 16 kNm** is the formula everyone remembers — but it applies **at the centre**, and the question asks about a point a quarter of the way along.

> **Read where the moment is wanted before reaching for a formula.**

**A check on the answer:**

> **At the quarter point of a UDL-loaded simply supported beam, M = 3wL²/32 = 3 × 64/32 = 6 kNm** ✓
>
> **That is 3/4 of the maximum** (16 × 0.75 = 12? no — 3/32 ÷ 1/8 = 3/4 × ... let us state it plainly: 6/16 = 0.375).

> **The moment at the quarter point is 37.5% of the maximum** — a useful proportion to carry, and it confirms 6 kNm is of the right size.

**The complete picture for this beam:**

| Quantity | Value |
|---|---|
| **Maximum BM (mid-span)** | **wL²/8 = 8 kNm** |
| **Maximum SF (at supports)** | **wL/2 = 4 kN** |
| **SF at mid-span** | **ZERO** |
| **Maximum deflection** | **5wL⁴/384EI** |
| SFD shape | **LINEAR** |
| BMD shape | **PARABOLIC** |

> **Wait — check that maximum:** **wL²/8 = 1 × 8²/8 = 8 kNm**, not 16. **Option (d), 16 kNm, is therefore not even the mid-span moment** — it is **wL²/4**, or twice it, which is the fixed-end/cantilever confusion. **The mid-span moment is option (c), 8 kNm.**

> **So both (c) and (d) are recognisable wrong answers**: (c) is the maximum moment at the wrong location, and (d) is twice that.

**The relations that govern the diagram shapes:**

> **w = −dV/dx** and **V = dM/dx**

| Applied | SFD | BMD |
|---|---|---|
| **UDL** | **Linear** | **Parabolic** |
| **Point load** | **Jump** | **Kink** |
| **Couple** | **No change** | **Jump** |
| **No load** | **Constant** | **Linear** |

> **The maximum moment occurs where the SHEAR CROSSES ZERO**, since V = dM/dx. **For this symmetric beam that is mid-span**, which is why wL²/8 sits there and nowhere else.

examTip.trick: **M(x) = wx(L − x)/2** needs no reactions: 1 × 2 × 6/2 = **6 kNm**. It also shows the parabola directly — zero at both ends, maximum at mid-span.
examTip.trap: **Option (c), 8 kNm, is R_A × x with the UDL's own moment forgotten** — and it happens to equal wL²/8, the MID-SPAN maximum. Read *where* the moment is wanted before reaching for a formula.
examTip.mnemonic: **Maximum moment sits where the SHEAR CROSSES ZERO**, because V = dM/dx. And at the quarter point of a UDL beam, M = 3wL²/32 — **37.5% of the maximum**.

questions.stem: The degree of a curve is the central angle subtended by an arc of length:
questions.solution:
**30 m.**

**The definition:**

> **The DEGREE OF CURVE (D) is the CENTRAL ANGLE subtended by a standard ARC — 30 metres in Indian and Nepali practice.**

**The working relation:**

> **A full circle is 360° and subtends a circumference of 2πR. So:**
>
> **D/360 = 30/(2πR)**
>
> **D = 30 × 360/(2πR) = 10800/(2πR) = 1718.9/R**

> **The familiar form: D ≈ 1719/R**, with R in metres — and the reverse, **R = 1719/D.**

> **The constant 1719 is not arbitrary**: it is **10800/2π**, and knowing that means the relation can be rebuilt from scratch if the number is forgotten.

**Why a "degree of curve" is used at all, when the radius says the same thing:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Historical — chain surveying** | The curve was **SET OUT by chords of a standard length** |
| **Convenient in the field** | **A larger D means a SHARPER curve** — an intuitive direct measure |
| Fits a curve table | Tabulated by degree, not radius |

> **The relation is INVERSE: sharp curve → small radius → LARGE degree.** A 1° curve has R = 1719 m and is very gentle; a 10° curve has R = 172 m and is sharp.

> **That inversion is the thing to hold on to**, because radius and degree move in opposite directions and it is easy to reason the wrong way.

**The standard arc length differs by country and by era**, which is why the question has four plausible-looking options:

| Practice | Standard length |
|---|---|
| **India / Nepal (metric)** | **30 m** |
| Older Indian (imperial) | **100 ft ≈ 30.5 m** |
| **USA — arc definition** | **100 ft** |
| USA — chord definition | 100 ft chord |

> **The metric 30 m was chosen precisely because it is close to 100 ft**, so existing curve tables and field practice carried over with minimal disruption. **Option (a), 20 m, is a genuine chain length in some contexts but not the degree-of-curve standard.**

**And the ARC versus CHORD definition** matters for sharp curves:

> **Under the arc definition D subtends a 30 m ARC; under the chord definition, a 30 m CHORD.**

> **For flat curves the two are indistinguishable**, since a short arc and its chord are nearly equal. **For sharp curves they diverge**, and a specification must say which is meant.

**Where the degree of curve is used:**

| Element | Relation |
|---|---|
| **Radius** | **R = 1719/D** |
| **Tangent length** | **T = R tan(Δ/2)** |
| **Curve length** | **L = πRΔ/180** |
| **Long chord** | **2R sin(Δ/2)** |
| **Mid-ordinate** | **R[1 − cos(Δ/2)]** |
| **Apex distance** | **R[sec(Δ/2) − 1]** |

> where **Δ** is the deflection angle between the two tangents.

**And the design constraint that fixes R in the first place:**

> **R = V²/(127(e + f))**, with **e** the superelevation and **f ≈ 0.15** the lateral friction coefficient.

> **The radius follows from the design SPEED, and the degree of curve then follows from the radius** — so the degree is a descriptive convenience, not a design parameter in its own right.

examTip.trick: **D = 1719/R**, and the 1719 is simply **10800/2π** — so the relation can be rebuilt if the number is forgotten. The standard arc is **30 m** in Indian and Nepali practice.
examTip.trap: **Radius and degree move in OPPOSITE directions**: sharp curve → small radius → LARGE degree. A 1° curve has R = 1719 m; a 10° curve has R = 172 m.
examTip.mnemonic: **The metric 30 m was chosen because it is close to 100 ft**, so existing curve tables carried over. And for sharp curves, **arc and chord definitions diverge** — a specification must say which.

questions.stem: If the radius of a horizontal curve is 120 m, calculate the safe allowable speed.
questions.solution:
**60 km/h.**

**The governing relation:**

> **R = V²/(127(e + f))**, so **V = √(127 R (e + f))**

| Term | Value used |
|---|---|
| **e** | **0.07** — maximum superelevation in plain terrain |
| **f** | **0.15** — the standard lateral friction coefficient |
| **e + f** | **0.22** |

**Working:**

> **V² = 127 × 120 × 0.22 = 3352.8**
>
> **V = √3352.8 = 57.9 km/h**
>
> **Rounded to the nearest standard design speed: 60 km/h** ✓

**Where the 127 comes from** — worth knowing, because it is the only awkward number in the formula:

> **The mechanics give R = v²/(g(e + f))** with **v in m/s.**
>
> **Converting to km/h: v = V/3.6, so v² = V²/12.96.**
>
> **R = V²/(12.96 × 9.81 × (e+f)) = V²/(127.1(e+f))** ✓

> **127 = 3.6² × 9.81.** It is a unit conversion, not a physical constant — which is why it disappears if the calculation is done in m/s.

**The two design values, and why they are what they are:**

| Parameter | Value | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **e_max (plain and rolling)** | **7%** | Higher would be unsafe for **slow or stationary** vehicles, which could slide inward or overturn |
| **e_max (hilly, not snow-bound)** | **10%** | Speeds are lower, so the risk to slow vehicles is smaller |
| **e_max (snow-bound)** | **7%** | **Ice destroys the friction that a steep cross-fall relies on** |
| **f** | **0.15** | A **conservative** value — actual tyre–road friction is far higher, but it must hold on a **wet, worn, poorly maintained** surface |

> **The limit on superelevation is set by the SLOW vehicle, not the fast one** — which is counter-intuitive and worth holding on to. **A vehicle stopped on a steeply banked curve in the wet has nothing but friction holding it from sliding down the slope.**

> **And f = 0.15 is deliberately low.** Design must be safe for the worst tyre on the worst surface in the rain, not for a new car on dry asphalt.

**The three-step design procedure** in practice (IRC):

> **Step 1 — assume the full speed is taken by superelevation alone at 75% of design speed: e = V²/(225R).**
>
> **Step 2 — if e exceeds 7%, cap it at 7% and check that friction can take the rest.**
>
> **Step 3 — if friction is inadequate, RESTRICT THE SPEED.**

> **Note the 225 in step 1: it is 127 ÷ 0.75²**, the same constant adjusted for designing at three-quarters of the full speed — an allowance for slow-moving vehicles that the simple formula ignores.

**The other provisions that go with the curve** — all needed together:

| Provision | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Superelevation** | **e = V²/(225R)**, capped at e_max |
| **Extra widening** | **nl²/(2R) + V/(9.5√R)** |
| **Transition length** | **GREATEST of three criteria** |
| **Grade compensation** | **(30 + R)/R %**, max **75/R** |
| **Set-back for sight distance** | Clearance on the inside of the curve |

> **A transition curve (a spiral or clothoid) is needed so the radius changes GRADUALLY**, allowing the superelevation to be introduced and the centrifugal force to build up progressively. **An abrupt change from straight to circular arc would require an instantaneous steering input, which no driver can supply.**

examTip.trick: **V = √(127 R (e + f))** with e = 0.07 and f = 0.15. Here √(127 × 120 × 0.22) = √3352.8 = 57.9, rounded to the standard design speed **60 km/h**.
examTip.trap: **127 = 3.6² × 9.81 — a UNIT CONVERSION, not a physical constant.** It vanishes entirely if the calculation is done in m/s rather than km/h.
examTip.mnemonic: **e_max is limited by the SLOW vehicle, not the fast one** — a car stopped on a steep banked curve in the wet has only friction holding it. And f = 0.15 is deliberately low: worst tyre, worst surface, rain.

questions.stem: A reinforced concrete beam having a width of 250 mm and an effective depth of 400 mm is reinforced with Fe 415 steel. As per the provisions of IS 456 : 2000, the minimum amount of tensile reinforcement is:
questions.solution:
**205 mm².**

**The IS 456 clause 26.5.1.1 requirement:**

> **A_s/(b d) = 0.85/f_y**

**Working:**

> **A_s = 0.85 × b × d / f_y**
>
> **A_s = 0.85 × 250 × 400 / 415**
>
> **A_s = 85,000/415 = 204.8 ≈ 205 mm²** ✓

**Note the depth used:**

> **The clause uses the EFFECTIVE depth d, not the overall depth D** — which is what the question supplies. **Using an overall depth would give a larger and wrong answer.**

**As a percentage:**

> **205/(250 × 400) = 0.205%** — and for **Fe 415 the minimum is always 0.205%**, since **0.85/415 = 0.00205** regardless of the section.

| Steel grade | Minimum percentage |
|---|---|
| **Fe 250** | **0.34%** |
| **Fe 415** | **0.205%** |
| **Fe 500** | **0.17%** |

> **Higher-grade steel needs LESS minimum area**, because the requirement is about **FORCE**, not area — a smaller area of stronger steel carries the same force.

> **Carrying the 0.205% figure lets any Fe 415 beam be checked in one multiplication**, which is faster than re-deriving the fraction each time.

**Why a minimum exists at all — this is the substance of the clause:**

> **The steel must be able to carry MORE force than the concrete carried just before it cracked.**

> **If it cannot, the moment that cracks the section immediately yields and fractures the steel — the beam fails SUDDENLY and COMPLETELY at first cracking**, with no warning and no deflection to give warning.

> **That is a BRITTLE failure, and it is the one mode reinforced concrete design exists to prevent.**

> **Minimum reinforcement therefore guarantees DUCTILITY**, not strength. A beam with adequate minimum steel cracks, deflects visibly, and only then approaches failure — which gives occupants time to leave.

**The maximum, and the reason for it:**

| Limit | Value |
|---|---|
| **Minimum tension steel** | **0.85 bd/f_y** |
| **Maximum tension steel** | **4% of the GROSS area (0.04 bD)** |
| Maximum compression steel | 4% |
| Maximum in a column | 6% (4% preferred) |

> **The maximum is a CONSTRUCTIBILITY limit, not a structural one** — beyond about 4%, bars cannot be spaced far enough apart for concrete and vibrator to pass between them, and the result is honeycombing.

> **Note the maximum uses the GROSS area bD while the minimum uses bd** — a genuine inconsistency in the code, and one that is easily missed.

**The related provisions:**

| Provision | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Minimum shear reinforcement** | **A_sv/(b s_v) ≥ 0.4/(0.87 f_y)** |
| **Maximum stirrup spacing** | **0.75d or 300 mm**, whichever is less |
| **Side face reinforcement** | **0.1% of the web** if **D > 750 mm** |
| **Minimum in a slab** | **0.15% (Fe 250), 0.12% (Fe 415)** of gross area |

> **Slab minimum reinforcement is specified on the GROSS area and serves a different purpose** — controlling **shrinkage and temperature cracking** rather than ensuring flexural ductility, which is why the percentage and the reference area both differ.

**A check on the answer's size:** **205 mm² is roughly two 12 mm bars (2 × 113 = 226 mm²) or three 10 mm bars (236 mm²)** — both realistic bottom bars for a 250 × 400 beam, which confirms the result is of the right order.

examTip.trick: **A_s = 0.85bd/f_y = 0.85 × 250 × 400/415 = 205 mm².** For Fe 415 the minimum is always **0.205%** of bd, so any beam is checked in one multiplication.
examTip.trap: **The minimum uses EFFECTIVE depth d; the maximum (4%) uses GROSS area bD.** A genuine inconsistency in the code, and easily missed.
examTip.mnemonic: **Minimum steel guarantees DUCTILITY, not strength** — without it the section cracks and the steel fractures in the same instant, with no warning. The 4% maximum is about **fitting bars in**, not about strength.

questions.stem: A three-hinged parabolic arch is subjected to a load w at L/4 distance from the left support. The rise of the crown is 4 m, the span is 20 m and w is 80 kN. The horizontal support reaction at the left support is:
questions.solution:
**50 kN.**

**Step 1 — vertical reactions, by moments about B.**

> The load sits at **L/4 = 5 m** from A, so it is **15 m** from B.
>
> **V_A × 20 = 80 × 15  →  V_A = 60 kN**
>
> **V_B = 80 − 60 = 20 kN**

**Step 2 — the third equation: moment about the CROWN HINGE is zero.**

> **The crown hinge is at mid-span, x = 10 m, at the rise y = 4 m.**
>
> **Taking moments of everything to the LEFT of the crown, about the crown:**
>
> **V_A × 10 − 80 × (10 − 5) − H × 4 = 0**
>
> **60 × 10 − 80 × 5 − 4H = 0**
>
> **600 − 400 = 4H**
>
> **H = 200/4 = 50 kN** ✓

**The general form, which is the fastest route:**

> **H = M_c / r**

> where **M_c is the BENDING MOMENT AT THE CROWN OF AN EQUIVALENT SIMPLY SUPPORTED BEAM** of the same span and loading, and **r is the rise.**

> **Check: the beam's mid-span moment is 60 × 10 − 80 × 5 = 200 kNm; H = 200/4 = 50 kN.** ✓

> **This is THE formula for a three-hinged arch**, and it reduces every such problem to a beam calculation followed by one division.

**Why the third hinge is what makes this possible:**

> **An arch with two supports has FOUR unknown reactions (two components at each) but only THREE equations of statics — so it is indeterminate to the first degree.**

> **The crown hinge supplies the fourth equation: ΣM = 0 at the hinge, because a hinge transmits no moment.**

> **That is why a THREE-hinged arch is DETERMINATE and a two-hinged arch is not.** The hinge is put there deliberately to make the structure calculable — and, more importantly in practice, **insensitive to support settlement and temperature change.**

**The crucial insight about H, and the reason arches exist:**

> **H depends INVERSELY on the RISE.**

| Rise | H |
|---|---|
| **4 m (here)** | **50 kN** |
| 2 m | **100 kN** |
| 8 m | **25 kN** |

> **A FLATTER arch produces a much LARGER horizontal thrust**, which must be resisted by the abutments or by a tie.

> **This is why flat arches need massive abutments or rock foundations**, and why an arch on poor ground must be built with a generous rise or given a **tie rod** — a tied arch resists its own thrust internally and behaves, at the supports, like a simply supported beam.

> **Inadequate abutments are the classic cause of arch failure**: the springings spread, the rise reduces, the thrust increases, and the process accelerates.

**The parabolic arch's special property:**

> **Under a UDL over the whole span, a PARABOLIC arch is the FUNICULAR shape — the bending moment is ZERO everywhere and the arch carries the load in PURE COMPRESSION.**

> **That is the ideal**, because concrete and masonry are strong in compression and weak in tension. **The parabola is the shape a cable would take under the same load, inverted.**

> **Under any OTHER loading — including this point load — bending moments do appear**, and the arch is no longer purely compressive. **Which is why the shape is chosen to suit the DOMINANT load case**, usually the dead load, and the rest is treated as a departure from it.

**And for reference, the arch bending moment:**

> **M_arch = M_beam − H·y**

> **The arch action REDUCES the beam moment by H·y at every point** — that is the whole benefit of an arch, and it is greatest where the arch is deepest.

examTip.trick: **H = M_c/r** — the equivalent simply supported beam's moment at the crown, divided by the rise. Here (60×10 − 80×5)/4 = 200/4 = **50 kN**. Every three-hinged arch reduces to this.
examTip.trap: **Take moments about the CROWN HINGE, not mid-span of the load.** The hinge supplies the fourth equation (a hinge carries no moment), which is exactly what makes a three-hinged arch determinate.
examTip.mnemonic: **H is INVERSELY proportional to the RISE** — halve the rise and the thrust doubles. Flat arches need massive abutments or a tie, and **spreading springings are the classic arch failure**: rise falls, thrust rises, it accelerates.

questions.stem: The weight of a person on Earth is 100 N. The weight will be _____ N if the person is on a planet having acceleration due to gravity 1/6th that of Earth.
questions.solution:
**16.67 N.**

**Working:**

> **W = m g**, and the **MASS m is unchanged** by moving to another planet.
>
> **W_planet = W_earth × (g_planet/g_earth) = 100 × 1/6 = 16.67 N** ✓

**The distinction the question exists to test:**

| | **MASS** | **WEIGHT** |
|---|---|---|
| Definition | **Quantity of matter** | **Gravitational FORCE on that matter** |
| **Unit** | **kilogram (kg)** | **newton (N)** |
| **Varies with location?** | **NO — constant everywhere** | **YES — proportional to g** |
| Measured by | **Beam balance** | **Spring balance** |
| Scalar or vector | **Scalar** | **Vector** |

> **A BEAM BALANCE compares two weights, so gravity cancels and it reads the same MASS on any planet.**

> **A SPRING BALANCE measures FORCE, so it reads one sixth as much** — the same object, a different reading.

> **That contrast is the cleanest way to fix the distinction**, because it is a physical consequence rather than a definition to memorise.

**The person's mass, for completeness:**

> **m = W/g = 100/9.81 = 10.19 kg** — unchanged on both planets.

> **Note that option (a), 10.66 N, is close to that mass value in kilograms** — a distractor built for anyone who divides by g somewhere they should not, and who then reports a mass as though it were a weight.

**Why option (c), 166.7 N, is the more instructive error:**

> **It is 100 × 6 — MULTIPLYING by six instead of dividing.**

> **The physical check catches it at once: WEAKER gravity must give LESS weight.** A planet pulling one sixth as hard cannot make a person heavier.

> **Always ask which way the answer should move before doing the arithmetic.** In this case the direction alone eliminates half the options.

**Why this matters in civil engineering** — the same distinction runs through the whole subject:

| Quantity | Symbol | Relation |
|---|---|---|
| **DENSITY** (mass per volume) | **ρ** | kg/m³ — **independent of g** |
| **SPECIFIC WEIGHT** (weight per volume) | **γ = ρg** | N/m³ — **varies with g** |
| Specific gravity | **S** | **Dimensionless — a ratio** |

> **For water: ρ = 1000 kg/m³ and γ = 9810 N/m³.** The two are constantly interchanged, and the factor between them is exactly **g**.

> **Specific gravity is dimensionless, so it is the SAME on any planet** — which is why it is such a convenient way to characterise a material.

**And the practical consequence in soil mechanics:**

> **Unit weights are always quoted as WEIGHT per volume (kN/m³)**, because it is force that produces stress. **γ_water = 9.81 kN/m³** appears in every effective-stress calculation.

> **σ′ = σ − u** — and both terms are forces per unit area, which is why the specific weight, not the density, is the quantity carried into the calculation.

**A last note on the units:** **the answer is asked in NEWTONS, and 16.67 N is a force.** Reporting 10.19 kg would answer a different question — which is exactly what option (a) tempts a candidate into doing.

examTip.trick: **Mass is unchanged; only g changes.** W = 100 × (1/6) = **16.67 N**. A beam balance would read the same on both planets; a spring balance would read one sixth.
examTip.trap: **Option (c), 166.7 N, multiplies instead of dividing** — but weaker gravity must give LESS weight. The direction check alone eliminates half the options before any arithmetic.
examTip.mnemonic: **ρ (density, kg/m³) is independent of g; γ = ρg (specific weight, N/m³) is not.** Water: 1000 and 9810. And **specific gravity is dimensionless — the same on any planet**.

questions.stem: A soil has a porosity of 30%. Its void ratio in the loosest and densest states is 0.92 and 0.35 respectively. What will be its density index?
questions.solution:
**0.861.**

**Step 1 — convert porosity to void ratio.**

> **e = n/(1 − n) = 0.30/0.70 = 0.4286**

**Step 2 — apply the density index formula.**

> **I_D = (e_max − e)/(e_max − e_min)**
>
> **I_D = (0.92 − 0.4286)/(0.92 − 0.35)**
>
> **I_D = 0.4914/0.57 = 0.8621 ≈ 0.861** ✓

**Step 1 is the whole question:**

> **The porosity is given, but the formula needs the VOID RATIO.** Substituting 0.30 directly gives **(0.92 − 0.30)/0.57 = 1.088** — a density index greater than 1, which is **impossible**, since I_D is bounded by 0 and 1 by definition.

> **The impossible result is itself the check.** If a density index comes out above 1 or below 0, the conversion has been missed.

**The two conversions, and how to keep them straight:**

> **e = n/(1 − n)** and **n = e/(1 + e)**

| Quantity | Definition | Range |
|---|---|---|
| **Void ratio e** | **V_v/V_s** — voids over **SOLIDS** | **0 to ∞** |
| **Porosity n** | **V_v/V** — voids over **TOTAL** | **0 to 1 (0–100%)** |

> **Porosity is bounded because the voids are part of the total; the void ratio is not, because the solids can be vanishingly small.**

> **And e is ALWAYS greater than n** for the same soil, since the denominator is smaller. **Here e = 0.4286 > n = 0.30** ✓ — a two-second check that the conversion went the right way.

**What the DENSITY INDEX (relative density) means:**

> **It measures where a COHESIONLESS soil sits between its loosest and densest possible states.**

| I_D | State |
|---|---|
| **0** | **LOOSEST possible (e = e_max)** |
| 0 – 0.15 | Very loose |
| 0.15 – 0.35 | Loose |
| 0.35 – 0.65 | Medium |
| **0.65 – 0.85** | **DENSE** |
| **0.85 – 1.0** | **VERY DENSE** ← 0.861 |

> **So this soil is VERY DENSE**, and that classification carries real engineering meaning.

**Why it applies only to COHESIONLESS soils:**

> **e_max and e_min are determined by standard laboratory procedures — pouring loose, and vibrating to maximum density.**

> **Those procedures are meaningful for sand and gravel. For clay they are not**, because a clay's structure depends on its stress history and water content rather than on packing. **Clay's equivalent measure is CONSISTENCY INDEX, based on the Atterberg limits.**

**What density index predicts:**

| Property | Dense sand (high I_D) | Loose sand (low I_D) |
|---|---|---|
| **φ** | **HIGH — 35–45°** | Low — 28–32° |
| **Volume change on shearing** | **DILATES (expands)** | **CONTRACTS** |
| Stress–strain curve | **Peak then softening** | Gradual to a plateau |
| **LIQUEFACTION risk** | **LOW** | **HIGH** |
| Settlement | Small | Large |

> **The dilation of dense sand is the key mechanical difference**: the grains must ride over one another to shear, which requires extra work and gives the **peak strength** that loose sand does not have.

> **And it explains the liquefaction contrast directly.** **Loose sand CONTRACTS on shearing; under rapid (undrained) loading the water cannot escape, so the pore pressure RISES, effective stress falls toward zero, and the soil LIQUEFIES.**

> **Dense sand tries to DILATE, which reduces pore pressure and increases effective stress** — so it is inherently resistant.

> **This is precisely why liquefaction was so severe in parts of the Kathmandu Valley in 2015**: loose, saturated, fine-grained lake-bed deposits are the exact combination that liquefies, and **densification is the standard remedy.**

examTip.trick: **Convert porosity to void ratio FIRST: e = n/(1−n) = 0.3/0.7 = 0.4286.** Then I_D = (0.92 − 0.4286)/0.57 = **0.861**.
examTip.trap: **Substituting n = 0.30 directly gives I_D = 1.088 — impossible**, since I_D is bounded by 0 and 1. The absurd result is itself the check that the conversion was missed.
examTip.mnemonic: **e is ALWAYS greater than n** (smaller denominator) — a two-second check. And **loose sand CONTRACTS and liquefies; dense sand DILATES and resists** — which is why densification is the standard remedy.

questions.stem: For a uniformly loaded circular area of radius 1000 m, the vertical pressure σ_z at a depth of 10 m is 80 kN/m² with an influence factor k = 1. Find the intensity of the applied load.
questions.solution:
**80 kN/m².**

**The relation:**

> **σ_z = k · q**, so **q = σ_z/k = 80/1 = 80 kN/m²** ✓

**Why the influence factor is 1 here — the physics behind the arithmetic:**

> **The loaded radius is 1000 m and the depth is only 10 m — a RADIUS-TO-DEPTH RATIO of 100.**

> **At that ratio the loaded area is effectively INFINITE in extent.** A point 10 m below the centre of a 2 km-wide load sees the ground surface as an unbounded loaded plane.

> **So there is NO spreading of stress at all, and the full applied pressure reaches that depth undiminished: σ_z = q.**

**The exact Boussinesq expression confirms it:**

> **k = 1 − [1/(1 + (R/z)²)]^{3/2}**
>
> **With R/z = 100: (R/z)² = 10,000, so k = 1 − (1/10,001)^{3/2} ≈ 1 − 0.000001 = 1.000**

> **The influence factor is 1 to six decimal places** — which is why the question can simply state k = 1.

**How the influence factor behaves with depth** — the pattern worth carrying:

| **R/z** | **k** | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| **0.5** | **0.28** | Deep relative to the load — heavy spreading |
| **1.0** | **0.65** | Depth equals radius |
| **2.0** | **0.91** | — |
| **3.0** | **0.97** | Nearly full pressure |
| **100** | **1.00** | **Effectively an infinite loaded area** |

> **Below a depth of about twice the loaded radius, the stress has already dropped substantially** — which is the basis of the **"significant depth"** rule.

**The practical consequence — the 2B rule:**

> **Stress becomes negligible (below about 10–20% of the applied pressure) at a depth of roughly TWICE THE WIDTH of the loaded area.**

> **That is why a SOIL INVESTIGATION must extend to 1.5 to 2 times the foundation width**, and no further — deeper soil is not stressed enough to matter.

> **And it explains a result that surprises people: a WIDE raft stresses the soil FAR DEEPER than a narrow footing carrying the same pressure.**

| Foundation | Pressure | Significant depth |
|---|---|---|
| **2 m footing** | 100 kPa | **~4 m** |
| **20 m raft** | 100 kPa | **~40 m** |

> **A soft layer at 15 m depth is irrelevant to the footing and critical to the raft** — the same contact pressure, an entirely different problem. **This is one of the most consequential ideas in foundation engineering**, and it is exactly what this question's extreme geometry illustrates.

**Boussinesq's assumptions**, for completeness:

> The soil is **homogeneous, isotropic, elastic and semi-infinite**, and **weightless** (self-weight is handled separately).

> **Real soil is none of these**, particularly the isotropy — most deposits are **layered and stiffer horizontally than vertically**. **Westergaard's solution** was developed for exactly that case and gives **lower stresses at depth** than Boussinesq.

> **Boussinesq is nevertheless used almost universally**, because it is conservative for settlement and because the errors are small compared with the uncertainty in the soil parameters themselves.

**The point-load form**, for reference:

> **σ_z = 3Q/(2πz²) × [1/(1 + (r/z)²)]^{5/2}**

> **Directly beneath the load (r = 0): σ_z = 0.4775 Q/z²** — and note the **inverse SQUARE of depth**, which is why stress dies away so quickly beneath a concentrated load.

examTip.trick: **R/z = 1000/10 = 100 — the loaded area is effectively INFINITE.** No spreading occurs, so the full pressure reaches that depth: σ_z = q = **80 kN/m²**.
examTip.trap: **Boussinesq's k = 1 − [1/(1+(R/z)²)]^{3/2} equals 1.000 to six decimals here** — so the stated k = 1 is exact, not an approximation. The other options are spreading calculations that do not apply.
examTip.mnemonic: **The 2B rule: significant stress reaches about twice the loaded WIDTH.** So a 20 m raft stresses the soil to ~40 m while a 2 m footing at the same pressure reaches only ~4 m — the same contact pressure, a different problem entirely.

questions.stem: The compound in ordinary Portland cement chiefly responsible for the early strength gain in the first seven days is:
questions.solution:
**C₃S — tricalcium silicate.**

**The four Bogue compounds and what each does:**

| Compound | Abbreviation | Typical % | Contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Tricalcium silicate** | **C₃S (alite)** | **45 – 55%** | **EARLY strength — up to 7 days**; moderate heat |
| **Dicalcium silicate** | **C₂S (belite)** | **20 – 30%** | **LATER strength — beyond 28 days**; low heat |
| **Tricalcium aluminate** | **C₃A (celite)** | **8 – 12%** | **FLASH SET; HIGHEST heat**; contributes little strength |
| **Tetracalcium alumino-ferrite** | **C₄AF (felite)** | **6 – 10%** | **Colour (grey)**; little strength |

> **The two SILICATES supply essentially all the strength; the two ALUMINATES supply heat and colour.** That single division organises the whole topic.

**C₃S versus C₂S — the pair the question turns on:**

| | **C₃S** | **C₂S** |
|---|---|---|
| **Hydrates** | **FAST** | **SLOWLY** |
| **Strength timing** | **EARLY (≤ 7 days)** | **LATE (beyond 28 days)** |
| **Heat of hydration** | **500 J/g** | **260 J/g — about half** |
| Ultimate strength | High | **Equally high, eventually** |

> **Both reach a similar ultimate strength — they differ in WHEN, not HOW MUCH.**

> **That is why cement types are made by adjusting the ratio between them**, rather than by adding something new.

**How the cement types follow directly:**

| Type | Composition change | Result |
|---|---|---|
| **RAPID HARDENING** | **MORE C₃S, finer grinding** | Early strength; **more heat** |
| **LOW HEAT** | **LESS C₃S and C₃A, MORE C₂S** | **Low heat — for MASS CONCRETE (dams)** |
| **SULPHATE RESISTING** | **C₃A limited to under 5%** | Resists sulphate attack |

> **LOW HEAT cement exists because mass concrete cannot shed its heat.** The interior of a large pour rises in temperature while the surface cools, and the differential causes **THERMAL CRACKING** — so the heat must be reduced at source.

> **SULPHATE RESISTING cement works by limiting C₃A**, because sulphates attack the hydrated aluminate to form **ETTRINGITE**, which is expansive and disrupts the concrete from within.

**Why C₃A also needs GYPSUM:**

> **C₃A alone would cause a FLASH SET — the cement would stiffen within minutes and be unusable.**

> **Gypsum (3–5%) is INTERGROUND with the clinker to retard it**, giving the initial setting time the code requires.

| Setting time (IS 269) | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Initial set** | **NOT LESS than 30 minutes** |
| **Final set** | **NOT MORE than 600 minutes (10 hours)** |

> **Note the directions differ**: the initial set has a **minimum** (time to place and compact) and the final set a **maximum** (so the works can proceed). **Reversing them is a common slip.**

**And the fineness effect:**

> **Finer grinding gives a larger surface area, so hydration is faster and early strength higher — but the heat is released faster too, and shrinkage increases.**

> **Minimum fineness: 225 m²/kg** by the Blaine air-permeability test.

examTip.trick: **The two SILICATES give strength; the two ALUMINATES give heat and colour.** Within the silicates, **C₃S is early (≤7 days) and C₂S is late (beyond 28)** — they differ in WHEN, not how much.
examTip.trap: **C₃A produces the most heat but almost no strength**, and alone it would cause a **flash set** — which is why 3–5% gypsum is interground to retard it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Initial set NOT LESS than 30 min; final set NOT MORE than 600 min.** The directions differ — one gives time to place, the other lets the works proceed. And **low-heat cement (less C₃S, more C₂S) exists because mass concrete cannot shed its heat.**

questions.stem: The section modulus of a rectangular section of width b and depth d, about the axis of bending, is:
questions.solution:
**bd²/6.**

**Derivation — it is one division, not a formula to memorise:**

> **Z = I/y_max**
>
> **I = bd³/12** and **y_max = d/2**
>
> **Z = (bd³/12)/(d/2) = bd³/12 × 2/d = bd²/6** ✓

**The DIMENSIONAL check settles it instantly:**

> **A section modulus has dimensions of LENGTH³ (it is I ÷ a length, so L⁴/L = L³).**

| Option | Dimensions | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| (a) bd³/12 | **L⁴** | **This is I, not Z** |
| **(b) bd²/6** | **L³** ✓ | **Correct** |
| (c) bd²/12 | L³ | Right dimensions, wrong coefficient |
| (d) bd³/6 | **L⁴** | Wrong dimensions |

> **Two of the four options are eliminated on dimensions alone**, which halves the problem before any recall is needed.

> **Option (a), bd³/12, is the SECOND MOMENT OF AREA** — the quantity Z is derived from. Offering I as a distractor for Z is the standard trap in this topic, and the dimensional check defeats it every time.

**Why Z matters — it is what bending design actually uses:**

> **σ = M/Z**

> **The section modulus is the single number that converts a bending moment into a maximum stress**, which is why steel section tables list Z for every rolled section.

> **Larger Z means less stress for the same moment** — so the design task is to obtain the largest Z for the least material.

**The key consequence — depth matters far more than width:**

> **Z = bd²/6 is LINEAR in width but goes as the SQUARE of depth.**

| Change | Effect on Z |
|---|---|
| **Double the WIDTH** | **Z doubles (× 2)** |
| **Double the DEPTH** | **Z QUADRUPLES (× 4)** |

> **And for stiffness the effect is stronger still: I = bd³/12 goes as the CUBE of depth, so doubling the depth makes the beam EIGHT TIMES stiffer.**

> **This is why beams are deep and narrow, why joists are laid on edge rather than flat, and why an I-section puts most of its material in the flanges** — as far from the neutral axis as possible.

> **A 50 × 200 timber joist laid FLAT has one sixteenth the section modulus it has laid ON EDGE** (the b and d swap, and the ratio is (200/50)² ÷ ... — plainly, Z_edge/Z_flat = (200²×50)/(50²×200) = 4). **Four times the strength and sixteen times the stiffness, from the same piece of timber turned through 90°.**

**Standard section moduli:**

| Shape | Z |
|---|---|
| **Rectangle b × d** | **bd²/6** |
| **Circle diameter D** | **πD³/32** |
| **Hollow circle** | **π(D⁴ − d⁴)/(32D)** |
| Triangle (about base) | bd²/24 |

**And a caution about UNSYMMETRICAL sections:**

> **A T-section or channel has TWO different values of y**, and therefore **two section moduli — Z_top and Z_bottom.**

> **The smaller Z governs**, because it produces the larger stress. **For a T-beam in sagging, y is larger to the bottom fibre, so the bottom governs in tension** — which is exactly where concrete needs reinforcement.

**Where Z is used:**

> **Elastic design: M = σ_allowable × Z.** In **plastic design** the equivalent is the **plastic modulus Z_p**, and the **SHAPE FACTOR Z_p/Z** is **1.5 for a rectangle** and about **1.12–1.15 for an I-section** — the reserve of strength beyond first yield.

examTip.trick: **Z = I/y_max = (bd³/12)/(d/2) = bd²/6.** One division — no need to memorise it separately from I.
examTip.trap: **Z has dimensions L³, I has L⁴.** Options (a) and (d) are dimensionally wrong and fall at sight — and (a), bd³/12, is I itself, the standard distractor in this topic.
examTip.mnemonic: **Z goes as depth SQUARED, I as depth CUBED.** Double the depth: 4× the strength, 8× the stiffness. That is why joists go on edge — and a flat joist has a quarter of the strength of the same timber turned 90°.

questions.stem: In levelling, the method that eliminates the errors due to collimation, curvature and refraction is:
questions.solution:
**Reciprocal levelling.**

**What it is:**

> **Where a level cannot be set up midway between two points — across a river, a ravine or a wide road — reciprocal levelling takes TWO sets of observations, one from NEAR EACH point, and averages them.**

**Why the averaging cancels the errors:**

> **Set the instrument near A and read A (short sight) and B (long sight).** Any collimation, curvature or refraction error affects the **long sight to B** almost entirely, and the short sight to A hardly at all.

> **Then set up near B and repeat.** Now the same error affects the **long sight to A**.

> **The error enters the two results with OPPOSITE SIGNS, so the mean is free of it.**

> **True difference = (ΔH₁ + ΔH₂)/2**

**The three errors it removes:**

| Error | Cause |
|---|---|
| **COLLIMATION** | The line of sight is **not truly horizontal** — instrument maladjustment |
| **CURVATURE of the earth** | The level surface **falls away** from the horizontal line |
| **REFRACTION** | The line of sight **bends downward** through the atmosphere |

> **All three are proportional to the SIGHT DISTANCE**, which is exactly why reversing the setup reverses their effect.

**The combined correction, when it must be computed instead:**

> **Curvature: c = 0.0785 d² (m)** — the sight appears **too HIGH**, so the correction is **negative**
>
> **Refraction: r = c/7** — acts **opposite** to curvature
>
> **Combined: 0.0673 d²**, with **d in kilometres**

> **Refraction offsets one seventh of curvature**, which is why the combined coefficient 0.0673 is slightly less than 0.0785. **At 1 km the combined effect is 67 mm** — negligible over short sights, serious over long ones.

> **This is also why the ordinary remedy is simply to BALANCE the sight distances**: with equal backsight and foresight lengths, all three errors cancel automatically at every setup. **Reciprocal levelling is the method for when that balancing is impossible.**

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Method | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **FLY levelling** | **Carrying a level from one point to a distant one** by a series of setups; no error cancellation of this kind |
| **CHECK levelling** | **Verifying a line by re-levelling it**, usually by returning to the start — detects error, does not eliminate it |
| **PROFILE levelling** | **Longitudinal section along a route** — a purpose, not an error-control technique |

> **Check levelling DETECTS a misclosure; reciprocal levelling PREVENTS a specific class of error.** The distinction between detection and elimination is the point.

**And refraction is the least reliable of the three:**

> **Curvature is a fixed geometric quantity; refraction varies with temperature, pressure and time of day**, and is worst **near the ground in the early afternoon** when the air is most unstable.

> **Which is why long sights are avoided, sights are kept above about 0.5 m from the ground, and reciprocal observations are taken as nearly SIMULTANEOUSLY as possible** — so that the refraction is at least the same in both directions.

**The permissible misclosure** for ordinary work: **±12√K mm** (K in kilometres), tightening to **±3√K mm** for precise levelling.

examTip.trick: **All three errors are proportional to SIGHT DISTANCE**, so reversing the setup reverses their sign and the mean cancels them. That is the whole mechanism.
examTip.trap: **Check levelling DETECTS error; reciprocal levelling ELIMINATES it.** Detection and elimination are different things, and only one of the four options does the second.
examTip.mnemonic: **Combined curvature + refraction = 0.0673 d² (d in km) — 67 mm at 1 km.** Refraction offsets one seventh of curvature. Normally you just **balance the sight distances**; reciprocal levelling is for when you cannot.

questions.stem: In the analysis of rates, the percentage normally added to the cost of materials and labour to cover the contractor's profit and overheads is about:
questions.solution:
**10 to 15%.**

**What ANALYSIS OF RATES is:**

> **Working out the cost of ONE UNIT of a finished item of work** — one cubic metre of concrete, one square metre of plaster — from its constituents.

**The components of a rate:**

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **MATERIALS** | Quantities per unit, at market rates, **including wastage** |
| **LABOUR** | Skilled and unskilled, from standard **outturn/task-work** figures |
| **Plant and machinery** | Hire or depreciation |
| **Transport** | Carriage of materials to site |
| **Overheads and CONTRACTOR'S PROFIT** | **10 – 15%** ← |
| **Water charges** | **1 – 2%** |
| Contingencies | **3 – 5%** |

> **Note that option (a), 1–2%, is the WATER CHARGE**, another standard percentage in the same table — which is what makes it a convincing distractor. **Each percentage belongs to a specific line, and they must not be interchanged.**

**Why a percentage at all, rather than a computed figure:**

> **Overheads cannot be attributed to a particular item of work.** Site establishment, supervision, insurance, security, temporary works and head-office costs serve the whole contract.

> **So they are recovered as a percentage spread across every item**, which is simple, transparent and auditable.

**What the 10–15% actually covers:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **Site overheads** | Supervision, site office, temporary works, plant standing |
| **Head office overheads** | Estimating, accounts, directors |
| **Insurance and financing** | Including the cost of retention money withheld |
| **RISK** | Weather, ground conditions, price movement |
| **Profit** | The actual return |

> **Risk is the part most often underestimated.** A contractor bidding at a rate with no allowance for risk is not bidding cheaply — they are bidding on the assumption that nothing goes wrong, and that assumption fails often enough to bankrupt firms.

> **This is why an ABNORMALLY LOW BID is a warning rather than a bargain**: the shortfall must be recovered somewhere, usually through claims, substituted materials, or abandonment.

**The estimate types and their accuracy:**

| Estimate | Purpose | Accuracy |
|---|---|---|
| **Plinth area / cube rate** | Preliminary; **administrative approval** | **±15 – 20%** |
| **DETAILED** | Item by item; **technical sanction** | **±5%** |
| **REVISED** | When the sanctioned amount is exceeded by **> 5%** | — |
| **SUPPLEMENTARY** | **ADDITIONAL work** not originally included | — |

> **REVISED = the SAME work costing more. SUPPLEMENTARY = ADDITIONAL work.** The test is whether the **scope** changed or only the **cost**.

**Standard measurement units** — a common companion question:

| Item | Unit |
|---|---|
| **Earthwork, concrete, brickwork** | **m³** |
| **Plastering, painting, flooring, formwork** | **m²** |
| **Skirting, cornice, railing** | **m (running)** |
| **Doors, windows** | **Number** or m² |
| **Reinforcement** | **kg or quintal** |

> **Anything with an appreciable THICKNESS is measured by VOLUME; anything applied as a SURFACE by AREA; anything essentially LINEAR by LENGTH.** That principle covers almost every item without a table.

**And the approval sequence:** **administrative approval → TECHNICAL SANCTION → expenditure sanction → tender.**

> **Technical sanction is the engineer's certification that the estimate is sound**, which is why the detailed estimate must reach ±5%.

examTip.trick: **10–15% covers overheads AND profit together**, because overheads cannot be attributed to any single item — they are spread across every item as a percentage.
examTip.trap: **Option (a), 1–2%, is the WATER CHARGE** — another standard percentage from the same table. Each figure belongs to a specific line: water 1–2%, contingencies 3–5%, overheads and profit 10–15%.
examTip.mnemonic: **Volume for anything thick, AREA for anything applied as a surface, LENGTH for anything linear.** That covers almost every measurement unit without a table. And **REVISED = same work dearer; SUPPLEMENTARY = extra work.**

questions.stem: In a direct shear test on dry sand, the shear strength parameter obtained is:
questions.solution:
**φ only, because a dry sand has c = 0.**

**The Mohr–Coulomb equation:**

> **τ_f = c + σ tan φ**

> **For a clean dry sand there is NO COHESION — the grains are not bonded — so c = 0 and τ_f = σ tan φ.**

> **The failure envelope therefore passes THROUGH THE ORIGIN**, and its slope is φ. **A single test at one normal stress is enough to find φ**, since the line's position is already fixed.

**The parameters for the common soil types:**

| Soil | c | φ |
|---|---|---|
| **Clean sand / gravel (cohesionless)** | **0** | **28 – 45°** |
| **Saturated clay, UNDRAINED** | **c_u > 0** | **φ_u = 0** |
| Clay, drained (effective) | **c′ ≈ 0** | **φ′ = 20 – 30°** |
| Silt, partly saturated | Small apparent c | Moderate |

> **Sand and undrained clay are the two mirror-image cases**, which is why they are examined together: **sand is purely frictional, saturated clay in undrained loading is purely cohesive.**

**Why φ_u = 0 for a saturated clay** — the point worth understanding:

> **In undrained loading no water can escape, so the VOLUME cannot change.**

> **Any increase in total stress goes entirely into PORE PRESSURE, leaving the EFFECTIVE stress unchanged** — and since strength depends on effective stress, the strength does not change either.

> **So the undrained envelope is HORIZONTAL: τ_f = c_u, independent of the applied normal stress.** It is a consequence of the physics, not a property of clay in itself.

**The direct shear test — its strengths and its real limitations:**

| Advantage | Limitation |
|---|---|
| **Simple and quick** | **Failure plane is FORCED — it may not be the weakest** |
| **Cheap apparatus** | **Stress distribution is NON-UNIFORM** |
| **Drainage is rapid in sand** | **Pore pressure CANNOT be measured** |
| **Good for sands** | **Poor for clays** — drainage cannot be controlled |

> **The forced failure plane is the fundamental objection**: the specimen must fail along the split between the two halves of the box, whether or not that is the weakest surface in the sample.

> **The TRIAXIAL test avoids this** — the specimen chooses its own failure plane, pore pressure can be measured, and the drainage conditions (UU, CU, CD) can be controlled. **That is why triaxial testing is standard for clays and direct shear is reserved mainly for sands**, where drainage is never in doubt.

**What φ depends on:**

| Factor | Effect on φ |
|---|---|
| **Density (I_D)** | **Denser → HIGHER φ** |
| **Particle ANGULARITY** | **Angular → higher φ than rounded** |
| **Grading** | **Well graded → higher** than uniform |
| Particle size | Slight |
| **Water content** | **Almost NONE for a clean sand** |

> **That last row is worth noting**: a clean sand has nearly the same φ wet or dry, because the friction is between grains and water does not lubricate them appreciably. **What water changes is the EFFECTIVE STRESS, not φ.**
